units.la: ACTA etiam est controuersia inter Theologos Augustanæ confessionis de Persona Christi: quæ tamen non inter ipsos primùm coepit; sed initium à Sacramentariis sumpsit. Nam euicta à Luthero contra Sacramentarios vera & substantiali præsentia corporis & sanguinis Christi in Cœna firmissimo fundamēto ex verbis institutionis: obiectū ei fuit à Cinglianis: Si corpus Christi semel & simul in cælo & in terra in Cœna adsit: non posse illud verè humanum corpus esse. Talem enim Maiestatem soli Deo propriam esse: cuius corpus Christi non sit capax. Huic obiectioni cùm D. Lutherus contradiceret & fortiter eam confutaret: sicut ipsius Apologetica & Agoniftica scripta de Cœna Domini commostrãt: quæ nos manifestè perinde atque alia didascalica amplectimur: post obitum ipsius quidam Augustanæ confessionis Theologi, licet pedem aperte & expressè in castra Sacramentariorum de Cœna Domini figere noluerint: eandem fundamenta de persona Christi, quibus Sacramentarij veram & substantialem præsentiam corporis & sanguinis Christi ex sua Cœna tollere conati sunt, in crebro víu habuerút: quòd scilicet humanæ naturæ in Christo non attribui debeant ea quæ sunt sua & contra ipsius naturæ essentiales proprietates. Insuper doctrinã Lutheri, omnésque eos, qui illam vt verbo Dei responden-tem sequuntur, insimulatione omnium penè veterum prodigiosarum hæresium onerarunt.
units.tr: A controversy about the Person of Christ has also arisen among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession. It did not begin among them, however, but took its start from the Sacramentarians. For when Luther had established, against the Sacramentarians, the true and substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Supper on the firmest foundation of the words of institution, the Zwinglians objected: if the body of Christ is present in the Supper once and at the same time in heaven and on earth, then it cannot be a truly human body, since such majesty belongs to God alone and the body of Christ is not capable of it. Luther answered this objection and refuted it vigorously, as his Apologetic and Agonistic writings on the Lord's Supper show. We embrace these writings openly, as we do his other doctrinal works. After his death, however, some theologians of the Augsburg Confession, although they did not wish to plant their foot openly and expressly in the camp of the Sacramentarians on the Lord's Supper, frequently used the same arguments about the Person of Christ with which the Sacramentarians had tried to remove the true and substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ from their Supper. These arguments hold that the things which belong to the divine nature should not be attributed to the human nature in Christ, and that the things contrary to the essential properties of that nature should not be either. Moreover, they burdened Luther's doctrine, and all who follow it as agreeing with God's Word, with the charge of nearly all the monstrous ancient heresies.

units.la: Ad hanc controuersiam dextrè ex verbo Dei secundum analogiam simplicis nostræ fidei declarandã,& Deo fauente oĩo tollendam, est hæc nostra vnanimis fides, doctrina & cõfessio, vt sequitur. Nos credimus, docemus & cõfitemur, quanuis filij Dei alia, distincta, perfecte diuina, persona, atq.ita verus rus, essentialis, perfectus Deus cum Patre & Spiritu sancto ab æterno fuit: eum tamen expleto tempore humanam etiā naturam in vnitatem suæ personæ assumpsisse: nō quòd duæ sint personæ vel duo Christi: sed quòd Iesus Christus nunc in vna persona simul verus æternus Deus sit, à Patre ab æterno genitus: & verus homo ex benedicta virgine Maria natus, vt scriptū est Rom. 9.Ex quib. Christus venit secundum carnem, qui est Deus super omnia benedictus in secula.
units.tr: To explain this controversy properly from the Word of God, according to the analogy of our simple faith, and, God willing, to settle it, here is our unanimous faith, doctrine and confession, as follows. We believe, teach and confess that, although the Son of God, a distinct and perfectly divine person, was from eternity a true, essential and perfect God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, when the time was fulfilled, he also assumed human nature into the unity of his person. This is not because there are two persons or two Christs, but because Jesus Christ is now, in one person, at once true, eternal God, begotten from the Father from eternity, and true man, born of the blessed Virgin Mary, as it is written in Rom. 9: "Of whom Christ came according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever."

units.la: Nos credimus, docemus, & cōfitemur, in illa vna inseparabili personaChristi esse duas distinctas naturas, diuinam, quæ fuit ab æterno: & humanam, quæ in tempore humiliationis à Filio Dei assumpta est. Quæ duæ naturæ in persona Christi neque separantur, neque inter se confunduntur: neque altera in alteram transmutatur: sed quælibet suam naturam & essentiam in persona Christi in æternum retinet.
units.tr: We believe, teach and confess that in that one inseparable person of Christ there are two distinct natures: the divine, which was from eternity, and the human, which the Son of God assumed in the time of his humiliation. These two natures in the person of Christ are neither separated nor mingled with each other, and neither is changed into the other, but each retains its own nature and essence in the person of Christ for ever.

units.la: Nos credimus, docemus & confitemur etiam, sicut illæ duæ naturæ in suis naturis & essentiis inconfusæ & inextinctæ manent: quòd ita quælibet suas naturales & essentiales proprietates retineat: & in omnem æternitatem à se non deponat: neque vnius naturæ essentiales proprietates, alterius naturæ essentiales proprietates vnquam fiant.
units.tr: We believe, teach and confess also that, just as those two natures remain unconfused and unextinguished in their natures and essences, so each retains its natural and essential properties and does not lay them aside for all eternity, and the essential properties of one nature never become the essential properties of the other.

units.la: Ita credimus, docemus & cófitemur nos omnipotentem, æternum, infinitum, vbique simul esse naturaliter (hoc est, secundum pro prietatem naturæ & naturalis essentiæ, per se præsentem vbique esse) omnia scire, essen tiales proprietates esse diuinæ naturæ, quæ nunquam humanæ naturæ essentiales pro-prietates in omnem æternitatem fiant. Et contrà: Corporalem creaturam vel naturam esse, carnem & sanguinem esse, finitū & cir-cumscriptum esse, pati, mori, ascendere & descendere, de loco ad locum se mouere, esu rire, sitire, frigus & æstum pati, &c. esse pro-prietates humanæ naturæ, quæ diuinæ natu-ræ proprietates nunquam fiant.
units.tr: So we believe, teach and confess that the omnipotent, eternal, infinite God is everywhere at once naturally (that is, according to the property of his nature and natural essence, being present of himself everywhere), knows all things; these are the essential properties of the divine nature, which never become essential properties of the human nature for all eternity. And conversely: that a corporeal creature or nature, flesh and blood, to be finite and circumscribed, to suffer, to die, to ascend and descend, to move from place to place, to eat, to thirst, to endure cold and heat, and so on, are properties of the human nature, which never become properties of the divine nature.

units.la: Nos credimus, docemus, & confitemur etiam iam post incarnationem non vnaquan-que naturam in Christo per se ita consistere, vt quælibet sit persona, vel personam ef-ficiat: sed ita vnitas esse, vt vnam constituat personam, in qua simul personaliter est & consistit tam diuina quàm assumpta huma-na natura: Et sicut sine sua Deitate, ita etiam sine sua humanitate personam Christi aut fi-lii Dei incarnati, nō totam esse. Hinc Chri-stus non duę distinctę sed vna persona est: et-iamsi duę distinctę naturę in suis naturali-bus bus substantiis & proprietatibus inconfuse in ipsa inueniuntur.
units.tr: We believe, teach and confess also that, even after the incarnation, in Christ neither nature so subsists by itself that either is a person or makes a person; rather they are so united as to constitute one person, in which both the divine and the assumed human nature personally exist and subsist together. And just as the person of Christ, or of the incarnate Son of God, is not whole without his Deity, so neither is it whole without his humanity. Hence Christ is not two distinct persons but one person, even though two distinct natures are found in him, unconfused, with their natural substances and properties.

units.la: Nos credimus, docemus, & confitemur etiam assumptam humanā naturam in Christo non tantum suas naturales & essentiales ƒpprietates habere & retinere: sed pręter has propter personalem vnionem cum Deitate: & deinde propter glorificationem, esse ad dextram Maiestatis, virtutis & potentię super omne q nominari potest, non tantū in hac, sed etiam in futura vita, exaltatam.
units.tr: We believe, teach and confess also that the human nature assumed in Christ not only has and retains its natural and essential properties, but, besides these, on account of the personal union with the Deity, and then on account of its glorification, it is exalted to sit at the right hand of the Majesty, of power and might, above every name that can be named, not only in this life but also in the life to come.

units.la: Quantum ad hanc Maiestatem attinet, ad quam Christus secundum suam humanitatem exaltatus est: non accepit illam primùm post resurrectionem a mortuis, & ascensionem ad cælos: sed cùm in vtero matris suæ conciperetur, & homo fieret: atque diuina & humana natura simul personaliter vniretur. Quę personalis vnio non tamen ita intelligenda est, sicut quidam eam sinistrè accipiunt: quasi duę illę naturę diuina & humana simul adunatę sint, sicut duo asseres conglutinati: vt ipsę realiter, hoc est, re & facto nullam prorsus inter se communionem habeant. Nam hic error & hęresis Nestorij & Samosateni fuit: qui, vt Suidas & Theodorus Presbyter Rhetęlis testantur, docuerūt,
units.tr: As for this Majesty, to which Christ was exalted according to his humanity, he did not receive it first after his resurrection from the dead and ascension into the heavens, but when he was conceived in his mother's womb and became man, and the divine and human natures were personally united together. This personal union, however, is not to be understood as some people wrongly take it, as if those two natures, divine and human, were joined together like two boards glued together, so that they have really, that is in fact, no communion whatever with each other. For this was the error and heresy of Nestorius and Samosatenus, who, as Suidas and Theodore the Presbyter, the Lector, bear witness, taught

units.la: δύο φύσεις ἀκοινώνητως πρὸς ἑαυτὰς παραδόσιν hoc eft,naturas duas omnimodo incommu-nicabiles effe:qua locutione nature inter fe diuelluntur, & duo Chrifti fiunt:vt alius fit Chriftus,& alius fit Deus λόγος inChristo habitans.Sic enim fcribit Theodorus Presby-ter:Paulus quidā,iifdem quibusManes tem-poribus,Samofatenus quidem ortu,fed An-tiochię Syrię Antiftes , Dominum impiè di-xit nudum fuiffe homine, in quo Deus Ver-bum, ficut & in fingulisProphetis habitauit: ac proinde duas naturas feparatas & citra omnem prorfus inter fe communionem in Chrifto effe, quafi alius fit Chriftus, alius Deus Verbum in ipfo habitans. Contra hac damnatam herefin fancta Ecclefia femper fimpliciter credidit: Diuinam & Humanam naturam in perfona Chrifti ita vnitas effe, vt realem communionem inter fe habeant: qua naturę non in vnam fubftantiam,fed vt D.Lutherus fcribit, in vnam perfonam mi-fcentur : Ideo propter illam perfonalem v-nionem & communionem Orthodoxi ve-teris Ecclefię fępenumero ante & poft con-ciliū Chalcedonenfe vocabulūMixtionis in bono fenfu & difcrimine vfurparunt: ficut huius rei multa teftimonia, fi opus, proferri poffent: quę etiam fępe in noftrorum fcri-ptis obuiam veniunt. Et perfona lis vnio at-que que communio similitudine animæ & corpo ris, item ferri candentis explicatur. Nam cor pus & anima, sicut etiam ferrū & ignis non per phrasin aut modum loquendi, aut verba liter, sed verè & realiter communione inter se habent: neque tamen aliqua confusio fit, aut exequatio naturarum, quemadmodum quando ex melle & aqua fit mulsum: quod amplius non discretum mel aut aqua est, sed commixtus potus : vbi humanæ cum diui- na natura vnionis in persona Christi longè alia ratio est. Multo enim maior communio & ineffabilis vnio est inter diuinam & hu- manam naturam in persona Christi propter quam vnionem & communionem Deus est homo, & Homo est deus. qua tamen neque naturæ neque harum proprietates commi- scentur: sed quælibet natura retinet suâ es- sentiam & essentiales proprietates.
units.tr: δύο φύσεις ἀκοινώνητως πρὸς ἑαυτὰς παραδόσιν [two natures wholly incommunicable with respect to one another], that is, that the two natures are in every way incommunicable with each other. By such language the natures are torn apart, and there become two Christs: one is Christ, and another is the Word of God dwelling in Christ. For Theodore the Presbyter writes thus: a certain Paul, who lived in the same times as Manes, a Samosatene by birth but bishop of Antioch in Syria, impiously said that the Lord was merely a man in whom the Word of God dwelt, as in each of the prophets; and therefore that there are two natures in Christ, separate and without any communion whatever with each other, as if Christ were one and the Word of God dwelling in him another. Against this condemned heresy the holy Church has always simply believed that the divine and human natures in the person of Christ are so united that they have a real communion with each other; the natures are mingled not into one substance but, as Dr. Luther writes, into one person. Therefore, on account of that personal union and communion, the orthodox of the ancient Church, both before and after the Council of Chalcedon, frequently used the term "mixture" in a good sense and with a distinction. Many testimonies to this could be cited if needed, and they often occur in the writings of our own people. The personal union and communion is also explained by the likeness of soul and body, and by red-hot iron. For body and soul, just as iron and fire, have communion with each other not by a figure or manner of speaking, nor merely verbally, but truly and really; yet no confusion or equalizing of the natures takes place, as when mead is made from honey and water, which is no longer separate honey or water but a mixed drink. In the union of the human nature with the divine in the person of Christ the case is very different. For there is a far greater communion and an ineffable union between the divine and human natures in the person of Christ, on account of which union and communion God is man and man is God; yet neither the natures nor their properties are mingled, but each nature retains its own essence and essential properties.

units.la: Propter hāc personalē vnionē (quę absq. illa reali communicatione naturarū nec cogi- tari nec esse potest) nō nuda humana natura pro totius mūdi peccatis passa est: cuius pro prietas est pati & mori: sed ipse filius Dei rea liter, sed tamē secundū assumptā humanam naturā passus est: & est (vt habet cōstās & sim plex Fides nostra) verè mortuus, etiāsi diuina natura neq. pati neque mori potest: sicut D.
units.tr: Because of this personal union, which can neither be conceived nor exist without that real communication of the natures, it was not the bare human nature that suffered for the sins of the whole world, since suffering and dying belong to that nature. Rather, the Son of God himself suffered, really, yet according to the human nature he had assumed. And (as our constant and simple faith holds) he truly died, even though the divine nature can neither suffer nor die, just as D.

units.la: Lutherus hoc in sua magna confessione de Cœna Domini contra impia Alloeosin Cinglij, qua docuit natura altera pro altera debere sumi: quæ ceu ipsius diaboli doctrina in abyssum inferni damnatur, declarauit.
units.tr: Luther declared this in his great confession on the Lord's Supper against the impious alloeosis of Zwingli, by which Zwingli taught that the one nature must be taken for the other. That doctrine, as the very teaching of the devil, is condemned to the abyss of hell.

units.la: Quare etiam veteres, vtrunq; verbum κοινωνίαν & ἕνωσιν in expositione huius mysterij coniunxerunt & alteru per alteru expo-sue-runt. Irenæus lib. 4. cap. 3. Athanasius in epi-stola ad Epictetum. Hilarius de Trinitate li. 9. Basilius & Nissenus in Theodoret. Dama-scenus lib. 3. cap. 19.
units.tr: For this reason the ancients also joined the two words κοινωνία [communion] and ἕνωσις [union] in explaining this mystery, and explained one by means of the other. See Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 3; Athanasius, in his letter to Epictetus; Hilary, On the Trinity, book 9; Basil and Nyssen, in Theodoret; and Damascene, book 3, chapter 19.

units.la: Propter hanc personalem vnione & com-municatione diuinæ & humanæ naturæ in Christo, credimus, docemus & confitemur nos iuxta simplicé nostram fidé, quicquid de Maiestate Christi secundū humanitate suam ad dexteram omnipotentis virtutis Dei , & quæ inde consequuntur, dicitur: quæ omnia nihil essent, neq. consistere possent, nisi hæc personalis vnio & comunicatio naturarum in persona Christi realiter constaret.
units.tr: Because of this personal union and communication of the divine and human natures in Christ, we believe, teach and confess, according to our simple faith, whatever is said of the majesty of Christ according to his humanity at the right hand of the almighty power of God, and whatever follows from it. All of this would be nothing and could not stand, unless this personal union and communication of the natures really subsisted in the person of Christ.

units.la: Propter hanc personalé vnione & cómu-nicationem naturarū, Maria virgo benedi-cta non merū hominé, sed talem homine qui realiter est Filius Dei altissimi, peperit: vt An-gelus testatur: quod suam etiam diuina ma-iestatem in vtero matris patefacit, cū ex virgine illæsa virginitate natus est. Ideóque ipsa realiter Dei genitrix est, virgo tamen incorrupta.
units.tr: Because of this personal union and communication of the natures, the blessed Virgin Mary bore not merely a man, but such a man as is really the Son of the Most High God, as the Angel testifies. In this way his divine majesty was also revealed in the mother's womb, since he was born of a virgin whose virginity remained unharmed. Therefore she is really the Mother of God, and yet a virgin uncorrupted.

units.la: Per eam ipsam etiam omnia sua miracula operatus est: & hanc suam diuinam maiestatem pro suo beneplacito quando & quomodo voluit, & non primùm post suam resurrectionem & ascensionem sed etiam in statu humiliationis suæ manifestauit: vt in nuptiis Canæ Galileæ: Item cum 12. annos natus esset inter docentes: Itē cùm in horto vno verbo suos hostes ad terram prosterneret: similiter in morte, vbi nō simpliciter, sicut alius homo mortuus est: sed cùm & in morte peccatum, mortem, Diabolum, infernum & æternam damnationem deuicit: quæ humana natura sola nunquam præstare potuisset, si non cum diuina natura personaliter vnita fuisset, & communionē habuisset.
units.tr: Through that same union he also performed all his miracles, and he revealed this his divine majesty whenever and however he willed, and not first after his resurrection and ascension, but already in the state of his humiliation: as at the wedding in Cana of Galilee; likewise when he was twelve years old and among the teachers; likewise when in the garden he cast his enemies to the ground with a single word; and similarly in death, where he did not die simply as another man dies, but when in death also he overcame sin, death, the devil, hell and eternal damnation. The human nature alone could never have accomplished these things, had it not been personally united with the divine nature and had communion with it.

units.la: Hinc facta etiam est humanæ naturæ exaltatio post resurrectionem à mortuis super omnes creaturas in cælo & in terra: quæ nihil est aliud, quàm quod Christus formam serui in vniuersum deposituit, non depositā tamen humana natura, sed in æternum seruata atque in plenam possessionem & vsurpationem diuinæ Maiestatis collocata: quā Maiestatem tamen in sua conceptione & in vtero matris habuit: verùm, vt Apostolus te statur, ἐξεκένωσε, hoc est vt D. Lutherus explicat, in statu suæ humiliationis clam serua uit, & non semper sed quando voluit, vsurpauit. Iam verò postquam non simpliciter sicut alius quispiam sanctus in cælum, sed vt Apostolus attestatur, super omnes cælos cō scendit, etiā verè omnia implet, & vbiq. non tantum vt Deus, sed etiā vt Homo præsens regit à mari ad mare, & vsque ad fine mundi, vt Prophetæ sunt vaticinati & Apostoli testati, quod vbique cum ipsis operatus sit & ipsorum verba confirmauerit per subsequētia signa. Psal.8.& 93.Zach.9.Rom.15.
units.tr: Hence also came the exaltation of the human nature after the resurrection from the dead above all creatures in heaven and on earth. This is nothing other than that Christ put off the form of a servant entirely, yet not so that the human nature was laid aside; rather it was preserved for ever and placed in full possession and exercise of the divine majesty, which majesty he had already possessed in his conception and in the mother's womb. But, as the Apostle testifies, he ἐξεκένωσε [emptied himself]; that is, as D. Luther explains, he kept that majesty hidden in the state of his humiliation, and used it not always but when he willed. Now, since he ascended not simply as another holy man into heaven, but, as the Apostle attests, above all the heavens, he truly fills all things, and is present everywhere, ruling not only as God but also as man, from sea to sea and to the ends of the earth, as the prophets foretold and the apostles testified: that he has worked everywhere with them and confirmed their words by the signs that followed. Psal.8.& 93.Zach.9.Rom.15.

units.la: Neque tamen hoc terreno aliquo modo factum est, sed vt D. Lutherus exponit, ratione dexteræ diuinæ, quæ nullus certus locus est in cælo, quemadmodum Sacramentarij sine fundamento sacrarum literarum dicunt: Sed est nihil aliud quàm omnipotens virtus Dei, quæ cælum & terram implet: in qua Christus secundum suam Humanitatem realiter sine confusione & exæquatione naturarum in sua substantia & substantialibus proprietatibus collocatus est: ex qua communicata virtute, vt sonant verba Testamenti, ipse suo corpore & sanguine in sacra Cœna realiter præsens esse potest test, & est, quod aliâs nulli homini possibile est: quoniam nullus homo hoc modo cum diuina natura vnitus est, & in eam diuinam omnipotentem Maiestatem & virtutem Dei per & in personali vnione duarum naturarum in Christo collocatus, sicut Iesus fi lius Mariæ,in quo diuina & humana natura personaliter simul vnitæ suut, ita vt in Chri ito omnis Deitatis plenitudo corporaliter habitet.Colof.2.Et in hac personali vnione eiusmodi ineffabilem communionem habet,quam etiam ipsi Angeli mirantur,obstu pescunt,& in ea spectanda,vt S. Petrus testa tur, voluptatem & lætitiam capiunt: sicut hæc omnia suo loco fusius à nobis decla- rabuntur.
units.tr: Yet this has not happened in any earthly manner, but, as D. Luther expounds, by reason of the right hand of God, which is no fixed place in heaven, as the Sacramentarians say without any foundation in the sacred letters. It is nothing other than the almighty power of God, which fills heaven and earth. In this power Christ, according to his humanity, is really placed, without confusion or equalizing of the natures, in his substance and substantial properties. From this communicated power, as the words of the Testament sound, he can be, and is, really present with his body and blood in the holy Supper, which is impossible for any other man, because no other man is united with the divine nature in this way, nor is placed in that divine, almighty majesty and power of God through and in the personal union of the two natures in Christ. Jesus, the son of Mary, is so placed, in whom the divine and human natures are personally united together, so that in Christ all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. Col. 2. In this personal union he has such an ineffable communion as the very angels marvel at and gaze upon, and in contemplating which, as St. Peter testifies, they take pleasure and joy. As all these things will be set out more fully by us in their proper place.

units.la: Ex hoc fundamento,quemadmodum est iam indicatum, & vnio personalis declarat, hoc est quo modo diuina & humana natura in persona Christi simul vnitæ sint, vt non solum nomina communia, sed etiam realiter inter se &sine omni permixtione earum in sua substantia communionem habeant: oritur etiam doctrina de communicatione Idiomatum,hoc est de reali communione proprietatum naturarum, de qua deinceps copiosius dicetur.
units.tr: From this foundation, as has already been indicated, and as the personal union makes clear, that is, how the divine and human natures are united together in the person of Christ, there arises not only a common naming but also a real communion of the natures with one another in their substance, and without any mixing of them. From this also arises the doctrine of the communication of idioms, that is, of the real communion of the properties of the natures, of which more will be said at length below.

units.la: Quia enim verum est illud quòd propriū non egrediatur sua subiecta, hoc est, quod quælibet natura suas essētiales proprietates retineat, & eas à natura non separet, atque in alteram naturam, sicut aqua ex aliquo vase in aliud transfundatur: non posset aliqua communicatio proprietatum esse, nec consistere, si personalis vnio & communio naturarum in persona Christi non realis esset: quod iuxta articulum sanctæ Trinitatis longè maximum mysterium in cælo & in terra est, sicut Paulus ait, ὁμολογουμένως μέγα ἐστὶ τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον, Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκὶ 1. Tim.3. Nam quia Apostolus Petrus claris verbis testatur, etiam nos in quibus Christus ex gratia habitat propter hoc summum mysterium in Christo participes fieri diuinæ naturæ, quam communionem diuinæ naturæ hanc esse oportet, de qua Apostolus loquitur, quòd in Christo omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter habitet: ita vt Deus & homo una persona sit.
units.tr: For since it is true that a property does not go out from its subject, that is, that each nature retains its essential properties and does not separate them from itself, nor pour them into the other nature as water is poured from one vessel into another, there could be no communication of properties, nor could it stand, if the personal union and communion of the natures in the person of Christ were not real. This, according to the article of the holy Trinity, is by far the greatest mystery in heaven and on earth, as Paul says: ὁμολογουμένως μέγα ἐστὶ τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον, Θεὸς ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί [Without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh], 1 Tim. 3. For the Apostle Peter testifies in clear words that we also, in whom Christ dwells by grace, become partakers of the divine nature because of this highest mystery in Christ. This communion of the divine nature must be that of which the Apostle speaks, that in Christ all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, so that God and man are one person.

units.la: Sed quia permultum refert, vt doctrina de communicatione Idiomatū iusto discrimine tractetur & explicetur (propositiones enim aut prædicationes non habent omnes vnam eandémque naturam: & quando promiscuè sine discrimine de iis dicitur, confunditur ipsa doctrina: & simplex lector facilè perturbatur) sequens tractatus diligenter ob seruari debet: qui melioris & simplicioris intelligentie gratia non incommodè in tria capita diuidi potest.
units.tr: But since it matters greatly that the doctrine of the communication of idioms be treated and explained with the proper distinctions (for not all propositions or predications have one and the same nature, and when they are used indiscriminately, without distinction, the doctrine itself is confused and the simple reader is easily disturbed), the following treatise must be carefully observed. For the sake of a better and simpler understanding, it may conveniently be divided into three heads.

units.la: 1 Cùm in Christo duæ distinctæ naturæ in suis naturalibus substantiis & proprietatib. salvæ & inconfusæ sint & maneant: duarum autem naturarum una tantum persona sit, id quod proprium est vnius persone, non naturæ tantum tanquam separatæ sed toti personæ, quæ simul Deus & homo est (nominetur siue Deus siue Homo) attribuitur. Sed in hoc genere loquendi nō sequitur: quicquid personæ attribuitur, vt idipsum simul vtriusque naturæ proprium sit: sed distinctè declaratur, secundum quam naturam vnumquodque personæ attribuatur. Ita filius Dei natus est ex semine Dauidis secundum carnem Rom. 1. Item, Christus occisus est secundum carnem: & passus est in vel secundum carnem 1. Pet. 2. & 4.
units.tr: 1. Since in Christ the two distinct natures remain and abide whole and unconfused in their natural substances and properties, and since there is only one person of the two natures, what is proper to the one person, not to one nature alone as if separated but to the whole person, who is at once God and man (whether named God or man), is attributed to that person. Yet in this manner of speaking it does not follow that whatever is attributed to the person is therefore a property of both natures at once; rather, it is set out distinctly according to which nature each thing is attributed. Thus the Son of God was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, Rom. 1. Likewise, Christ was put to death according to the flesh, and suffered in or according to the flesh, 1 Pet. 2 and 4.

units.la: Quia autem sub verbis illis, quibus dicitur (toti personæ tribuitur quod vni naturæ proprium est) clandestini & manifesti Sacramentarij suum turpissimum errorem occultant (cùm totam quidè personā dicunt, sed tamè tantū nudè alteram naturā subintelligunt, alteramque prorsus excludunt: quasi nuda humana natura pro nobis esset passa: quemadmodum D. Lutherus in sua magna confessione deCœna Domini de Cinglij Allœosi scripsit)ipsius D.Lutheri verba hîc ponemus,quò Ecclesia Dei cōtra talem errorē etiam atque etiam præmuniatur. Verba eius ita sonant. Hoc vocat Cinglius Allœosin quando aliquid de Deitate dicitur, quod tamen humanitati competit: aut contrà: vt Luc. 24, An Christū nō oportebat pati,&sic intrare in gloriâ suam? Hïc somniat ille, Christum sumi pro humana natura.Caue,caue inquam tibi ab Allœosi ista:est enim Diaboli larua:& talem facit Christum,secundū quem nolim ego esse Christianus: videl.quodChristus in posterū nihil amplius sit nec faciat sua passione & vita, quàm alius simplex homo sanctus. Nam si hoc credo, quòd tantum humana natura pro me passa est,tum est mihi ille Christus vilis saluator:& opus est ipsi salvatore.In summa dici non potest, quid Diabolus sua Allœosi quærat.Et paulo post:Si vetula illa venefica domina ratio Allœoseos auiadixerit: At qui Deitas nō potest pati nec mori. Respondebis, Hoc verum est, sed quia Deitas & Humanitas est vna persona in Christo, propter talem personalem vnionem scriptura tribuit etiam Diuinitati omnia quæ Humanitati eueniunt, & contrà: Et ita se reuera habet. Nam hoc fatendum est,Persona(Christus)patitur,moritur: hæc persona sona est verus Deus: Ideo recte dicitur, Filius Dei patitur. Nam etiâsi una pars (vt sic dicam) vt Diuinitas non patitur, patitur tamen ea persona, quæ est Deus in altera parte, vt in Humanitate. Nam realiter est Filius Dei pro nobis crucifixus, hoc est illa persona quæ Deus est: nam ipsa, ipsa inquam persona est crucifixa secũdum humanitatem. Et iterũ paulo post. Quod si Allœosis vera est, quemadmodum Cinglius eam proponit, tum Christum oportebit duplicem esse personam, diuinam vnam, & humanam vnam: quandoquidem dicta de passione tantùm ad humanam naturam refert, & prorsus à Deitate abstrahit. Nam quando actiones diuiduntur & se parantur, tum etiam persona separabitur: quia omnes actiones siue passiones non natura sed personæ attribuuntur. Persona enim est, quæ omnia facit & patitur: hoc quidem secundum hanc naturam, illud verò secundum aliam naturam. Sicuti hæc omnia homines docti norunt. Ideóq. credimus Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum Deum & hominem in vna persona, non confundentes naturas, nec diuidentes personam.
units.tr: But since the secret and open Sacramentarians hide their most shameful error under those words, by which it is said that what belongs to one nature is attributed to the whole person (for they say "the whole person" but mean only the one nature in a bare sense and entirely exclude the other, as if bare human nature alone suffered for us, as Dr. Luther wrote in his great confession on the Lord's Supper against Zwingli's Alloeosis), we will set down here the very words of Dr. Luther himself, so that the Church of God may be ever more firmly guarded against such error. His words run thus: Zwingli calls it Alloeosis when something is said of the Deity that nevertheless belongs to the humanity, or the reverse, as in Luke 24: Ought not Christ to have suffered and so entered into his glory? There he dreams that Christ is taken for human nature. Beware, I say, beware of that Alloeosis, for it is the devil's mask, and it makes Christ such that I would not wish to be a Christian according to him, namely that Christ henceforth is nothing more and does nothing more by his passion and life than any other simple holy man. For if I believe that only human nature suffered for me, then that Christ is a worthless saviour to me, and he himself needs a saviour. In sum, it cannot be said what the devil seeks by his Alloeosis. And a little later: If that old witch, Lady Reason, has said of the Alloeosis: But the Deity cannot suffer or die. You will reply: This is true, but because the Deity and the humanity are one person in Christ, on account of this personal union Scripture attributes to the Deity also all that happens to the humanity, and the reverse. And so it really stands. For this must be confessed: the person (Christ) suffers and dies; this person is true God. Therefore it is rightly said that the Son of God suffers. For although one part (so to speak), namely the Deity, does not suffer, nevertheless that person who is God suffers in the other part, namely in the humanity. For truly the Son of God was crucified for us, that is, that person who is God; for it is that very person, I say, that was crucified according to the humanity. And again a little later: If the Alloeosis is true, as Zwingli puts it forward, then Christ would have to be two persons, one divine and one human, since he refers the things said about the passion only to the human nature and entirely separates them from the Deity. For when the actions are divided and set apart, then the person is also divided, because all actions or passions are attributed not to the nature but to the person. For it is the person who does and suffers all things: this indeed according to this nature, that according to the other nature. As learned men know all these things. Therefore we believe that our Lord Jesus Christ is God and man in one person, neither confusing the natures nor dividing the person.

units.la: Tom. 7. Viteb. f. 530.
units.tr: Vol. 7, Wittenberg edition, f. 530.

units.la: Item D. Lutherus de cōciliis & Ecclesiis. Nos Christianos scire oportet, nisi Deus ipse vnà fuerit in lance & pondus dederit, tum feremur nos cum nostra lance in profundum: hoc sic puto: ni dicatur, Deus est pro nobis mortuus, sed tantum homo, periimus. Quando autem Dei mors vel Deus mortuus in lance iacet, tum ille in profundum defertur, & nos sursum efferimur tanquam lanx facilis & inanis. Potest autem ille etiam iterum sursum elevari, vel sua lance exilire: non vero potest in lance sedere, nisi nobis similis homo factus: ut dici possit: Deus mortuus, Deus passus: Dei sanguis, Dei mors: Deus enim in sua natura non potest mori. Sed quando Deus & homo unitus est in unam personam, recte dicitur, Dei mors. Homo enim ille moritur, qui cum Deo unum sive una persona est. Hactenus Lutherus.
units.tr: Likewise Dr. Luther, on councils and churches: We Christians must know that unless God himself has been placed in the scale together with us, and has given weight, we shall be carried down with our scale into the depths. I think it is like this: if it is not said, "God has died for us, but only a man," we perish. But when the death of God, or God dead, lies in the scale, then that scale is carried down into the depths and we are lifted up like an empty, light pan. He, however, can again be raised up or leap out of his scale; yet he cannot sit in the scale unless he has been made a man like us, so that it can be said: God died, God suffered; the blood of God, the death of God. For God in his own nature cannot die. But when God and man are united in one person, it is rightly said, "the death of God." For that man dies who is one and the same person with God. Thus far Luther.

units.la: Hinc manifestum est, non recte dici, quando dicitur vel scribitur, illas locutiones Deus est passus, Deus est mortuus, esse tantum praedicationes verbales, hoc est esse tantum nuda verba & non realia. Nostra enim simplex fides demonstrat, Filium Dei fuisse incarnatum, pro nobis passum & mortuum, & suo sanguine nos redemisse.
units.tr: Hence it is plain that it is not right to say, when it is said or written, that those expressions "God has suffered" and "God has died" are merely verbal predications, that is, mere words and not realities. For our simple faith shows that the Son of God was incarnate, suffered and died for us, and redeemed us by his blood.

units.la: Secundo quod attinet ad consummationem officij Christi, agit & operatur persona nihil in, cum, per & secundum alterutram naturam solam, sed in, secundum, cum & per utramque naturam: vel sicut concilium Chalcedonense loquitur: Una natura opera-tur rur communicatione alicuius, quod est cuiusque proprium. Ita Christus est noster Mediator, Redemptor, Rex, Sacerdos, Caput, Pastor, &c. non secundū alterutram naturā tantùm siue ea sit diuina siue humana, sed secundum vtranque naturam: sicut hæc doctrina alibi vberius tractatur.
units.tr: Secondly, as regards the carrying out of the office of Christ, the person acts and works not in, with, through or according to one nature alone, but in, according to, with and through both natures; or, as the Council of Chalcedon puts it: each nature works in communion with the other what is proper to it. So Christ is our Mediator, Redeemer, King, Priest, Head, Shepherd, and so on, not according to one nature only, whether divine or human, but according to both natures. This doctrine is treated more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Tertiò est adhuc longè aliud, quando de eo interrogatur, dicitur aut agitur: an naturæ in personali vnione in Christo nihil magis quàm tantum suas naturales & essentiales proprietates habeant. (nam quod eas habeant & retineant supra est affirmatum.) Quod ad diuinam in Christo naturam attinet, quia apud Patrem nulla est mutatio Iac. 1. Deo suæ naturæ per incarnationem in essentia sua & proprietatibus nihil nec accessit nec decessit: Est in & per se, illa incarnatione, neque minor neq. maior facta. Quod autem attinet ad humanam assumptam naturam in persona Christi, contendere quidem voluerunt aliqui, quòd ea etiam in personali cum Deitate vnione aliud & amplius nihil habet quàm tantum suas naturales & essentiales proprietates, secundum quas suis fratribus per omnia similis sit: & quòd propterea humanæ naturæ in Christo non debeant nec possint ascribi, quæ sunt contra vel supra naturales suas proprietates, etiam si scripturæ testimoniaita sonent. Sed hanc opinionem falsam esse & iniustam, est exvei bo Dei tam clarum, vt etiam illorum contri bules iam iustum errorem reprehédant & re- iiciant. Sacra enim scriptura, & veteres ex sa cra scriptura recte testantur, quòd humana natura in Christo (ideo & inde, quia cum di uina natura in Christo personaliter est vni- ta, & deposita ferui forma & humiliatione est glorificata atque ad dexteram Maiesta- tis & virtutis Dei exaltata) iuxta & supra suas naturales & essentiales manentes pro- prietates, etiam alias immensas, supernatu- rales, imperscrutabiles, inenarrabiles, cæle- stes prærogatiuas in Maiestate, Sanctitate, Virtute & Potentia super omne nomen non tantum in hoc sed etiam in futuro mun do, acceperit: vt ita humana natura in Chri- sto ad actiones officij Christi suo modo vnà adhibeatur, & suam etiam efficaciam, hoc est virtutem & operatione habeat: non tan- tum ex & secundum suas essentiales pro- prietates, aut duntaxat quantum facultas patitur, sed præcipuè ex & secundum Maie- statem, gloriam, virtutem & potentia, quam ipsa personali vnione, glorificatione & exal tatione accepit. Et hoc non possunt etiam adueraduersarij negare: tantum disputant & certant esse dona creata, aut finitas qualitates, sicut in sanctis, quibus humana natura in Christo donata est & ornata. Et suis cogitationibus propriisque argumentationib. vel rationibus metiri & computare volüt, quid humana natura in Christo absque sui destructione capere vel non capere possit aut debeat. Verum optima, certissima, & tutissima via in hac controuersia est hęc, vid. Quod ea quæ Christus secundum suam assumptam naturam humanam personali vnione, glorificatione aut exaltatione accepit, & quę sua essentia humana natura supra naturales proprietates absque illarum destructione capere potest: Ea inquam, nemo melius & certius scire possit quàm ipse Christus. Is autē ea quæ nobis in hac vita sunt scitu necessaria in suo verbo manifestauit. De quibus igitur in hoc casu certa testimonia habemus, ea simpliciter debemus credere & nullomodo contra disputare, quasi possit humana natura in Christo eius non capax esse. Est quidem hoc certum & verum, quod de creatis donis humanæ naturæ in Christo data & communicatis, quòd ea illa per se habeat, dicitur: sed illa adhuc non attingunt Maiestatem, quam Scriptura & veteres ex scriptura assumptæ humanæ naturæ in Christo attribuunt. Viuificare enim, omne iudicium & omnem potestatem habere in cælo & in terra, omnia in suis manibus habere, omnia suis pedibus subiecta tenere, à peccatis mundare, non sunt creata dona, sed diuinæ, infinitæ proprietates, quæ tamen iuxta scripturas homini Christo datæ & communicatæ sunt. Ioh. 5. 6. Matth. 28. Dan. 7. Ioh. 3. & 13. Matth. 11. Eph. 1. Heb. 2. 1. Cor. 15. Ioh. 1. Et quod hæc communicatio non per phrasin aut modum loquendi (hoc est tantum verbis) de persona, solum secundum diuinam naturam, sed secundum assumptam humanam naturam intelligenda sit, demonstrant tria firma indissolubilia argumenta & fundamenta.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is quite another matter when it is asked, said or treated whether the natures in Christ's personal union have nothing more than their natural and essential properties. (That they have and retain these has been affirmed above.) As for the divine nature in Christ, since there is no change with the Father (James 1), nothing has been added to or taken from God in his nature, in his essence or his properties, by the incarnation: he remains in and through himself, neither made less nor greater by that incarnation. As for the assumed human nature in the person of Christ, some have wished to contend that it too, in its personal union with the Deity, has nothing more or other than its natural and essential properties, according to which it is in all things like its brethren; and that therefore those things which are against or above its natural properties ought not and cannot be ascribed to the human nature in Christ, even though the testimonies of Scripture sound so. But that this opinion is false and unjust is so clear from the Word of God that even those who hold it are now rebuking and rejecting their own mistaken error. For Holy Scripture, and the ancients from Holy Scripture, rightly testify that the human nature in Christ (for this reason too, that it is united personally with the divine nature in Christ, and having laid aside the form of a servant and its humiliation has been glorified and exalted to the right hand of the Majesty and power of God) has received, both alongside and above its natural and essential properties which remain, also other immense, supernatural, unsearchable, inexpressible, heavenly prerogatives in majesty, holiness, virtue and power above every name, not only in this world but also in the world to come; so that the human nature in Christ is also employed together, in its own way, in the actions of Christ's office, and has its own efficacy, that is, power and operation, not only from and according to its essential properties, or only as far as its capacity allows, but chiefly from and according to the majesty, glory, virtue and power which it has received through the personal union, glorification and exaltation. And this even the adversaries cannot deny; they only dispute and contend that these are created gifts, or finite qualities, as in the saints, with which the human nature in Christ has been endowed and adorned. And they wish to measure and reckon by their own thoughts and arguments or reasonings what the human nature in Christ can or should receive, or not receive, without its own destruction. But the best, most certain and safest way in this controversy is this: that those things which Christ has received according to his assumed human nature through the personal union, glorification or exaltation, and which that human nature in its essence can receive above its natural properties without their destruction, these, I say, no one can know better and more certainly than Christ himself. He has made known in his Word what we need to know in this life. Therefore, concerning those things for which we have certain testimonies in this matter, we ought simply to believe them and by no means dispute against them, as if the human nature in Christ could not be capable of them. It is indeed certain and true that it is said of the created gifts given to and communicated to the human nature in Christ that it has them of itself; but these do not yet reach the majesty which Scripture and the ancients from Scripture attribute to the assumed human nature in Christ. For to quicken, to hold all judgment and all power in heaven and on earth, to have all things in his hands, to have all things subject to his feet, to cleanse from sins, these are not created gifts but divine, infinite properties, which nevertheless according to the Scriptures have been given and communicated to the man Christ (John 5 and 6; Matt. 28; Dan. 7; John 3 and 13; Matt. 11; Eph. 1; Heb. 2; 1 Cor. 15; John 1). And that this communication is to be understood not by a figure of speech or manner of speaking (that is, only in words) concerning the person as regards the divine nature alone, but as regards the assumed human nature, three firm and indissoluble arguments and foundations demonstrate.

units.la: Primum est communis regula totius Orthodoxæ Ecclesiæ, quicquid sacra scriptura dicit Christum in tempore accepisse, non secundum diuinam naturam, secundum quam ipse omnia ab æterno habuit, sed secundum humanam intelligendum esse.
units.tr: This is the common rule of the whole orthodox Church: whatever Holy Scripture says Christ received in time must be understood not according to the divine nature, by which he had all things from eternity, but according to the human nature.

units.la: Secundum, testatur sacra scriptura aperte Ioh. 5. & 6. Virtutem viuificandi, & iudicium agendi Christo datam esse, ideo quia filius hominis est, & sicut carnem & sanguinem habet.
units.tr: Second, Holy Scripture plainly testifies in John 5 and 6 that the power of giving life and of executing judgment was given to Christ because he is the Son of Man and has flesh and blood.

units.la: Tertium, Dicit scriptura non tantùm in genere de persona filij hominis, sed loquitur etiam expresse de assumpta humana natura Ioh. 1. Sanguis Christi mundat nos ab omnibus peccatis: non tantum secundum meritum; quod in cruce est semel peractum: sed Ioannes loquitur in eo loco de eo, quòd nos in actu iustificationis nō tantum diuina natura in Christo, sed etiam suus sanguis per modum efficacię mundet nos ab omnibus peccatis. Sic Ioh. 6. Est caro Christi viuificās cibus; sicut ex eo etiam consilium Ephesinū conclusit, quòd caro Christi virtutem habeat viuificandi. Sicut de hoc articulo alia multa illustria testimonia veteris Orthodoxę Ecclesię alibi sunt proposita.
units.tr: Third, Scripture speaks not only in general of the person of the Son of Man but also expressly of the assumed human nature. In 1 John 1: "The blood of Christ cleanses us from all sins." This is not only according to the merit that was accomplished once for all on the cross. John is speaking there of the fact that, in the act of justification, it is not only the divine nature in Christ but also his blood that cleanses us from all sins, by way of efficacy. Likewise John 6: "My flesh is the living food." From this passage the Council of Ephesus also concluded that the flesh of Christ has the power of giving life. Many other clear testimonies of the ancient orthodox Church on this article have been set forth elsewhere.

units.la: Proinde quòd Christus iuxta suam humanam naturam hęc accepit & humanę naturę in Christo sint data & communicata, debemus & oportet nos secundum scripturam credere. Sed, sicut supra dictum est, quia duę illę naturę in Christo ita vnitę sunt, vt non inter se commixtę aut altera in alteram commutata sit: cuiuslibet etiā proprietates essent tiales alterius naturę proprietates nunquā fiant. Est hęc doctrina etiam rectè declaranda, & accuratè contra omnes hereses munienda. In qua nos nihil noui ex nobis ipsis fingimus: sed amplectimur & conseruamus declarationem, quam veteres Orthodoxę Ecclesię ex bono fundamento sacrę scripturę de hac re reliquerunt, videlicet, quòd diuina virtus, vita, potestas, Maiestas & gloria assumptę humanę naturę in Christo data sit: non ita sicut Pater filio secundum diuinam naturam suam essentiam & omnes diuinas proprietates ab æterno communicauit. Unde etiam unius essentię est cum Patre & Deo æqualis. Christus enim tantùm secundum diuinam naturam Patri æqualis est, sed secundum assumptam humanam naturam est infra Deum. Ex quo planum fit, nos nullam confusionem, æquationem, abolitionem naturarum in Christo facere. Præterea virtus vivificandi non ita est in carne Christi sicut in diuina natura, videlicet tanquam essentialis proprietas. Neque facta est hęc communicatio per essentialem aut naturalem aliquam transfusionē proprietatum diuinę naturę in humanam naturam, ita ut Christi humanitas eam per se & à diuina essentia separatam habeat: aut quasi per eam humana natura in Christo suas naturales proprietates omnino depositerit: & iam vel in Deitatem mutata sit vel his communicatis proprietatibus in & per se æqualis facta: aut aut quòd nunc vtraque natura vna fit: aut denique æquales essentiales proprietates & actiones esse debeant.
units.tr: Therefore we must and ought to believe, according to Scripture, that Christ received these things according to his human nature, and that they are given and communicated to the human nature in Christ. But, as said above, the two natures in Christ are so united that they are not mixed together, nor is one changed into the other, so the essential properties of neither nature can ever become the properties of the other. This doctrine too must be rightly declared and carefully defended against all heresies. In this we invent nothing new of our own. Rather, we embrace and maintain the declaration which the ancient orthodox Church left on this matter, from the sound foundation of Holy Scripture: namely, that the divine power, life, authority, majesty and glory have been given to the assumed human nature in Christ, but not in the way that the Father from eternity communicated to the Son, according to his divine nature, his essence and all the divine properties. Hence the Son is also of one essence with the Father and equal to God. For Christ is equal to the Father only according to the divine nature, but according to the assumed human nature he is below God. From this it is plain that we make no confusion, equalization or abolition of the natures in Christ. Moreover, the power of giving life is not in the flesh of Christ as it is in the divine nature, namely as an essential property. Nor has this communication been made by some essential or natural transfusion of the properties of the divine nature into the human nature, so that the humanity of Christ would have them of itself and separated from the divine essence; or as if the human nature in Christ had through it laid aside its natural properties altogether and were now either changed into the Deity or, with these properties communicated, made equal in itself; or as if both natures now became one; or finally as if there must be equal essential properties and actions.

units.la: Hę & similes corruptelę in veteribus approbatis conciliis ex fundamento sacre scripturę merito reiectę & condemnatę. Minimè enim facienda vel admittenda est aut conuersio aut confusio, aut exęquatio siue naturarum in Christo siue essentialium proprietatum. Quo pacto etiam nos voces illas Realis communicatio vel realiter communicari nunquam de aliqua physica cōmunicatione vel essentiali trāsfusione intelleximus: sicut quidam illas peruersè & malignè, vt puram doctrinam suspectam redderent, contra conscientiam interpretati sunt: sed tantùm verbali comunicationi oppositiuimus, cum tales homines dixerunt, quòd tantum phrasis & modus sit loquendi, quam etiam adeò vrse runt, vt nullam aliam communicationem scire voluerint. E cōtra ad maiorem manifestatis Christi declarationem, quomodo hęc verba (de reali communicatione) vsurpentur, sic exponere voluimus: quòd hęc communicatio realiter, sine omni tamen permixtione naturarum & essentialium proprietatum facta sit.
units.tr: These and similar corruptions have been rightly rejected and condemned in the ancient approved councils, on the foundation of Holy Scripture. By no means may conversion, confusion or equalization be done or admitted, whether of the natures in Christ or of their essential properties. In this way too we have never understood those words real communication, or to be really communicated as referring to any physical communication or essential transfusion. Some have interpreted them perversely and maliciously, against their own conscience, in order to make pure doctrine suspect. We only opposed a merely verbal communication, which such men said was only a figure and manner of speaking, and which they pressed so hard that they wanted to know no other communication. On the contrary, to declare more clearly how these words (of real communication) are to be used, we wished to explain it thus: that this communication has been made really, yet without any mixture of the natures or of their essential properties.

units.la: Sentimus igitur & docemus nos cum ve teri Orthodoxa Ecclesia, sicut ea hanc do-ctrinam ex Scriptura tradidit: Humanam naturam in Christo illam maiestatem accepisse ratione personalis vnionis, videlicet quia tota plenitudo Deitatis in Christo habitat, non sicut in aliis sanctis hominibus aut Angelis, sed corporaliter vt in suo corpore proprio, q; cum omni sua maiestate, virtute, gloria, & operatione in assumpta humana natura liberrime, quando & quomodo vult, lucet: in, cum & per eam, suam diuinam potentiam, gloriam & actionem ostendit, exerit & perficit: sicut anima in corpore, & ignis in ardente ferro facit (his enim similitudinibus, sicut superius etiam est dictum, tota vetusta Ecclesia hanc doctrinam explicauit) Hoc tempore humiliationis fuit occultatum & absconditum, sed iam deposita ferui forma, fit hoc perfecte, efficaciter, & manifeste coram omnib. sanctis in coelo & in terra: & nos etiam in illa vita hanc suam Maiestatem a facie ad faciem spectabimus. Ioan. 17.
units.tr: We therefore feel and teach, with the ancient orthodox Church, as it handed this doctrine down from Scripture: the human nature in Christ has received that majesty by reason of the personal union, namely because the whole fullness of the Deity dwells in Christ. It dwells not as in other holy men or angels, but bodily, as in its own proper body. With all its majesty, power, glory and working, it shines most freely in the assumed human nature in Christ, when and how it wills. In, with and through that nature it shows, exerts and accomplishes its divine power, glory and action, just as the soul does in the body and fire does in a glowing iron. (For by these likenesses, as was said above, the whole ancient Church explained this doctrine.) In the time of humiliation this was hidden and concealed, but now, the form of a servant having been laid aside, it is done perfectly, effectively and manifestly before all the saints in heaven and on earth. We too in that life shall behold this majesty face to face. John 17.

units.la: Ita est, & manet in Christo tantum vna diuina omnipotentia, virtus, maiestas, & gloria, quæ tantum diuinæ naturæ propria est: eadem vero lucet, exerit & ostendit se perfecte, liberè tamen, in, cum, & per assumptam & exaltatam humanam naturam in Christo: sicut in cadente ferro non duplex vis est lucendi & ardendi: sed fa
units.tr: So it is: there remains in Christ only one divine omnipotence, power, majesty and glory, which belongs to the divine nature alone. Yet the same shines forth, exerts itself and shows itself perfectly, yet freely, in, with and through the assumed and exalted human nature in Christ. Just as in a glowing iron there is not a double power of shining and burning, but the power of shining and burning belongs to the fire itself.

units.la: Ioan. 17. cultas lucēdi & ardēdi est ignis ꝑpria. Quia autē ignis cū ferro vnitus est, exerit & often dit suā vim lucendi & ardendi in, cū, & per ipsum candēs ferrū: ita vt etiā ipsum candēs ferrum ex tali vnione vim habeat ardendi& lucendi sine transmutatione substantię & es sentialium proprietatum ignis & ferri.
units.tr: John 17. The faculty of shining and burning is the proper property of the fire. But since the fire is united with the iron, it exerts and shows its power of shining and burning in, with and through the glowing iron itself. So the glowing iron itself, from such a union, has the power of burning and shining without any change of the substance or essential properties of fire and iron.

units.la: Ergo intelligimus illa testimonia scriptu- ræ;quæ de Maiestate Christi loquuntur, ad quam humana natura est exaltata,non ita: quòd illa diuina Maiestas, quæ diuinæ natu- ræ Filij Dei propria est, in persona filii ho- minis simpliciter tantum secundum suam di- uinam naturam tribui debeat:aut quod illa Maiestas in humana natura Christi tantum hoc respectu esse debeat, quòd sua humana natura ab illa nūdum duntaxat titulum & nomē per phrasin & modum loquendi,hoc est, tantùm verbis,re verò ipsa nullam pror- sus communionem cum illa habeat. Hoc e- nim modo(quia Deus spiritualis, indiuisibi- lis essentia,& vbique presens, & in omnibus creaturis est:& in quibus est,potissimum au- tem in fidelibus & sanctis, habitat : ibidem suam maiestatem cum & apud se habeat) e- tiam verè dici posset,in omnibus creaturis, cum & in quibus Deus est, presertim autem in fidelibus & sanctis, in quibus Deus habitat, omnem plenitudinem Deitatis corporaliter habitare, omnes thesauros sapientiae & scientiae absconditos esse, omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra datam: quia ipsis Spiritus sanctus qui omnem potestatem habet, datur. Qua ratione inter Christum secundum suam humanam naturam & inter alios sanctos homines nullum discrimen esset: & ita Christus sua Maiestate, qua prę omnibus aliis creaturis ut homo vel secundum suam humanam naturam accepit, spoliaretur. Nulla enim alia creatura neq. homo neq. Angelus dicere poterit, nec debet: Mihi data est omnis potestas: cum tamen Deus tota plenitudine suae diuinitatis, quam ubique secum habet, in suis sanctis sit: sed non corporaliter in ipsis habitat, aut personaliter cum ipsis unitus est, sicut in Christo. Ex hac enim personali unione illud est, quod etiam Christus secundum suam humanam naturam dicit Matt. 28. Mihi data est, &c. Item Ioh. 13. cum Christus sciret a Patre sibi omnia in suas manus tradita esse. Item Colos. 2. In ipso habitat tota plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter. Item Gloria & honore coronasti eum, & collocasti eum super opera manuum tuarum: omnia subiecisti pedib. suis: & q subiecit illi omnia, nihil reliquit quod non subiectum sit illi. Heb. 2. excepto eo, qui ipsi ipsi omnia subiecit.1.Cor.15.
units.tr: Therefore we understand those testimonies of Scripture which speak of the majesty of Christ, to which the human nature has been exalted, not in such a way that the divine majesty which belongs to the divine nature of the Son of God should be attributed simply to the person of the Son of Man according to his divine nature alone. Nor should that majesty in the human nature of Christ be in this respect only, that his human nature has merely the title and name by a figure and manner of speaking (that is, only in words), while in reality it has no communion at all with that majesty. For in this way (since God is a spiritual, indivisible essence, present everywhere and in all creatures, and dwells especially in the faithful and holy in whom he is, and has his majesty with himself there), it could also truly be said that in all creatures in whom God is, and especially in the faithful and holy in whom God dwells, all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, and all power in heaven and on earth is given, because the Holy Spirit, who has all power, is given to them. By this reasoning there would be no difference between Christ according to his human nature and other holy men, and so Christ would be stripped of the majesty which, as man, or according to his human nature, he received above all other creatures. For no other creature, neither man nor angel, can say or ought to say: "All power is given to me." Yet God, with the whole fullness of his divinity, which he has with him everywhere, is in his saints, but he does not dwell in them bodily or become personally united with them as he is in Christ. For from this personal union comes what Christ also says according to his human nature in Matt. 28: "All power is given to me," etc. Likewise John 13, when Christ knew that the Father had given all things into his hands. Likewise Col. 2: "In him dwells all the fullness of the Deity bodily." Likewise: "You crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands; you put all things under his feet; for in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him," Heb. 2, "except him who put all things under him," 1 Cor. 15.

units.la: Nos credimus,docemus & cofitemur autem nequaquam talem effusionem Maiestatis Dei & omnium illarum proprietatum in humanam naturam Christi, qua diuina natura minor fiat: aut aliquid de suo alteri tradat, quod non per se seruet: aut quod humana natura in sua substantia æqualem maiestatem acceperit à natura & essentia filij separatam & distinctam, sicut quando ex vno vase in aliud aqua, vinum aut oleum transfunditur. Humana enim natura, sicut etiam nulla alia creatura neque in cœlo neque in terra tali ratione omnipotentiæ Dei nō capax est, vt per se omnipotes essentia fiat, vel omnipotentiæ proprietates in & per se habeat: qua certè humana natura in Christo negaretur, in Deitatémque omnino transmutaretur: quod nostræ fidei, & omniū Prophetarum Apostolorúmque doctrinæ repugnat.
units.tr: We believe, teach and confess that the majesty of God and all those properties are by no means so poured out into the human nature of Christ that the divine nature becomes less, or hands over to the other something it does not keep in itself, or that the human nature receives in its own substance an equal majesty, separated and distinct from the nature and essence of the Son, as when water, wine or oil is poured from one vessel into another. For the human nature, like every other creature in heaven or on earth, is not capable of the omnipotence of God in such a way that it becomes essentially omnipotent through itself, or has the properties of omnipotence in and of itself. Such a view would indeed deny the human nature in Christ and transform it wholly into deity, which is contrary to our faith and to the teaching of all the Prophets and Apostles.

units.la: Sed nos credimus,docemus & confitemur, Deum Patrem Filio suo Christo secundum assumptam naturam Spiritum S. ita dedisse (ideo enim quoque Messias, hoc est, vnctus appellatur) vt non ad mensuram, sicut reliqui sancti, illa dona acceperit. In Christo enim secundum assumptam humanam naturam (quia secundum diuinam naturam cum S. sancto vna est essentia) requiescit Spiritus sapientiae & scientiae, consilij, roboris, & cognitionis: non sic vt inde tanquam homo quaedam tantum sciat & possit, sicut alij sancti diuino Spiritu, qui tantum creata dona in ipsis operatur, sciunt & possunt. Sed quia Christus secundum Deitatem secunda persona est S. Trinitatis: ab eo, sicut etiam a Patre, Spiritus sanctus procedit: & ita filius & Patris proprius spiritus est & manet in aeternum a Filio Dei inseparabilis: Christo secundum carnem, quae cum filio Dei personaliter vnita est, tota plenitudo Spiritus (vt Patres aiunt) illa personali vnione communicata est: quae se libere omni virtute in ea, per eam, & cum ea ostendit & exerit: vt non tantum quaedam sciat & quaedam nesciat: quaedam possit & quaedam non possit: sed sciat & possit omnia: in quem Pater sine mensura Spiritu sapientiae & virtutis effudit, vt tanquam homo per illam personalem vnionem omnem scientiam, omnem potestatem reipsa & facto acceperit. & ita omnes thesauri sapientiae in ipso sint reconditi. Ita ei omnis potestas est data, & collocatus est ad dexteram Maiestatis & virtutis Dei. Et ex historiis scimus, tempore Imperatoris Valentis inter Arianos
units.tr: But we believe, teach and confess that God the Father has so given the Holy Spirit to his Son Christ according to the assumed nature (for this is why he is also called the Messiah, that is, the Anointed), that he did not receive those gifts by measure, as the other saints did. For in Christ, according to the assumed human nature (because according to the divine nature he is one essence with the Holy Spirit), there rests the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge, of counsel, of strength and of understanding. Not in such a way that he knows and can certain things only as a man, as the other saints know and can through the divine Spirit, who works only created gifts in them. But because Christ according to the Godhead is the second person of the Holy Trinity, the Holy Spirit proceeds from him as from the Father, and so the Son has and keeps the Spirit as his own, inseparable from the Son of God for ever. To Christ according to the flesh, which is personally united with the Son of God, the whole fullness of the Spirit (as the Fathers say) has been communicated by that personal union, which shows itself and works freely in every power in it, through it and with it, so that he does not know some things and not others, or can some things and not others, but knows and can all things. The Father poured out upon him the Spirit of wisdom and power without measure, so that, as man, through that personal union he has received in deed and in fact all knowledge and all power, and so all the treasures of wisdom are hidden in him. Thus all power has been given to him, and he has been placed at the right hand of the majesty and power of God. And from histories we know that in the time of the Emperor Valens, among the Arians, there was another sect, called the Agnoetae, because they pretended that the Son of the Father, the Word [λόγον], knows all things, but that his assumed nature is ignorant of many things. Gregory the Great also wrote against them.

units.la: nos aliam sectam fuisse, quę dicta fuit Agnoi tarum: propterea quòd finxerunt filium Patris λόγον quidem omnia scire, sed suam assumptam naturam multarum rerum esse ignorantem, contra quos etiā Gregorius magnus scripsit.
units.tr: There was another sect, called the Agnoetae, because they pretended that the Son of the Father, the Word [λόγον], knows all things, but that his assumed nature is ignorant of many things; against them Gregory the Great also wrote.

units.la: Propter hanc personalem vnionem, & quæ inde consequitur, communicationem, quam diuina & humana natura in persona Christi realiter inuicè habent, Christo secundum carnem attribuitur, quòd caro ipsius secundum naturam & essentiam per se non sit, & q; extra hanc vnionem Christus habere non posset, vt ipsius caro verè viuificans cibus, & sanguis verè viuificans potus sit, sicut illi 200 Patres concilij Ephesini testati sunt, Carnem Christi esse viuificam, seu viui ficantem. Vnde etiam hic homo solus, & alias nullus homo neq.in cœlo neque in terra dicere potest: Vbi duo vel tres in nomine meo congregati sunt sum in medio illorum. Item Semper sum vobiscum víque ad consummationē seculi. Quæ testimonia nos etiam non sic accipimus: quasi apud nos in fideli congregatione tantùm Deitas Christi presens sit: & talis presentia ad Christum secundum suam humanitatem nihil omnino attineat. Quo pacto etiam Petrus, Paulus, &
units.tr: On account of this personal union, and the communication that follows from it, which the divine and human natures really have with one another in the person of Christ, there is attributed to Christ according to the flesh that his flesh is not, by its nature and essence, of itself alone, and that Christ could not have this outside the union, so that his flesh is truly a life-giving food and his blood a truly life-giving drink. So the 200 Fathers of the Council of Ephesus testified that the flesh of Christ is life-giving, or makes alive. Hence this man alone, and no other man, neither in heaven nor on earth, can say: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." And: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age." We do not understand these testimonies as though the Godhead of Christ alone were present among us in the faithful congregation, and such presence had nothing at all to do with Christ according to his humanity. On that view Peter, Paul and

units.la: Ignoti: ut supra?
units.tr: Unknown: as above?

units.la: omnes sancti in coelo, quado Deitas vbique existens in ipsis habitat, etiam apud nos in terris effent. Quod tamen tantum de Chri- sto & de nullo alio homine sacra Scriptura affirmat. Verum nos credimus, his verbis, Maiestatem Christi declarari, quam Chri- stus secudum suam humanitatem in dextera Maiestatis & virtutis Dei accepit. quod ip- se scilicet etiam secundum & cum illa sua as sumpta humana natura presens esse potest, & etiam est, vbi vult. imprimis vero in sua Ecclesia in terris tanquam mediator, caput, rex & summus sacerdos, non ex dimidio tā- tum, sed tota persona Christi, ad quam per- tinent duę naturę, diuina & humana, adsit, non tantum secundum Deitatem, sed etiam secundum & cum humanitate, secundum quam frater noster est, & nos caro sumus de carne eius, & os de ossibus eius, sicut ad con- firmationem & consignationem huius rei suam sacram Cœnam instituit: quod etiam secundum eam naturam, secundum quam carnem & sanguinem habet, apud nos esse, in nobis habitare, operari & efficax esse velit.
units.tr: all the saints in heaven would also be present with us on earth, since the Godhead, existing everywhere, dwells in them. Yet holy Scripture affirms this only of Christ and of no other man. But we believe that by these words the majesty of Christ is declared, which Christ, according to his humanity, has received at the right hand of the majesty and power of God: namely that he himself, according to and together with that assumed human nature, can be present, and indeed is present, wherever he wills; above all in his Church on earth, as mediator, head, king and high priest, not in half only but in the whole person of Christ, to whom both natures belong, divine and human. He is present not only according to the Godhead but also according to and together with the humanity, according to which he is our brother, and we are flesh of his flesh and bone of his bones. He instituted his holy Supper to confirm and seal this matter. He also wills that, according to that nature by which he has flesh and blood, he be with us, dwell in us, work and be effective among us.

units.la: Tom. Viteb. 2. ger. sol. 191.
units.tr: Tom. Viteb. 2. ger. sol. 191.

units.la: In hoc solidum fundamentum D. Luthe- rus beatę memoriæ etiam de Maiestate scri- psit, secundum suam humanam naturam.
units.tr: On this solid foundation, the blessed Dr. Luther also wrote concerning the majesty, according to his human nature.

units.la: In magna enim cōfessione de persona Christi ita scribit de Cœna: Cùm autem talis homo est Christus, qui supernaturaliter cum Deo vna persona est,& extra hunc hominem nullus Deus est: necesse est sequi, vt etiam sit secundum tertiū modum supernaturalem & esse possit vbique vbi Deus est, & omnia per totum plena sint Christi etiam secundum humanitatem, non iuxta primum comprehensibilem modum, sed secundum supernaturalem diuinum modum. Hic enim cogeris dicere & fateri: Christus secundum Deitatem vbi vbi est, ibi naturalis diuina persona: & est quoque naturalis & personalis ibidem: sicut hoc demonstrat conceptio eius in vtero matris. Si enim debebat esse filius Dei, conueniebat eum naturaliter & personaliter in vtero matris esse & hominem fieri. Si est naturalis & personalis vbicunque est, necesse est vt ibi etiā homo sit: non enim sunt duæ distincta personæ, sed vna persona est, vbicūque ea est, ibi est vna inseparabilis persona. Et vbi dicere potes, Hic est Deus: cogeris etiam dicere ibi Christus homo quoque est. Et siquem locum ostenderis, vbi Deus sit & non homo, tum persona est separata. Si igitur vere dicere possem, Hic est Deus qui non est homo neq. vnquā homo est factus, talem Deū ego nō recipe rem. Hinc enim sequeretur quod spaciū & locus duas illas naturas separarēt& personā distraherent, cùm tamen neque mors neque omnes diaboli illas possint separare, neq. diuellere: debet enim tantum vnus Christus manere, qui non in pluribus quàm in vno loco simul & diuina & humana persona esset: & in omnib. aliis locis oporteret ipsum tantum nudum separatum Deum, & diuinam personam esse sine humanitate. Nõ mi homo, quò mihi Christum ponis, ibi & humanitatem mihi ponas necesse est: non sinunt se separari & seiungi: est vna persona facta: neque vnquam separatur diuina ab humana.
units.tr: In his great Confession concerning the person of Christ he writes thus about the Supper: When, however, Christ is such a man, who is supernaturally one person with God, and outside this man there is no God, it must follow that he is also, according to the third supernatural mode, and can be, everywhere where God is, and all things are full of Christ, even according to the humanity, not according to the first comprehensible mode, but according to the supernatural divine mode. For here you are forced to say and confess: Christ according to the Godhead, wherever he is, there the divine person is by nature; and he is also there by nature and personally, as his conception in the mother's womb shows. For if he was to be the Son of God, it was fitting that he should be in the mother's womb naturally and personally and become man. If he is by nature and personally wherever he is, it must be that there he is also man; for they are not two distinct persons, but one person, and wherever she is, there is one inseparable person. And where you can say, "Here is God," you are also forced to say that there Christ is also man. And if you show me a place where God is and not man, then the person is separated. If therefore I could truly say, "Here is God who is not man, nor has ever become man," I would not accept such a God. For from this it would follow that space and place separate the two natures and tear the person apart, whereas neither death nor all the devils can separate or pull them apart; for only one Christ must remain, who would not be, in more than one place at once, both divine and human person; and in all other places he would have to be only bare, separated God and divine person without humanity. "No, man, why do you set Christ before me? You must also set his humanity before me there: they do not allow themselves to be separated or divided; one person has been made; nor is the divine ever separated from the human."

units.la: Tom. 5. Viteb. ger. 545.
units.tr: Tom. 5. Viteb. ger. 545.

units.la: In libello de vltimis verbis Dauidis, quem D. Lutherus paulo ante mortem suam scripsit, ait ipse in hunc modum: Secundum alteram temporalem natiuitatem, est ei quoque æterna Dei potestas data, tamen temporaliter & non ab æterno. Humanitas enim Christi non fuit ab æterno, sicut Deitas, sed (vt numeratur & scribitur) Iesus Maria filius est hoc anno natus annos M. D. XLIII. A momento autem illo, quo Deitas & humanitas vnitæ sunt in vnam personam est & vocatur homo Maria filius, omnipotens æternus Deus, qui æternam potentiam habet, & omnia creauit & adhuc sustentat per communicationem Idiomatum. Ideò quòd cum Deitate vna persona & etiam verus Deus est. De eo loquitur Matt. vlt. Mihi data est omnis potestas, &c. Matt.11.Omnia mihi à Patre tradita sunt. Cui? Mihi Iesu Nazareno, filio Mariæ & homini nato: ab æterno habeo à Patre antequam homo fierem: sed cum homo fierem, temporaliter eã accepi secundum humanitatem, & clam seruaui vt que ad meam resurrectionem & ascensionem, quando manifestari & declarari oportuit. Sicut & Paulus Rom.1. inquit: Declaratus est filius Dei potenter. Ioh. 17. appellat Glorificationem. Similia testimonia in D. Lutheri scriptis, præsertim autem in libro, quòd hæc verba adhuc firma sunt: & in magna confessione de Cœna Domini, inueniuntur: ad quæ scripta seu ad bene fundatas declarationes Maiestatis Christi ad dexteram Dei, & sui testamenti nos breuitatis ergo in hoc articulo, sicut etiam in articulo de Cœna Domini, vt dictū est, referimus.
units.tr: In the little book on the last words of David, which Dr Luther wrote shortly before his death, he says the following: "According to the other, temporal birth, there was also given to him the eternal power of God, yet temporally and not from eternity. For the humanity of Christ was not from eternity, as the Deity was, but (as it is counted and written) Jesus of Mary, the son, was born this year 1543. From the moment, however, in which the Deity and humanity were united into one person, he who is called the man, Mary's son, is also the almighty, eternal God, who has eternal power and created all things and still sustains them, through the communication of properties. For he is, together with the Deity, one person and also the true God. Of him Matthew speaks at the end: 'All power is given to me,' etc. [Matt. 28]. Matthew 11: 'All things are delivered to me by the Father' [Matt. 11:27]. To whom? To me, Jesus of Nazareth, son of Mary and born man.
