Et in sexta Syn. sic legitur: Afferimus duas eius esse naturas in una eius radiates subsistentia. Ad eundem sane modum cæteræ Synodi & Patres unionem personalem intellexerunt.
units.tr: E.iij. the fifth general synod: the holy Church of God, casting out the impiety of both the perfidy of Nestorius and that of Eutyches, confesses the union of the Word of God to the flesh according to composition, which is according to subsistence. And in the following canon: If anyone does not confess that the Word of God is united to the flesh subsistentially, and therefore one subsistence or one person of it, and thus confesses that the holy Synod of Chalcedon confesses one subsistence of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema. In the synodal decrees of Martin I it is also thus held: If anyone does not confess, according to the holy Fathers, that properly and truly our Lord Jesus Christ is one and the same, from two natures, deity and humanity, united according to subsistence, unconfusedly and undividedly, let him be condemned. And in the sixth synod it is thus read: We affirm that there are two natures of him in one subsistence of his. In the same way the other synods and Fathers understood the personal union.

units.la: Nec ita tamen naturas illas in una hypostasi unitas existimare decet, qua si ex duab. subsistentiis, humana videlicet & diuina, tertia coaluerit aliqua, quæ partim diuina sit, partim humana. Non enim adiectionem personæ vel subsistentię (vt cum quinta Synodo loquamur) sancta Trinitas suscepit ex incarnato Dei verbo, sed vna est duntaxat eadémq. indiuidua in Christo domino subsistentia, ipsius nimirum Verbi propria, quæ propter im mensam Verbi perfectionem atque virtutem, hypostaticæs humanam subsistentat naturam, quam propria (vt sic dicamus) personalitate destitutam, sibi asciuit atque coniunxit. Vnde Damascenus, Ipsius Verbi hypostasis, vtriusque naturarū hypostasis existens, nullam insubsistentem esse permittit, neq. alterius esse hypostasis. Neque quandoque quidem huius, quandoque vero illius, sed semper vtriusque indiuisibiliter & inseparabiliter est hypostasis: tota huius, & tota illius, impartibiliter & plenissime. Non enim in propria subsistentia suscepta est Dei verbi caro, neque in alia hypostasi facta est, quàm in Dei verbi hypostasi, sed in ipso sustentata & subsistes potius, neque secundum propriam subsistens hypostasin facta est. Quapropter neq. in subsistens est, neque Trinitati superaddit hypostasin. Hæc ille
units.tr: Yet we ought not to think that those natures are united in one hypostasis in such a way that, if two subsistences, the human and the divine, were to coalesce, some third thing would result which is partly divine and partly human. For the holy Trinity did not take up an addition of person or subsistence (to use the words of the fifth synod) from the incarnate Word of God; rather there is only one and the same undivided subsistence in the Lord Christ, namely that of the Word itself, which, on account of the immense perfection and power of the Word, sustains the human nature hypostatically and has taken it to itself and joined it, though that nature was, so to speak, destitute of its own personality. Hence Damascene, who holds that the hypostasis of the Word itself, being the hypostasis of both natures, permits no nature to be without subsistence, nor to be of another hypostasis: it is not at one time of this and at another of that, but always indivisibly and inseparably the hypostasis of both, wholly of this and wholly of that, without division and most fully. For the flesh of the Word of God was not assumed into a subsistence of its own, nor was it made in another hypostasis than that of the Word of God, but it was sustained in him and rather subsists in him, and was not made subsisting according to its own hypostasis. Therefore it is neither subsisting in itself, nor does it add a hypostasis to the Trinity. These are his words.

units.la: 13 Atque hinc iam absque vlla difficultate intelligitur, quanta humanitatis cum diuinitate sit vnio. Non enim tanta est, quanta trium personarum in vna essentia diuina, neq; tam parua etiam quàm ea est, quæ in solius gratiæ, gloriæ, virtutis, autoritatis, dignitatis aut potestatis communicatione consistit, aut quæ alio quouis accidentario modo efficitur. Nam neque persona, in qua vniuntur, neque naturæ ipsæ, accidës aliquod censeri debent aut possunt.
units.tr: 13 And from this it is now understood, without any difficulty, how great the union of the humanity with the divinity is. It is not as great as that of the three persons in the one divine essence, nor is it as slight as that which consists only in the communication of grace, glory, virtue, authority, dignity or power, or which is effected by any other accidental mode. For neither the person in whom they are united nor the natures themselves can or should be regarded as an accident.

units.la: 14 Imò si rem, in qua vnio hæc facta est, penitius intucâre, haud facile parem in rerum natura comperias vnionem. Etenim diuina illa substantia, in qua naturæ conueniunt, si per se consideretur, rerum omnium, quæ exister e possunt, est simplicissima: quamuis si naturas ipsas vnitas spectes, cöpositæ quodammodo dici queat, eò quòd in duab. substantiis naturis.
units.tr: 14 Indeed, if you examine more closely the thing in which this union has been made, you will hardly find a like union in the nature of things. For that divine substance in which the natures meet, considered in itself, is the most simple of all things that can exist; although, if you look at the natures themselves as united, it can in a certain way be called composite, because it is in two substances, natures.

units.la: 15 Est autem hæc vnio vsqueadeo singularis, vt nullo prorsus exemplo satis commodè explicari queat. Nam licet vnio animi cum corpore, vt cætera omittamus, nonnullam cum diuina illa vnione affinitatem habere videatur, & idcirco ad eandem explicandam à sanctis Patribus interinterdū assumatur, quatenus in vtraq. v-ttione duę res diuisę in vna hypostasi sine vlla mixtione, confusione ac conuersio-ne sustentantur: tamen si rem omnem re-ĉte perpendas, longissimo hæc distant in-teruallo: animꝰ enim &corpus nequaquā integræ & perfectæ sunt essetiæ, sed vnius essentiæ partes: diuina verò &humana na-tura in Christo, essentiæ sunt, sic integræ atque perfectæ, vt nulla ratione vnā ter-tiam essentiam absoluere possint.
units.tr: 15 This union is so singular that it cannot be explained adequately by any example at all. For although the union of soul with body, to omit other things, seems to have some affinity with that divine union, and for this reason the holy Fathers sometimes adopt it to explain the latter, inasmuch as in each union two distinct things are sustained in one hypostasis without any mixture, confusion or conversion, yet if you weigh the whole matter correctly, these are very far apart. For the soul and the body are not complete and perfect essences, but parts of one essence; whereas the divine and human natures in Christ are essences so complete and perfect that by no reasoning can they make up a third essence.

units.la: 16 Hæc quibusdam erunt obscura fortasse, sed scitu sanè digna, vt ex hac personalis vnionis explicatione confute-tur impius Sabellius, & intelligatur non Patrem, qui solus ingenitus est, nec Spiritum sanctum, qui ex Patre Filióque procedit, sed solum Filium, Deiꝰ verbum, Deum verum de Deo vero, genitum, non factum, Patri ὁμοούσιον, in plenitudine temporis hominem factum esse, nobis non modo ὁμοούσιον, sed etiam per omnia similem absque peccato, eúmque solū pro nobis passum fuisse.
units.tr: 16 These things will perhaps be obscure to some, but they are certainly worth knowing, so that from this explanation of the personal union the impious Sabellius may be refuted, and it may be understood that not the Father, who alone is unbegotten, nor the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, but only the Son, the Word of God, true God of true God, begotten not made, of one substance [ὁμοούσιον] with the Father, was made man in the fullness of time, of one substance with us not only, but also like us in all things apart from sin, and that he alone suffered for us.

units.la: 17 Nam etsi vna omnino Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti οὐσία sit & ἐξουσία, Maiestas quoque & dignitas: non tamē in essentia aut quacunq. essetiæ perfectio-
units.tr: 17 For although the essence [οὐσία], power [ἐξουσία], majesty and dignity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are altogether one, yet that union was not made in the essence, or in any essential perfection of the essence,

units.la: Hebr.2.4.Con.Nicenū;Const.1.2.3.Ephe.1. Chalce. &c. cCon.Tolet.6.c.1, ne siue essentiali aliqua proprietate ( quæ omnia toti Trinitati sunt communia)sed in solius Filij hypostasi,qua à patre & Spiritu sancto re ipsa distinguitur , vnionem illam factam esse cuncti in Ecclesia proferentur.
units.tr: Heb. 2.4. Nicene Creed; Constantinople 1, 2, 3; Ephesians 1; Chalcedon, etc.; Toledo 6, c. 1, (which are all common to the whole Trinity), but in the hypostasis of the Son alone, by which he is really distinguished from the Father and the Holy Spirit, as all in the Church declare.

units.la: 18 Quòd si in sola essentia aut in essentiali aliqua perfectione vnio illa facta fuisset,totavtiq. Trinitas incarnata(quod sentire sit nefas) pari ratione affirmaretur:cum essentia & quæuis essentialis per sectio in tribus illis personis ex æquo reperiatur.
units.tr: 18 But if that union had been made in the essence alone, or in some essential perfection, then by the same reasoning the whole Trinity would be affirmed to be incarnate (which it is wicked even to think), since the essence and any essential attribute are found equally in all three persons.

units.la: 19 Liquet etiam ex iam dictis insaniuisse Nestorium, Nestorianiq. dogmatis sectatores omnes, contra quos cum Ephesina Synodo aperte profitendum est, non duas Christi personas, aut duos filios, alterū videlicet Dei, alterum Virginis Matris,totidémve Christos,sed vnā duntaxat personam, vnum Filiū,vnúmque Christum, qui verus Deus& verus homo sit, constituendum & adorandum esse:quia non duas,sed vnam tantummodo hypostasin in eodem Christo agnoscimus ac veneramur.
units.tr: 19 It is also clear from what has been said that Nestorius went mad, and all the followers of the Nestorian doctrine, against whom we must openly profess, with the Council of Ephesus, that there is to be acknowledged and worshipped not two persons of Christ, or two sons, one of God and the other of the Virgin Mother, nor as many Christs, but only one person, one Son and one Christ, who is true God and true man; because in the same Christ we acknowledge and venerate not two hypostases but only one.

units.la: 20 Ex his præterea,confirmamur in Christiana & necessaria cōfessione,quam approbauit sacra Chalcedonensis Synodus contra Eutychetem, nimirum: Vnigenitum Dei filium in duabus naturis inconfusè, inconuertibiliter, indiuisè, inseparabiliter exist-ere, nunquam sublata dif-ferētia naturarum propter vnionem, sed potius salua vtriusque naturæ proprieta-te. Quandoquidem non conuersione di-uinitatis in carnem, aut carnis indininita tē sed assumptione humanitatis in Deū, non confusione, aut transfusione substan-tiæ, aut vnius tertiæ naturę cōpositione, sed vnitate personæ, siue subsistētiæ, vnus est manetq. Christus, in duabus subsistens naturis.
units.tr: 20 Further, from these things we are confirmed in the Christian and necessary confession which the holy Council of Chalcedon approved against Eutyches, namely: that the only-begotten Son of God exists in two natures, unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably, the difference of the natures never being taken away by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved. For the one Christ is and remains one, subsisting in two natures, not by conversion of the divinity into flesh, nor by change of the flesh into the divinity, but by the assumption of the humanity into God; not by confusion or transfusion of substance, nor by the composition of a third nature, but by the unity of the person, or subsistence.

units.la: 21 a Itaque sicut in Deo vna est substantia & tres personæ: ita in Christo vna est persona & duæ substantiæ siue naturæ.
units.tr: 21 a Therefore, just as in God there is one substance and three persons, so in Christ there is one person and two substances or natures.

units.la: 22 b Ex quo illud etiam contra Monothelitas euidenti ratione consequitur, vt, quemadmodum in Domino nostro Iesu Christo duas naturas indiuisè inconuertibiliterque vnitas esse confitemur, ita & duas proprietates duásque naturales operationes (vt sextæ Synodi verbis vtamur) indiuisè, inconfusè, inseparabiliter, in eodem Christo agnoscere debeamus, ac venerari, alteram videlicet humanam, alteram vero diuinam.
units.tr: 22 b From this, against the Monothelites, the following also follows by evident reasoning: just as we confess that in our Lord Jesus Christ two natures are united indivisibly and unchangeably, so we ought to acknowledge and venerate in the same Christ two properties and two natural operations (to use the words of the Sixth Synod) indivisibly, unconfusedly and inseparably, namely the one human and the other divine.

units.la: 23 Quod profecto Monothelitæ minimè negauissent, si Philosophiæ præceptionibus mediocriter saltem fuissent instructi. Nam ratione naturali perspicuum est, essentiales seu naturales proprietates ac operationes, nō ex persōnæ, sed ex naturæ seu formæ vnitate & distinctione, vnitatem & distinctionem sortiri. Id quod supernaturali quoque Trinitatis exemplo aperte confirmari potest, vbi propter naturæ vnitatem, vna essentialis proprietas vnáque operatio in tribus illis sanctis personis reperitur, secundum illud Theologicum axioma: Opera Trinitatis ad extra sunt indiuisa.
units.tr: 23 The Monothelites certainly would not have denied this, had they been at least moderately instructed in the precepts of philosophy. For it is clear by natural reason that essential or natural properties and operations receive their unity and distinction not from the unity and distinction of the person but from that of the nature or form. This can also be clearly confirmed by the supernatural example of the Trinity, where, on account of the unity of the nature, one essential property and one operation are found in those three holy persons, according to the theological axiom: the external works of the Trinity are undivided.

units.la: 24 Atque hinc rursus manifestum euadit, de neutra in Christo natura alterius proprietates dici posse, manet enim inconfusa in Christo tam carnis, quàm diuinitatis proprietatum contemplatio, cùm vtraque natura absque vlla confusione, mixtione aut conuersione proprietates suas distinctas omnino incolumésque retinuerit.
units.tr: 24 And from this again it becomes plain that the properties of neither nature can be predicated of the other in Christ; for the contemplation of the properties of the flesh and of the divinity remains unconfused in Christ, since each nature, without any confusion, mixture or conversion, has retained its own distinct properties entirely intact.

units.la: 25 Quapropter sicut humanitas, diuinissima hac vnione diuinam naturam non reddidit infirmiorem nec natura diui-na na humanitate omnipotente effecit, cum nec forma serui, Dei formam in Christo ademerit, nec forma Dei formā serui minuerit, vt D. Leo eleganter dixit.
units.tr: 25 Therefore, just as the humanity did not make the divine nature weaker by this most divine union, nor did the divine nature make the humanity omnipotent, since the form of a servant did not take away the form of God in Christ, nor did the form of God diminish the form of a servant, as St Leo elegantly said.

units.la: 26 Verum quāuis post admirandā hāc vnione duæ in Christo naturæ earūmq. proprietates distincte impermixteq. perstiterint, tamen, quoniā vna est persona Christi in illis duabus naturis subsistens, eidem Christo velut vni eidemq. personæ ascribimus voces omnes, tam diuinas quàm humanas, quæ vel in Euangelicis, vel Apostolicis scripturis, vel in Patrum monumentis passim reperiuntur: tametsi inter se pugnare videantur, & reuera pugnent, propter naturarum, quas concernunt, diuersitatem.
units.tr: 26 Indeed, although after this admirable union the two natures in Christ and their properties have remained distinct and unmixed, nevertheless, since there is one person of Christ subsisting in those two natures, we ascribe to the same Christ, as to one and the same person, all the expressions, both divine and human, which are found everywhere in the Gospel or Apostolic writings or in the monuments of the Fathers, even though they seem to contend with one another, and indeed do contend, on account of the diversity of the natures they concern.

units.la: 27 Et hęc ipsa persone vnitas, in causa est vt quæ Dei sunt propria, sępe in scripturis ascribātur homini: e contrario quæ carnis sunt propria, attribuantur Deo.
units.tr: 27 And this very unity of person is the cause why what belongs to God is often ascribed in Scripture to the man, and conversely what belongs to the flesh is attributed to God.

units.la: 28 Vnde non potest nō aperte cōstare, quòd veré prorsus & Catholicè vnus & idem Christus, Deus & homo dicatur, i- demque mortalis & immortalis, Patri æqualis & minor Patre, Creator & creatura, omnipotens & infirmus, vbique exi stens &certo loco circūscriptus, ętern⁹ & in tempore natus. Demum ob hanc eandem personæ vnitatem,& hominem Dei filium, Creatorem etiam & omnipotentem,ediuerso verò Deum, Virginis Filiũ, passum quoque & crucifixum, rectissime confitemur. Non enim interest (inquit Leo)ex qua Christus substantia nominetur:cùm inseparabili manēte vnitate personæ,idem sit & totus hominis filius propter carnem, & totus Dei filius propter vnam cum Patre deitatem.
units.tr: 28 Hence it cannot but be plainly established that the one and the same Christ is truly, entirely and catholicly called God and man, and the same mortal and immortal, equal to the Father and less than the Father, Creator and creature, almighty and weak, existing everywhere and circumscribed in a certain place, eternal and born in time. Lastly, on account of this same unity of person, we most rightly confess both that man is the Son of God, also Creator and almighty, and conversely that God is the Son of the Virgin, also suffered and crucified. For, as Leo says, it makes no difference from which substance Christ is named, since, the unity of the person remaining inseparable, he is both wholly the Son of man on account of the flesh and wholly the Son of God on account of the one deity he shares with the Father.

units.la: 29 Quæ cùm ita sint,non est Grammatica tantum, seu verbalis ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία in persona Christi: in natura verò,ne Grammatica quidem seu verbalis fieri potest.Siquidem vni & eidem Christi personæ, in qua naturæ sunt vnitæ, vtriusque naturæ attributa reipsa conuenium,cùm eadem sit hypostasis vtriusque naturæ: in neutra verò natura, alterius proprietates insunt, sed nec inesse queút: cùm neq.in natura, neque in naturæ proprietate aliqua, vnio aut confusio facta fuerit,aut etiam fieri possit.
units.tr: 29 Since these things are so, there is not merely a grammatical or verbal communication of properties [ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία] in the person of Christ; but in the nature, not even a grammatical or verbal one can be made. For the attributes of both natures truly belong to the one and the same person of Christ, in whom the natures are united, since the hypostasis of both natures is the same; but the properties of the one nature do not inhere in the other, nor can they inhere, since neither in the nature, nor in any property of the nature, has any union or confusion been made, or can even be made.

units.la: 30 Accuratè ergo obseruandum est, quæ nomina personam, & quæ naturam significent, ne ex verbis aut malè prolatis, aut falsò intellectis, error in re tanta perniperniciosissimus forte oriatur. Nam cum hæc naturarum vnio in persona facta sit, non in natura, nominibus non naturam, sed personam significantibus perpetuò vtendum est ad idiomatum communicationem.
units.tr: 30 We must therefore observe carefully which names signify the person and which the nature, so that a most pernicious error in so great a matter does not arise from words either badly uttered or wrongly understood. For since this union of the natures was made in the person, not in the nature, we must always use, for the communication of idioms, names that signify the person and not the nature.

units.la: Propterea enim enunciationes hæ veræ sunt & catholicæ, homo est Deus, omnipotens, immortalis, impatibilis: Item, Deus est homo, infirmus, mortalis, patibilis: falsæ sunt itidem hæ, simul & hæreticæ: humanitas est Deus vel Deitas: humanitas est omnipotens, immortalis, impatibilis: Item, deitas est homo, vel humanitas: Deitas est infirma, mortalis. Neque id alia sanè ratione, quàm quòd modò concretis, modò abstractis vtamur nominibus. quæ in concreto sumpta θεος, in abstracto verò θεοτης significant, si ad vim & proprietatem sermonis attendamus. Vnde sic ait Damascenus: Diuinitatem dicentes, non de illa nominamus ea, quæ humanitatis sunt propria, neque de carne, id est, humanitate prædicamus ea, quę diuinitatis sunt propria. Non enim dicimus deitatem aut passibilem aut creatâ, neque dicimus carnem, id est, humanitatem increatam. At verò de θεοτοκος siue
units.tr: For this reason the following statements are true and catholic: "man is God, almighty, immortal, impassible"; likewise "God is man, weak, mortal, passible." These are false, and at the same time heretical: "the humanity is God or the Deity"; "the humanity is almighty, immortal, impassible"; likewise "the deity is man or the humanity"; "the Deity is weak, mortal." This comes about for no other reason than that we use now concrete and now abstract names, which, if we attend to the force and proper meaning of the words, signify God [θεος] when taken concretely and deity [θεοτης] when taken abstractly. Hence Damascene says thus: "When we speak of the Deity, we do not name of it the things that are proper to the humanity, nor do we predicate of the flesh, that is, of the humanity, the things that are proper to the Deity. For we do not say that the Deity is passible or created, nor do we say that the flesh, that is, the humanity, is uncreated. But when we name the Theotokos [θεοτοκος] either from both natures or from one of the natures,

units.la: lib.3.c.4 (marginal reference) ex vtraque siue ex vna naturarum, eam nominemus, vtriusque naturarum propria illi adiicimus. Hæc Damascenus.
units.tr: lib.3.c.4 we add to her the properties of both natures." This is Damascene.

units.la: 32 Ceterùm licet vni & eidem Christi persónæ, vtriusque naturæ proprietates & operationes, indiuisè & inseparabiliter adscribantur, tamen (vt rectè monet Leo) intelligendum est, & syncerè fidei contemplatione cernendum, ad quæ pro uehatur humilitas carnis, & ad quæ inclinetur altitudo diuinitatis. Enimuero necesse est (teste Cyrillo) reddere Deo quæ sunt Dei, & humanitati, quæ ei debentur, & ne id, quod creatum est ad diuinam deducentes essentiam, aut id quod est diuinæ naturæ, ad locum qui creaturis congruit, deponentes, in aliquem incidamus errorem.
units.tr: 32 Moreover, although the properties and operations of both natures are ascribed indivisibly and inseparably to the one and the same person of Christ, nevertheless (as Leo rightly warns) we must understand, and discern with the sincere contemplation of faith, to what the lowliness of the flesh is raised and to what the loftiness of the Deity inclines. Indeed it is necessary (as Cyril testifies) to render to God the things that are God's, and to the humanity the things that are due to it, and, lest we bring what is created into the divine essence, or place what belongs to the divine nature in the place that suits creatures, we fall into some error.

units.la: 33 Non enim alio ex fonte Arrius, Paulus Samosatenus, Photinus, & cæteri id genus hæretici suos hauserunt errores, quàm ex præpostera peruersa intelligentia, quæ in Scripturis sacris Christo attribuuntur: quod nescierunt aut noluerunt inter ea secernere, quæ ratione diuinitatis, & quæ ratione humanitatis, de vno eodemque Christo passim dicta leguntur. Hinc Athanasius contra Arrium scribens, bens: Vtriusq.igitur naturæ opus(inquit) noscentes & vtraq.ab vna persona agi vi dentes, rectè credemus,& nunquâ errabi mus. Nec aliud ferè idē beatus Pater contĕdit,quâ vt prædicta discretio inter Christi attributa conuenienter adhibeatur. Huc etiam illud S. Ambrosij spectat: Ser- uemus (inquit) distinctionem diuinitatis & carnis: vnus in vtraque loquitur Dei Filius,quia in eodem vtraque natura est: &si idē loquitur, non vno semper loquitur modo:intende in eo nunc gloriā Dei nunc hominis passiones, quia quasi Deus loquitur quæ sunt diuina, quia Verbum est:quasi homo, dicit quæ sunt humana, quia in mea substantia loquebatur. Sic quoque Grego.Nazian . iis verbis admonet: Vno autem capitulo moneo, vt altio ra quidem adscribas diuinitati,humiliora autem naturæ humanæ attribuas, quæ ex parte infirmitatis nostræ assumpta est. Nec dissentit his D. Augustt.dicens: Distin guamus, quid in Scripturis sonet,secun- dum formam Dei,& quid,secundum formam serui. Quid autem,& propter quid, & quid secundum quid dicatur, prudens & diligens & pius Lector intelliget. Er ibidem. Non itaque immeritò scriptura
units.tr: 33 For Arius, Paul of Samosata, Photinus and others of that kind drew their errors from no other source than from a perverse and backward understanding of the things ascribed to Christ in the holy Scriptures: they either did not know or would not distinguish between those things that are said of the one and the same Christ everywhere in the texts according to the Deity and those according to the humanity. Hence Athanasius, writing against Arius, says: "Knowing therefore the work of each nature, and seeing that both are performed by the one person, we shall believe rightly and never err." Nor does the blessed Father contend for anything else than that the aforesaid distinction be applied fittingly to the attributes of Christ. To this also pertains that saying of St Ambrose: "Let us keep (he says) the distinction between the Deity and the flesh: the one Son of God speaks in both, because both natures are in the same one; and although he speaks as the same, he does not always speak in the same way. Attend in him now to the glory of God, now to the sufferings of man: for as God he speaks of the things that are divine, because he is the Word; as man he speaks of the things that are human, because he was speaking in my substance." Gregory Nazianzen likewise admonishes in these words: "In one chapter I advise you to ascribe the loftier things to the Deity and to attribute the lowlier things to the human nature, which was assumed on account of our weakness." Augustine, too, does not disagree with these, saying: "Let us distinguish what in the Scriptures is said according to the form of God and what according to the form of a servant. But what is said, and on account of what, and in what respect, the prudent, diligent and pious reader will understand."

units.la: F vtrunque dicit:& æqualem Patri Filium, & Patrem maiorem Filio:illud enim propter formam Dei,hoc autem propter formā serui,sine vlla confusione intelligitur.
units.tr: And in the same place: "Not without reason therefore does Scripture say both things: that the Son is equal to the Father, and that the Father is greater than the Son. For the former is understood on account of the form of God, the latter on account of the form of a servant, without any confusion."

units.la: 34 Et hîc locum habet regula catholicæ fidei,cuius Beda post Augustinum meminit:Cùm aliqua in Scripturis dicuntur de Filio,quibus demõstratur quòd Patre sit minor,ea secundum humanitatem intelligantur. Cùm verò ea dicuntur, quibus Filius Patri demonstratur æqualis, secundum quòd Deus est accipiatur, nec aliter sanè Patres omnes docuêre.
units.tr: 34 And here applies the rule of the catholic faith, which Bede, after Augustine, recalls: "When some things are said in the Scriptures of the Son by which it is shown that he is less than the Father, they are to be understood according to the humanity. When those things are said by which the Son is shown to be equal to the Father, they are to be taken according as he is God." And indeed all the Fathers taught nothing otherwise.

units.la: 35 Ex quibus omnibus manifestè deducitur,eos grauissimè errare, naturarum que proprietates confundere,qui contra Patrum omnium definitionem & cõsuetudinê,vel humana diuinitati adscribunt vel humanitati diuina.
units.tr: 35 From all these things it is clearly deduced that those err most gravely, and confuse the properties of the natures, who, contrary to the definition and custom of all the Fathers, either ascribe human things to the divinity or divine things to the humanity.

units.la: 36 Superest vt concludamus ex superioribus genuinam, sanam & orthodoxā de Maiestate hominis Christi sententiam quæ breuiter in eo consistit: Dominū nostrum Iesum Christum, in forma Dei,æqualem esse cum Patre, imò eandem omnino gloriam,Maiestatem,potentiam,sapientiam,&c.sicut & οὐσίαν communem habere,eadémque Maiestate & prouidétia,
units.tr: 36 It remains that we conclude from what has gone before the genuine, sound and orthodox opinion concerning the majesty of the man Christ, which consists briefly in this: that our Lord Jesus Christ, in the form of God, is equal to the Father, indeed altogether the same in glory, majesty, power, wisdom, etc., and that he has the same essence in common with the Father, and has the same majesty and providence,

units.la: Sapientiæ 8. tia, qua Patrem, reb. omnib. & singulis, etiam minimisουσιωδῶς præsentem adesse. Sic Catholici credimus, & ingenuè profitemur. Vnde Ambrosius ait: Eadē Verbi gloria, eadē Patris gloria est, sicut scriptū est: Dominus Iesus Christus in gloria est Dei patris. Ita igitur secūdùm diuinitatē, Dei Filius suā gloriā habet, vt Patris & Filij vna sit gloria. Nō est ergo minor in claritate, quia vna gloria: nō minor in diuinitate, quia plenitudo diuinitatis ī Christo est
units.tr: Wisdom 8. by which the Father is present to all things and to each one, even the smallest, essentially [ουσιωδῶς]. Thus we Catholics believe, and frankly profess. Hence Ambrose says: "The glory of the Word is the same as the glory of the Father, as it is written: the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. So then, according to the Deity, the Son of God has his own glory, such that the glory of the Father and of the Son is one. He is therefore not less in brightness, because the glory is one; not less in divinity, because the fullness of the Deity is in Christ."

units.la: 37 Addimus etiam, eundem Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, propter inexplicabilem illam, & arcanam naturarum vnionē, nulla ratione secundùm humanitatem diuinitati æqualem euasif-se: quin potius non sola essentia, sed etiā gloria, Maiestate, potestate ceterisque attributis omnibus & proprietatibus Deo minorem permansisse: vt vniuersi Patres, diuinis scripturis instructi, vnanimi consensu profitentur. Ita enim humana natura donis gratuitis in Christo exornata est, vt creaturę tamen limites nullatenus excesserit.
units.tr: 37 We add also that the same Lord our Lord Jesus Christ, on account of that inexplicable and secret union of the natures, did not in any way become equal to the Deity according to the humanity; rather, not only in essence but also in glory, majesty, power and all the other attributes and properties he has remained less than God, as all the Fathers, instructed by the divine Scriptures, profess with one consent. For the human nature was so adorned in Christ with gratuitous gifts that yet it in no way exceeded the limits of a creature.

units.la: 38 Non tamē hinc sequitur, in Christo Domino, nihilo plº dignitatis aut emi nētiæ, quàm in quibuslibet aliis hominibus bus inueniri.Nam inter diuinam illam al titudinem seu excellentiam,& eam digni tatem, quę communi hominum generi obtingere solet, singularis quædam eminentia intercedit, quam soli Christo propter vnionem illam hypostaticam, secun dum humanitatem, vt par est, attribu- mus.
units.tr: 38 Nevertheless it does not follow from this that in the Lord Christ there is found nothing more of dignity or eminence than in any other men. For between that divine loftiness or excellence and the dignity that usually falls to the common run of men there intervenes a certain singular eminence, which we properly ascribe to Christ alone, according to the humanity, on account of that hypostatic union.

units.la: 39 Nec ea quidem ratione Christum, secundum naturam assumptā, redigimus in sanctorum angelorum aut beatorum hominum ordinem, vt cum illis vlla ex parte(quod ad dona gratuita attinet)adę quemus. Absit hæc impia suspicio: quin illum singulari quadam gloria& honore coronatum,supra omnem Principatum, & Potestatem,& Virtutem, & Dominationem,& super omne nomen, quod nominatur non solùm in hoc seculo,sed etiā in futuro,agnoscimus ac veneramur.
units.tr: 39 Nor indeed do we, for this reason, reduce Christ, according to the assumed nature, to the order of the holy angels or of blessed men, so that we are equal to them in any respect (as far as the gratuitous gifts are concerned). Far be this impious suspicion: rather we acknowledge and venerate him as crowned with a singular glory and honour, above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the future.

units.la: 40 Nam solus is est primarium fundamentum, Caput omnis Ecclesiæ, Primo genitus in multis fratribus, in omnibus primatum tenens,Mediator Dei & homi num,in quo instaurata ac pacificata sunt omnia,siue quæ in cœlis, siue quę in terris existunt,Dominus omnium, Legisla tor & iudex viuorum & mortuorum. Et ne multis. Solus is ita plenus gratia & ve-ritate, tantísque spiritus S.donis repletus, tanta Maiestate, gloria, potestate & auto-ritate cumulatus est, vt nulla gratia, nulla veritas, nullum Spiritus S.donum, nec ma ior Maiestas, gloria, potestas, aut authori-tas in hac ipsa Christi humanitate deside-rari queat. Quippe quæ affatim sortita sit quę natura finita, qualis ipsa post perso-nalem illam vnionem permansit, sortiti aut capere potest.
units.tr: 40 For he alone is the primary foundation, the Head of the whole Church, the firstborn among many brethren, holding the primacy in all things, the Mediator between God and men, in whom all things are restored and reconciled, whether those in heaven or those on earth, the Lord of all, the Lawgiver and Judge of the living and the dead. And not to be long: he alone is so full of grace and truth, and so filled with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, so heaped with majesty, glory, power and authority, that no grace, no truth, no gift of the Holy Spirit, nor any greater majesty, glory, power or authority can be desired in this very humanity of Christ. Indeed it has received abundantly whatever a finite nature such as it remained after that personal union has received or can receive.

units.la: 41 Que sane dignitas, & incomparà bilis eminentia, quamuis ab immensa Dei celsitudine quàm longisime distet, tamè in alia creatura nulla, quęcunque tandè illa sit, locum vllum obtinet. In ceteris e-nim, etsi gratię & Spiritus sanđi dona re-periuntur, non tamen coaceruatim & cu-mulatim, vt in Christo, sed diuisim, & iux-ta mensuram donationis Christi, de cuius plenitudine nos omnes accepimus.
units.tr: 41 This dignity, and incomparable eminence, although it stands as far as possible from the immense loftiness of God, yet holds no place in any other creature, whatever it may be. For in the others, although the gifts of grace and of the Holy Spirit are found, they are not found heaped up and abundant as in Christ, but divided, and according to the measure of Christ's gift, from whose fullness we have all received.

units.la: 42 Excellit igitur Christus secundum humanitatem Maiestate, potestate, gra-tia & gloria, cetersque donis gratuitis, creaturas omnes, & mirum in modū ex-cellit, sed manet nihilominus secundum eandem humanitatem creature limitibus circunscriptus, & minor patre, eidémquē subiectus, qui omnia ei dedit atque subiecit.
units.tr: 42 Christ therefore excels all creatures in his humanity, in majesty, power, grace and glory, and in the other free gifts, and he excels them in a wonderful manner; yet, according to that same humanity, he remains circumscribed by the limits of a creature, lesser than the Father, and subject to him who gave and subjected all things to him.

units.la: 43 Atque hæc est omnis illa ἐξουσία in cœlo & in terra, hic Spiritus non ad mensuram, hæc sessio ad dexteram Patris, quæ Christo, quatenus homo est, attribui sentiunt Orthodoxi.
units.tr: 43 And this is all that authority [ἐξουσία] in heaven and on earth, this Spirit not given by measure, this sitting at the right hand of the Father, which the Orthodox hold to be ascribed to Christ as he is man.

units.la: 44 Neque tamen negamus ex his iam allatis Scripturæ locis vel aliis similibus, æqualem cum Patre potestatem, Maiestatem, gloriam, aut quiduis aliud diuinæ naturæ proprium Christo attribui posse, & à quibusdam Patribus in explicatione Scripturæ attributum esse. Sed adhibeatur necesse est Catholicæ fidei regula, quam iidem Patres diligenter obseruant, vt istiusmodi omnia de Christo secundum diuinitatem interpretemur, ne perperam alioquin, quisquis diuinitatis propria, humanæ naturæ admiscuerit, vtriusque naturæ proprietates, cum Monothelitis confundat. Atque hactenus si fortasse prolixè, at certè quidem non inutiliter explicata sunt, quæ ad Christi Maiestatem & gloriam ritè cognoscendam imprimis conferunt.
units.tr: 44 Yet we do not deny that from the passages of Scripture already cited, or from others like them, an power equal to the Father's, majesty, glory, or anything else proper to the divine nature, can be ascribed to Christ, and that some Fathers have ascribed it to him in their exposition of Scripture. But the rule of the Catholic faith must necessarily be applied, which these same Fathers carefully observed, so that we interpret all such things concerning Christ according to his divinity; otherwise, whoever mingles the properties of the divinity with human nature, he confounds the properties of both natures with the Monothelites. And so far, if perhaps at some length, yet certainly not without profit, those things have been explained which above all contribute to rightly knowing the majesty and glory of Christ.

units.la: THESES
units.tr: THESES

units.la: THESES CONFVTATO RIAE AD IMPIAS SCHMIdelini opiniones disiiciendas & explodendas:
units.tr: THESES REFUTING THE IMPIOUS OPINIONS OF SCHMIDELINUS, TO BE OVERTHROWN AND DRIVEN OUT

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: VNC vt alterum caput, quod in confutatione aduersariæ opinionis est positum, aggrediamur: Non potest sane vllo modo constare, q; Schmidelinus nouus Theologus nouis Thesibus firmare & persuadere conatur, in quibus quid loquatur, aut de quibus affirmet, prorsus ille non intelligit, vt ex his quę in explicatoriis Thesibus constituimus satis constat, & iamiam clarius cuincemus.
units.tr: Now let us take up the second point of the refutation of his opposing opinion. Schmidelinus, the new theologian, tries to establish and persuade with new theses. Certainly, it cannot in any way stand that he does not understand what he is saying or what he affirms, as is sufficiently clear from what we have set out in our explanatory theses, and as we shall now show more clearly.

units.la: 2 Definit personalem vnionē, vt sit communicatio plenitudinis omnis Deitatis. De hac inquit Apostolum ita loqui, In quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ & scientiæ abscondite: Et iterum: In ipso inhabitat omnis plenitudo diuinitatis corporaliter. Plenitudinem vero diuinitatis vocat, totius præsentiæ Dei secundum ἐνέργειαν in Christum effusionem, ita vt
units.tr: 2. He defines the personal union as a communication of the fullness of all the Deity. Of this he says that the Apostle speaks thus: "In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" [Col. 2:3]; and again: "In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily" [Col. 2:9]. He calls the fullness of the Godhead the outpouring of the whole presence of God according to the energy [ἐνέργειαν] into Christ, so that

units.la: F.iiij.
units.tr: F.iiij.

units.la: iam extra ipsum nihil, sed in homine, & per hominem Christum omnia in omnibus operetur.Et postea eandem diuinitatis plenitudinem appellat æqualitatem Maiestatis, glorię & potentię cum Verbo,ita vt humana in Christo natura, non iam potens tantum sit,sed etiam omnipotens,humana inquam, natura, non sola diuina,propterea quòd diuinitas realiter (vt ipsius verbis nobis loqui liceat) suas proprietates humanitati communicauerit, suásque perfectiones in eam effuderit & quasi transfuderit, & hac sola ἰδιω-μάτων κοινωνία hypostaticam vnionem definiendam esse docet. Igitur si mirabilem huius autoris sententiam recipiamus nihil erit aliud hypostatica seu personalis duarum naturarum in Christo vnio, quàm quędam totius energię diuinę in humanitatę effusio, aut quędam æqualis potentię,glorię & Maiestatis cómunicatio.
units.tr: now nothing works outside him, but in the man and through the man Christ all things work in all. Afterwards he calls the same fullness of the Godhead the equality of majesty, glory and power with the Word, so that the human nature in Christ is no longer merely powerful but also almighty. I say the human nature, not the divine alone, because the divinity has really (to use his own words, if we may speak so) communicated its properties to the humanity, and poured out and as it were transfused its perfections into it. He teaches that the hypostatic union is to be defined by this communication of properties alone [ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία]. So if we accept this author's remarkable opinion, the hypostatic or personal union of the two natures in Christ will be nothing other than a certain outpouring of the whole divine energy into the humanity, or a certain equal communication of power, glory and majesty.

units.la: 3 His iactis porro fundamentis, quę sunt verè putrida, progreditur ad colligendum humanam Christi naturam, ex vi personalis illius vnionis, eadem omnino Maiestate qua diuinitatem, corporaliter vbique adesse præsentem. Vt omit mittamus alia eiusdē farinę deliramenta, quę quæ hic Neotheologus attexit posteà, vt absurdum vnum ex alio deducat.
units.tr: 3. Having laid these foundations, which are truly rotten, he goes on to infer from the force of that personal union that the human nature of Christ is present everywhere, bodily, with exactly the same majesty as the divinity. To pass over the other nonsense of the same kind which this new theologian adds afterwards, drawing one absurdity from another.

units.la: 4 Iam ad fabricandâ hanc egregiam (si superis placet) personalis vnionis doctrinam, nullius Concilij definitionem, nullius Patris sententiam, nullam ratio-nem, autoritatem denique nullam, hic supercilij Artifex producit, sed vno tantùm Scripturæ loco fraudulenter exposito, hoc phantasma suum adumbrare conatur,& non tam persuadere, quàm fidei articulum sua solius autoritate id efficere sperat.
units.tr: 4. Now, to fabricate this splendid doctrine of the personal union (if the gods approve), this artificer of arrogance produces no definition of any council, no opinion of any Father, no reasoning, and in short no authority at all. He relies on a single passage of Scripture, fraudulently expounded, and tries to sketch out this phantom of his. He hopes to accomplish by his own authority alone what he does not so much persuade as make into an article of faith.

units.la: 5 Verùm, vt simul & imperitia & impietas noua coarguatur, Primùm ostendemus istiusmodi potentiæ & Maiestatis vnionem, aut plenitudinis diuinitatis communicationem, qualem ille fingit, minimè factam fuisse, imò ne fieri quidem vllo pacto potuisse. Tum vt concedamus factam illam fuisse, tamen eam nec personalem esse, nec ad personalem constituendam sufficere docebimus. Postremò Christum secùdum assumptam naturam non vbique, sed in cælo tantùm, & in Eucharistiæ sacramento præsentem adesse planum faciemus.
units.tr: 5. But, so that both his ignorance and his new impiety may be exposed together, we shall first show that a union of power and majesty of this kind, or a communication of the fullness of the Godhead such as he imagines, was never made, and indeed could not have been made in any way. Then, granting that it was made, we shall teach that it is neither personal nor sufficient to constitute a personal union. Lastly, we shall make it plain that Christ according to the assumed nature is present not everywhere, but in heaven only and in the sacrament of the Eucharist.

units.la: 6 Quòd igitur humana in Christo natura parem aut eandem cum diuina potentiam, Maiestatem, gloriam, aut quamuis aliam perfectionem sortita nō fuerit,ex eo manifeste constat, quòd naturæ post hypostaticam illam vnionem, absque vlla permixtione,confusione aut conuersione, proprietates suas saluas & distinctas retinuerint, vt ex Conciliis & Patribus supra docuimus: ita nimirum, vt nec humanitati, diuinæ proprietates: nec diuinitati,humanæ adaptari queant. Id quod nulla constare ratione posset, si diuina natura suas proprietates humanitati communicasset, aut illas in humanitatem effudisset aut transfudisset. Id enim alteri dicitur communicari, quod alteri commune efficitur. Id autem quod duobus ex æquo commune factum est, alterius proprietas dici non potest. Vnde non aliud profecto sacris Conciliis aut Patrib.est, naturarū proprietates in Christo confundere (vt docti horum) quàm vel humanas adscribere diuinæ naturæ, vel ediuersò diuinas humanæ, vel eosdem vtrique attribuere, quemadmodum iste palàm facit.
units.tr: 6. That the human nature in Christ did not obtain an equal or the same power, majesty, glory, or any other perfection as the divine nature is clearly established by this: after that hypostatic union the natures, without any mixture, confusion or conversion, retained their properties safe and distinct, as we have taught above from the Councils and the Fathers. So neither can the divine properties be fitted to the humanity, nor the human to the divinity. This could not be upheld by any reasoning if the divine nature had communicated its properties to the humanity, or poured them out or transfused them into it. For that is said to be communicated to another which becomes common to the other. But what has been made common to two equally cannot be called the property of one of them. Hence, to confuse the properties of the natures in Christ is in truth nothing other for the sacred Councils and the Fathers (as the learned know) than either to ascribe human properties to the divine nature, or conversely divine ones to the human, or to attribute the same to both, as this man openly does.

units.la: 7 Hoc vero incōmodum hic Theologaster subodoratus,errori suo patrocinium nium aucupatur hac oratione. Cum(inquit)dicitur, vnionem duarum naturarum in Christo factam hypostaticam, seruatis vtriusque naturæ proprietatibus, sobriè admodum intelligendum est & explicandum. Neque enim ita diuinitas Verbi sua energia, quæ ipsa est simplicissima, sese intra se continet, vt nullam in naturam humanam quasi transfundat perfectionem, quin potius humanitas plenitudinis omnis particeps diuinæ naturæ, duarum naturarum in Christo, hac sola ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνία, hypostatica vnio definienda est.Hæc ille, fidus scilicet & so brius admodum interpres, qui lucem inferre vult venerandis sanctorumPatrum & Conciliorum decretis: sed clariora illa sunt, quàm vt aliena, & falsò emendicata luce indigeant, vt ex his, quæ suprà copiosè citatissimus satis constat. Quod si adhuc plura & clariora desideras testimonia, quæ ex diametro cum huius Noua-toris doctrina pugnent, audi Hieronymum sic loquentem: Illorum quoque similiter execramur blasphemiam, qui nouo sensu asserere conantur, à tempore susceptæ carnis, omnia quæ erant deitatis in hominem demigrasse, & rursum quæ erant humanitatis in Deum esse trasfusa, vt quod nulla vnquam hæresis dicere ausa est, videatur hac confusione, vtraque exinanita substantia, Deitatis scilicet & humanitatis, & à proprio statu in aliud esse commutata. Hactenus ille. Audi iterum Damasce. Diuinitatem, inquit, dicentes, nō de illa nominamus, quę humanitatis sunt propria: neque de carne, id est, humanitate prædicamus ea, quæ Deitatis sunt propria. Hæc Damasce. Sic quoque reliqui Patres loquuntur.
units.tr: 7. This pseudo-theologian, having sniffed out this difficulty, seeks a defence for his error in the following words: "When it is said that the union of the two natures in Christ is hypostatic, with the properties of each nature preserved, it must be understood and explained very soberly. For the divinity of the Word does not so keep itself within itself by its energy, which is itself most simple, as not to transfuse some perfection into the human nature. Rather, the humanity, a partaker of all the fullness of the divine nature, is to be defined as the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ by this communication of properties alone." So he says. A faithful and very sober interpreter indeed, who wants to bring light to the venerable decrees of the holy Fathers and Councils! But those decrees are clearer than that they need a light borrowed from elsewhere and falsely begged, as is sufficiently clear from what we have quoted at length above. But if you still desire more and clearer testimonies which fight directly against the doctrine of this innovator, hear Jerome speaking thus: "We likewise curse the blasphemy of those who try to assert in a new sense that from the time of the assumed flesh, all that belonged to the Deity has migrated into man, and again that what belonged to the humanity has been transfused into God, so that, which no heresy has ever dared to say, both substances, that of the Deity and that of the humanity, are emptied by this confusion and changed from their own state into something else." Thus he. Hear again Damascene: "When we speak of the Deity, we do not name those things which are proper to the humanity; nor do we predicate of the flesh, that is the humanity, those things which are proper to the Deity." Thus Damascene. The other Fathers speak in the same way.

units.la: 8 Quod vt clarius intuearis, adde. Quòd si vna eadémque in Christi Domini humanitate & diuinitate potentia constituitur, vna etiam constituenda erit operatio. Rursum, si diuina natura suas proprietates & attributa in humanitatem effudit aut trăsfudit (vt iste somniat) sequetur, & illud necessario, vt vnum communémque vtriusque naturæ intellectum & voluntatem defendamus, cum hæc ad naturales diuinæ essentiæ proprietates pertineant, & vnum & idem omnino cum omnipotentia existant.
units.tr: 8. So that you may see this more clearly, add this. If in the humanity and the divinity of Christ the Lord there is one and the same power, then one operation will also have to be posited. Again, if the divine nature has poured out or transfused its properties and attributes into the humanity (as he dreams), it will follow, and necessarily so, that we must maintain one common understanding and will of both natures, since these belong to the natural properties of the divine essence and are altogether one and the same with omnipotence.

units.la: 9 Quare huius sententia hac in parte non modò falsa est, verùmetiam damnatam Monothelitarum hæresin sapit, cùm vtriusque naturæ proprietates atq. operationes in Christo confundat impie. piè. Atque hinc forsan accidit, vt cùm aliarum priscarum, & iam olim profligatarum hæresium in suis Thesibus meminerit, nullam tamen omnino Monotheli tarum fecerit mentionem.
units.tr: 9. Therefore the doctrine of this man is not only false in this respect, but also savours of the condemned heresy of the Monothelites, since he impiously confuses the properties and operations of both natures in Christ. And perhaps from this it happens that, although he mentions other ancient heresies, long since overthrown, in his theses, he makes no mention at all of the Monothelites.

units.la: 10 Quòd autem vult diuinitatem per proprietatum suarum seu perfectionum communicationem, effusionem, aut quasi transfusionem, humanæ naturæ essे coniunctam: Quid est hoc aliud tandè, quàm affirmare humanitatem in vna aliqua, vel in omnibus diuinæ naturæ perfectionibus, quæ tribus personis communes sunt, diuinitati esse coniunctam?
units.tr: 10. But when he wills that the divinity is joined to the human nature by a communication, outpouring, or as it were transfusion of its properties or perfections, what else, pray, is this than to affirm that the humanity is joined to the divinity in some one, or in all, of the perfections of the divine nature, which are common to the three persons?

units.la: 11 Hîc illi opponimus Oecumenica Concilia & Orthodoxos Patres, quorū est vna eadémque semper in hac re sententia, ex diuinarum scripturarum auctoritate pendens, nimirum: Naturarum in Christo vnionem, non secundùm essentialem aliquam diuinitatis perfectionē, toti trinitati communem, sed secundùm subsistentiam, quæ Verbo propria est (vt ante quoque non semel meminimus) factam esse.
units.tr: 11. Here we oppose to him the Ecumenical Councils and the orthodox Fathers, whose opinion on this matter has always been one and the same, resting on the authority of the divine Scriptures: namely, that the union of the natures in Christ was made not according to some essential perfection of the divinity common to the whole Trinity, but according to the subsistence which is proper to the Word (as we have recalled more than once before).

units.la: 12 Et quis inter Christianos adeò sit rudis rerúmque omnium ignarus, qui creaturam vllam, quantalibet excellentia præditam,omnipotenté esse statuat: aut in gloria & Maiestate, aut in quacunque alia perfectione eam exæquet creatori? Facit hoc tamen Schmidelinus, dum humanam Christi naturâ, quam creaturam esse fatetur,non solùm in omnipotentia, sed etiam in gloria, sapientia, Maiestate, & autoritate,Patri Deo audet exæquare.
units.tr: 12. And who among Christians is so rude and ignorant of all things as to hold that any creature, however excellent, is almighty, or to equal it to the Creator in glory and majesty or in any other perfection? Yet Schmidelinus does this, while he dares to make the human nature of Christ, which he confesses to be a creature, equal to God the Father not only in omnipotence but also in glory, wisdom, majesty and authority.

units.la: 13 Nec intelligit,in quameunq.tandem partem sese proripuerit, se captum & comprehensum teneri, vt elabi non possit,quin hac κυριοδοξία concedere cōstringatur,duas esse naturas omnipotentes:duos item creatores: Creaturam ipsam, creatorem esse, & omnipotentem: Denique creatorem quendam recentem , & nouum in tempore factum esse. Verum hæc omnia, cum expressis sacræ scripturæ testimoniis,cum Apostolorum & Conciliorum Symbolis,& cum perpetuo totius Ecclesiæ consensu plane pugnant.Et vbi legas probatum vllum autorem, qui vel somniauerit alium, præter Deum,creatorem &omnipotentem esse?
units.tr: 13 Nor does he see that, wherever he throws himself, he is held captured and cornered, so that he cannot escape without being forced to concede this "lordship of glory" [κυριοδοξία]: that there are two omnipotent natures, likewise two creators, the creature itself being a creator and omnipotent, and finally a certain recent creator, made new in time. But all these things plainly clash with the express testimonies of Holy Scripture, with the creeds of the Apostles and the Councils, and with the constant consensus of the whole Church. And where would you find any approved author who has even dreamed that anyone other than God is creator and omnipotent?

units.la: 14 Quapropter piis & mediocriter peritis rerum sacrarum , persuasum id semper fuit,Christum secundum naturam divinam,creatorem esse,& omnipotétem, per quem omnia facta sunt: At secudum humanitatem non creatore esse, sed crea turam, non infinitę virtutis aut omnipo- tentem, sed infirmum, humilem, sitiente, esurientem, flentem, tædio, pauori, sudo- ri, tristitiæ, morti, aliisque miseriis, & af- flictionibus humanis obnoxiū, vt qui ve- re languores nostros ipse tulerit, & pro- pter viscera misericordię suæ dolores no- stros in sua carne portauerit, vt à tyrannide ca dęmonis seruitute nos liberaret: vt e- tiam per omnia fratribus assimilatus ab- sque peccato, infirmitatibus nostris com- pati posset, & eis qui tentantur auxiliari. Quæ omnia simul cum omnipotentia, cęterisq.diuinis perfectionib.in vna natu- ra existere neutiquam possunt. Ex quibus proinde sancti Patres duas Christi natu- ras colligebant.
units.tr: 14 Therefore pious men with moderate learning in sacred things have always been persuaded that Christ, according to the divine nature, is creator and omnipotent, through whom all things were made; but according to the humanity he is not creator but creature, not of infinite power or omnipotent, but weak, humble, thirsty, hungry, weeping, subject to weariness, dread, sweat, sadness, death and other human miseries and afflictions. He truly bore our sicknesses and carried our sorrows in his flesh, through the bowels of his mercy, so that he might free us from the tyranny and servitude of the devil; and so that, made like his brothers in all things apart from sin, he might be able to sympathize with our weaknesses and help those who are tempted. All these things cannot in any way exist together in one nature, along with omnipotence and the other divine perfections. From these things the holy Fathers accordingly inferred two natures in Christ.

units.la: 15 Quod si Christus secundū humanitatem potentia & cęteris naturę diuinę perfectionib. diuinitati equalis est, iam neq.Patri usq.ad mortem obediens,neq. matri & Iosepho subditus esse, neq. sibi vel nobis mereri, neq.Mediator Dei & homīnū esse aut dici potuit. Siquidē hęc & id genus similia, quę in Scripturis passim occurrunt, inequalitate sonant, nō solū in essentia, sed etiā in potetia, vnde hęc opera proficiscuntur.
units.tr: 15 But if Christ according to the humanity is equal to the divinity in power and in the other perfections of the divine nature, then he could neither have been obedient to the Father even unto death, nor subject to his mother and Joseph, nor merit for himself or for us, nor be, or be called, Mediator between God and men. For these and similar things, which occur everywhere in the Scriptures, speak of inequality, not only in essence but also in power, from which these works proceed.

units.la: 16 Et quidé vel ex hoc solo aperte con uinci potest humanitatem Christi haud esse omnipotentem,quòd plurima possit Deus,& ante ipsam etiam Christi humanitatem conditam potuerit & fecerit, quę humanitas nulla ratione efficere potest,nec vnquam potuit. Etenim vt cęte-ra innumera omittamus, non potuit humanitas ipsa se fingere,neque resuscitare neque se nunc potest in nihilum redigere.non est igitur humanitas diuinę naturæ in potentia vllo pacto exęquanda.
units.tr: 16 And indeed from this alone it can be clearly proved that the humanity of Christ is not omnipotent: God can do very many things, and could and did do them even before the humanity of Christ itself was created, which humanity can by no means effect, nor ever could. For, to omit countless other things, the humanity itself could not form itself, nor raise itself, nor can it now reduce itself to nothing. The humanity is therefore in no way to be made equal to the divine nature in power.

units.la: 17 Qui ergo cum Schmidelino errare nolint,Paulum ducem sequantur , & vtriusque naturę proprietates & operationes ita distinguant, vt tribuant humanitati quidem , infirmitatem : diuinitati vero, virtutem,in quaChristus Dominus prędestinatus est Filius Dei.Et sicut duas voluntates & duas itidem operationes, singulas in singulis naturis esse credunt cum Ecclesia: ita quoque duas virtutes seu potentias alteram infinitam in diuinitate,alteram finitam in humanitate,sine vlla permixtione, confusione, transfusione, effusione vel infusione, cum eadem sancta & Apostolica Ecclesia simpliciter pliciter confiteantur.
units.tr: 17 Those therefore who do not wish to err with Schmidelin should follow Paul as their leader, and so distinguish the properties and operations of each nature that they ascribe weakness indeed to the humanity, but virtue to the divinity, in which Christ the Lord was predestined to be the Son of God. And just as they believe, with the Church, that there are two wills and likewise two operations, each in its own nature, so too they simply confess, with that same holy and Apostolic Church, two powers or abilities: one infinite in the divinity, the other finite in the humanity, without any mixture, confusion, transfusion, effusion or infusion.

units.la: 18 Abutitur autem quibusdam Scripturæ locis nouus iste Macarius, vt probet humanitatem potentia, autoritate, Maiestate, gloria, scientia & sapientia diuinitati æqualem esse. Tametsi enim largiamur illi, quòd in citatis locis aliqua cum Deo æqualitas Christi designetur, hinc tamen non sequitur illud, humanitatem diuinitati æqualem esse. Aliud enim est, si dicas (vt ante declarauimus) Christo omnem datam esse potestatem in cœlo & in terra, aliud humanæ eius naturæ donationem eam factam fuisse. Nam personæ diuinæ, quæ Christi nomine significatur, omnipotentia & quæcunque alia diuina perfectio vere ascribi potest, creatæ verò naturæ, qualis est Christi humanitas, non potest.
units.tr: 18 But this new Macarius abuses certain passages of Scripture to prove that the humanity is equal to the divinity in power, authority, majesty, glory, knowledge and wisdom. Even if we grant him that in the passages cited some equality of Christ with God is indicated, it does not follow from this that the humanity is equal to the divinity. For it is one thing to say (as we declared above) that all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ, and another that this gift was made to his human nature. For omnipotence and any other divine perfection can truly be ascribed to the divine person signified by the name of Christ, but not to the created nature, such as the humanity of Christ is.

units.la: 19 Certè si omne illud, quod vel in Scripturis sacris, vel in Patrum monumentis, quocunque modo Christo ascribitur, humanitati Christi statim tribuatur, profectò & Catholicè affirmare licebit, humanitas Christi est Deus, increata, æterna, per quam omnia facta sūt, vnum & idem cum Patre, splendor Patris & figura substantiæ eius, quoniam hæc omnia de Christo verissimè prædicantur.
units.tr: 19 Certainly, if everything that is ascribed to Christ in any way, whether in the holy Scriptures or in the writings of the Fathers, were at once attributed to the humanity of Christ, then one could also affirm catholically that the humanity of Christ is God, uncreated, eternal, through whom all things were made, one and the same with the Father, the brightness of the Father and the image of his substance, since all these things are most truly predicated of Christ.

units.la: 2o Imprudentius verò & insulsius colligitur, Apostolus asserit plenitudinē diuinitatis in Christo corporaliter inha-bitare,&omnes in eo thesauros sapientię & scientiæ reconditos esse,igitur plenitu-do diuinitatis,id est,æqualis gloria,Maie-stas, sapientia & potentia, humanitati Christi est communicata, & in eam effu-sa,aut quasi transfusa: ita vt iam humani-tas Christi, veré sit & dicatur omnipo-tens, sicut ipse Deus, humana, inquam, natura,non sola diuina,æqualíque gloria & Maiestate cum Deo ipso prædita.
units.tr: 20 More imprudently and foolishly he infers: the Apostle asserts that the fullness of the divinity dwells bodily in Christ, and that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him; therefore the fullness of the divinity, that is, equal glory, majesty, wisdom and power, has been communicated to the humanity of Christ and poured into it, or as it were transfused into it; so that now the humanity of Christ truly is, and is called, omnipotent just as God himself is: human nature, I say, not the divine nature alone, endowed with glory and majesty equal to God himself.

units.la: 21 Hîc monendus est Lector,vt ob-seruet, personam Christi cum natura ma-nifestè ab hoc Theologo confundi,quā-doquidem ex eo,quòd quippiam inChri-sto esse dicitur,concludit,idipsum quóq. in eius humanitate statui oportere.
units.tr: 21 Here the reader is to be warned to observe that this theologian plainly confuses the person of Christ with his nature, since from the fact that something is said to be in Christ, he concludes that the same must also be established in his humanity.

units.la: 22 Deinde,vt fingamus Apostolum dixisse, plenitudinem diuinitatis in hu-manitate Christi corporaliter inhabitare omnésque thesauros sapientiæ & scien-tiæ diuinæ in eadem humanitate recon-ditos latere, quod à Diuo Paulo dictum non est, tametsi Catholicè id affirmari posse nouerimus,cùm tota & plena diui-nitas nitas humanitati personaliter sit vnita, & in ea lateat abscondita. Cæterùm falsò inde colligitur,ergo æqualis Maiestas,sapientia & potentia,&c. humanitati Christi est communicata,ita vt humanitas dicatur omnipotens,quemadmodũ Deus. Eodem enim argumētationis genere deduceretur,Deitatem naturæ humanæ cõmunicatam esse, ita vt humanitas Deus veré dici possit, sicut omnipotens: cùm verissimè asseueretur diuinitatem ipsam in humanitate Christi corporaliter inhabitare.Præsertim cũ nihil sit aliud Deitatis plenitudo,q; Deitas plena atq. pfecta.
units.tr: 22 Next, let us suppose that the Apostle had said that the fullness of the divinity dwells bodily in the humanity of Christ, and that all the treasures of wisdom and divine knowledge lie hidden in that same humanity. This was not said by the divine Paul, although we know it can be affirmed catholically, since the whole and full divinity is personally united with the humanity and lies hidden in it. But it is falsely inferred from this: therefore equal majesty, wisdom and power, etc., have been communicated to the humanity of Christ, so that the humanity is called omnipotent just as God is. For by the same kind of argument it would be deduced that the Deity has been communicated to the human nature, so that the humanity could truly be called God, just as it is called omnipotent; since it would be most truly asserted that the divinity itself dwells bodily in the humanity of Christ. Especially since the fullness of the Deity is nothing other than the Deity full and perfect.

units.la: 23 Adde,quòd cùm anima rationalis in corpore humano corporaliter inhabitet, non solum hypostatica vnione illi coniuncta,sed etiam essentiali:si huius autoris explicationem sequimur, integrum erit inferre, animam cum omnibus suis facultatibus & affectionibus, ad eum modum corpori communicatam esse,vt corpus perinde atque anima intelligens sit & volens, arte Mathematica & Medica, cæterísque scientiis præditum. Quis autē nisi stultus id fateatur?
units.tr: 23 Add that, since the rational soul dwells bodily in the human body, joined to it not only by hypostatic union but also essentially, then if we follow this author's explanation, it will entirely follow that the soul, with all its faculties and affections, has been communicated to the body in such a way that the body is as intelligent and willing as the soul, and endowed with mathematical and medical skill and the other sciences. But who, except a fool, would admit this?

units.la: 24 Imò vero cũ domos corporaliter inhabitemus,sequetur etiā nos illis ita cõ municatos esse, vt eisdem proprietatibus & perfectionibus domus affectæ dicantur, quibus nos ipsi affecti sumus. Qualis ergo est autoris huius explicatio, qua pro eodem inhabitationis & communicationis nomen audet vsurpare?
units.tr: 24 Indeed, since we dwell bodily in houses, it will follow that we too are communicated to them in such a way that the houses are said to be affected by the same properties and perfections by which we ourselves are affected. What, then, is the worth of this author's explanation, which dares to use the same name of indwelling and communication for both?

units.la: 25 Nec obstat, quòd aliter diuinitas in humanitate habitet, nimirum hypostatice cum illa coniuncta. Nam licet id verum sit, non ideo tamen consequitur, idem esse, aliquid in altero corporaliter inhabitare, & illi communicatum aut hypostatice coniunctum esse. Vnde Cyrillus sic ait: Neq. idem fuerit dicere, Verbum factum fuisse hominem, & putare, Deum habitare in homine, etiamsi, vt est, vera beati Pauli vox est, quòd complacuit in ipso habitare omnem plenitudinem Deitatis corporaliter. Sed vnum inquit esse Deum Patrem & Filium Dominum Iesum Christum, per quem omnia. Et hinc est quòd Nestorius, qui hypostaticam diuinitatis cum humanitate vnione reiicebat, libenter eo testimonio vteretur, quòd videret aliud esse, aliquid in altero inhabitare, & illi hypostaticos coiunctum esse.
units.tr: 25 Nor does it stand in the way that the divinity dwells in the humanity in another way, namely, hypostatically joined to it. For although that is true, it does not follow that it is the same thing for something to dwell bodily in another and for it to be communicated to that other or hypostatically joined to it. Hence Cyril says: "Nor would it be the same to say that the Word was made man and to think that God dwells in man, even though, as it is, the true word of the blessed Paul is that it pleased [God] that all the fullness of the Deity should dwell bodily in him. But," he says, "there is one God the Father and the Son the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." And hence it is that Nestorius, who rejected the hypostatic union of the divinity with the humanity, would gladly use that testimony, because he saw that it is one thing for something to dwell in another and another for it to be hypostatically joined to it.

units.la: 26 Quocunque ergo modo hic interpretetur Scripturæ testimonia, siue de per-
units.tr: 26 Therefore, however one interprets the testimonies of Scripture here, whether they concern the per-

units.la: Coloss. 2. ; 1.Cor. 7. ; Ioh. 4. persona, siue de natura Christi, nullum inde firmum satis praesidium petere potè rit,cùm vtrouis modo accepta,longè qui dem aliter explicari debeant, & à Patri-bus secus explicentur, quàm ab hoc au-tore intelliguntur.
units.tr: Coloss. 2. ; 1.Cor. 7. ; Ioh. 4. son or the nature of Christ, no firm enough support can be sought from them, since, understood in either way, they must be explained quite differently, and the Fathers explain them otherwise than this author understands them.

units.la: 27 Nec tamen ideo, quòd diuinitas proprietates suas humanæ naturæ non communicaucrit,consequens est, Gram-maticam tantùm seu verbalem idiomatū diuinæ naturę communicationem in per sona Christi fieri, vt hic homo inferre co natur,eadem enim omnino ratione con-uinceretur, idiomatum humanæ naturæ communicationem,cum persona diuina nullatenus esse factam.Nam vt fides Or-thodoxa docet,& Schmidelinus quoque aperte confitetur, humana Christi natu-ra proprietates suas diuinæ naturæ nullo pacto communicauit.
units.tr: 27 Yet it does not follow, merely because the divinity did not communicate its properties to the human nature, that the communication of the divine nature's attributes to the person of Christ is only grammatical or verbal, as this man here wishes to infer. By the very same reasoning one would be convinced that the communication of the human nature's attributes to the divine person has in no way taken place. For, as the Orthodox faith teaches, and Schmidelin himself openly confesses, the human nature of Christ in no way communicated its properties to the divine nature.

units.la: 28 Sicut ergo Deus dicitur hominis Filius, infirmus,crucifixus,mortuus & se pultus, &c. propter naturam humanam sibi personaliter vnitam: ita etiam homo Christus, Dei Filius appellatur, omnipo-tens,æternus,immortalis,&c.nō propter aliquam effusionem aut transfusionem, sed propter inconfusam vnionem, qua humana natura cum diuinitate coniun-ƈta est in vnitate personæ.
units.tr: 28 Just as God is therefore called the Son of man, weak, crucified, dead and buried, and so on, on account of the human nature personally united to him, so also the man Christ is called the Son of God, almighty, eternal, immortal, and so on. This is not because of any outpouring or transfusion, but because of the unconfused union by which the human nature is joined with the divinity in the unity of the person.

units.la: 29 Dicet aliquis inter idiomatum diuinorum & humanorum communicationem multum interesse discriminis; quoniam diuina non solùm voce, sed etiam re ipsa de humana natura dicuntur, humana verò idiomata, non re sed voce tantùm diuinitati ascribuntur, id quod haud obscurè quidem & ille hisce verbis subindicat. Diligenter verò discernendum est, inter idiomata humanæ naturæ, quæ propter vnionem personalem diuinæ tribuuntur, & idiomata diuinæ naturæ, quæ propter eandem vnionem humanæ ascribuntur. Humanitas enim diuinitatè non assumpsit, sed ipsa assumpta est à diuinitate in vnitatem personæ, quam infirmam reddere non potest: etsi verè & rectè dicitur persona, quæ Deus & homo est, laborare & mori. Cùm econtra humanitas à diuinitate perficiatur, quæ realiter suas proprietates humanitati communicat, vt sit non modò viua, sed viuificatrix quoque, non potens tantùm, sed etiã omnipotês: humana inquã natura, nõ sola diuina. Hæc ille insignis scilicet disputator.
units.tr: 29 Someone will say that there is a great difference between the communication of divine and of human attributes, since the divine attributes are predicated of the human nature not only in word but also in fact, whereas the human attributes are ascribed to the divinity not in fact but only in word. This our author also hints at, not obscurely, in these words: We must carefully distinguish between the attributes of the human nature, which are ascribed to the divine nature on account of the personal union, and the attributes of the divine nature, which are ascribed to the human nature on account of the same union. For the humanity did not assume the divinity; rather, the humanity itself was assumed by the divinity into the unity of the person, and the divinity cannot be made weak. Yet it is truly and rightly said that the person who is God and man suffers and dies. On the contrary, the humanity is perfected by the divinity, which really communicates its properties to the humanity, so that it is not only living but also life-giving, not only powerful but also omnipotent: the human nature, I say, not the divine alone. So says that distinguished disputant, to be sure.

units.la: 30 Primùm hic explicandũ erat apertius de persona, an de natura loquatur. nam vtram-
units.tr: 30 First, he should have explained more clearly here whether he is speaking of the person or of the nature, for he confuses each of them

units.la: Thesi 19. vtramque passim more suo confundit,& vtriusq. vocabulis citra vllum delectum abutitur. Quòd si de natura loquatur, vt sanè loqui videtur, non minus falsum est, quod ait, diuinas proprietates humanæ naturæ realiter esse communicatas, quàm ediuerso, communicatas esse humanas diuinæ naturæ, vt ex his quæ antea diximus liquidò constat: etenim nec voce nec re ipsa vnius naturæ proprietates alteri conueniunt, nec de altera dici queunt. Nec minùs repugnat, humanam naturam diuinis affici proprietatibus, quàm diuinitatem humanis infirmitatibus obnoxiam fieri.
units.tr: Thesis 19. throughout, after his own fashion, and abuses the terms of both without any distinction. But if he is speaking of the nature, as he certainly seems to be, it is no less false to say that the divine properties are really communicated to the human nature, than conversely that the human properties are communicated to the divine nature, as is clear from what we said above. For neither in word nor in fact do the properties of one nature belong to the other, nor can they be predicated of the other. Nor is it any less inconsistent for the human nature to be affected by divine properties than for the divinity to be made subject to human infirmities.

units.la: 31 Si verò de persona disserit, vt ibidem quoque facit, dum inquit: Etsi verè & recte dicitur, persona quæ Deus & homo est, laborare & mori: non minus & id falsum est, scilicet idiomata humana, voce duntaxat, non re ipsa, de persona, quæ revera diuina & humana est, affirmari, cùm vni eidemque personæ vtriusque naturæ attributa re ipsa conueniant. Quòd autem fieri nequeat, vt voce & non re ipsa humana idiomata de persona Verbi enuncientur, id ex peruulgato illo Philosophi dictoclare intelligitur: Ab eo, quòd res est vel non est, oratio dicitur vera vel falsa. Vnde omnibus compertum est nō posse aliquid voce de altero affirmari, fi res ipsa aliter habeat, quàm voce fignifi- cetur.
units.tr: 31 If, however, he is discussing the person, as he also does in the same place when he says: Yet it is truly and rightly said that the person who is God and man suffers and dies, then this too is no less false: that human attributes are predicated of the person, who is really divine and human, merely in word and not in fact, since the attributes of both natures really belong to one and the same person. That this cannot happen, namely that human attributes are pronounced of the person of the Word in word and not in fact, is made clear by that well-known saying of the Philosopher: a statement is called true or false according as the thing is or is not. Hence it is known to all that nothing can be affirmed of another in word if the thing itself is otherwise than the word signifies.

units.la: 32 Ex eo verò, quòd humanitas diuinitatem non affumpserit, sed ipsa af- sumpta sit à diuinitate in vnitatem per- sonę,& diuinitas infirmari nequeat, hu- manitas autem à diuinitate perficiatur: nequaquam sequitur,ipsam Verbi perso- nam,infirmitates humanas non sustinuisse, aut humanam naturam ęquè perse- ctam esse,atque diuinam:sed hoc tantùm hinc inferri potest: nihil imperfectionis ex ea vnione diuinitatem accepisse, hu- manitati verò maximam accessisse perse- ctionem,qua particeps, non ęqualis esse- cta est diuinę naturę,vt D.Basilius his ver- bis docet: Humana Domini caro, ipsa participauit deitati, non propriam debi- litatem diuinitati distribuit.
units.tr: 32 But from the fact that the humanity did not assume the divinity, but was itself assumed by the divinity into the unity of the person, and that the divinity cannot be weakened while the humanity is perfected by the divinity, it by no means follows that the person of the Word did not bear human infirmities, or that the human nature is as perfect as the divine. Only this may be inferred from it: that the divinity received no imperfection from that union, while the humanity received the greatest perfection, by which it was made a partaker, though not an equal, of the divine nature. St Basil teaches this in these words: The human flesh of the Lord shared in the deity; it did not distribute its own weakness to the divinity.

units.la: 33 Vnde quòd ad naturas ipsas atti- net, rectè quidem hoc discrimen statui poteit, quòd ex hypostatica diuinitatis cū humanitate vnione, nihil omnino im- perfectionis diuinę obtigerit naturæ: hu- manę verò magna quædam & singularis excel
