units.tr: 33 Hence, as far as the natures themselves are concerned, this distinction may rightly be laid down: from the hypostatic union of the divinity with the humanity, no imperfection at all befell the divine nature, whereas to the human nature there came a certain great and singular excellence.

units.la: Concione de Natiuit. excellentia obuenerit. Sed interim hæc perfectio, quæ ex vnione illa humanæ accessit naturæ, non est idioma diuinum, sed humanum, non quidem naturale sed gratuitum.
units.tr: Sermon on the Nativity. But this perfection, which accrued to the human nature from that union, is not a divine attribute but a human one, not indeed natural but gratuitous.

units.la: 34 Quantum verò spectat ad idioma-tum communicationem in persona, citra vllum omnino discrimen, & diuina homi-ni, & humana Deo, tanquam vni & eidem personæ, in diuina & humana natura sub-sistenti, non voce tantùm, sed & re ipsa re ＆tissimè attribuuntur, cùm vna reuera sit Dei & hominis persona. At verò idioma-ta diuina neque voce neque re ipsa naturæ humanæ possunt ascribi, sicut nec hu-mana diuinæ, quòd, secundùm sacrorum Conciliorum sanctiones & Patrum tradi-tione, naturæ semper distinctæ & imper-mixtæ cum suis proprietatibus permanserint.
units.tr: 34 As far as the communication of attributes in the person is concerned, without any distinction at all, both divine attributes are ascribed to the man, and human attributes to God, as to one and the same person subsisting in the divine and the human nature, not only in word but also in fact most truly, since there is really one person of God and man. But divine attributes can be ascribed to the human nature neither in word nor in fact, nor human attributes to the divine nature, since, according to the decrees of the sacred Councils and the tradition of the Fathers, the natures have always remained distinct and unmixed, each with its own properties.

units.la: 35 Nunc vide obsecro huius Theolo-gi imperitiâ impiâ, & impietatē imperitâ, qui dum nouū quoddâ & hactenus inau-ditum discrimen comminiscitur, ab omni Christiana veritate in re tanta discedit. Nam attributa diuina palàm humanæ as-scribit naturæ, ediuersò verò humana non reuera, sed voce solùm diuinæ perfonæ accommodat.
units.tr: 35 Now, I beg you, consider the impious ignorance of this theologian, and the ignorant impiety of him who, while he devises a certain new and hitherto unheard-of distinction, departs from all Christian truth in a matter of such importance. For he openly ascribes divine attributes to the human nature, but conversely does not really apply human attributes to the divine person, only in word.

units.la: 36 Iam illud est expediendum,& scil uata quidem methodo:huiusmodi Maiestatis, potentiæ,sapientiæ communicatio nem,quam iste confingit,ne fieri quidem potuisse.Primùm enim certissimũ est nulli us omnino proprietatem , in alteram naturam seu speciem transferri posse.Et-enim vt erudite Cyrillus dixit, & ratio ipsa dictat : Quorum operatio & virtus indifferenter vna est, iis necesse est speciei vnitatem seruare . Quis enim diceret aptitudinem ad disciplinas capiendas , ad ridendum,ad ratiocinandum, quæ hominis propria,lapidi aut trunco infundi posse? Multò minùs vero diuina proprietas, quę infinita est,natures finitę & creatę poterit communicari , cùm in confesso sit, quod res finita certisq. terminis conclusa rem infinitam &immensam intra se capere nequeat.
units.tr: 36 Now this must be set out, and in a fitting method: that such a communication of majesty, power and wisdom as this man invents could not even have taken place. For first it is most certain that the property of no nature whatsoever can be transferred into another nature or kind. For, as Cyril learnedly said, and reason itself dictates: those whose operation and power are indistinguishably one must necessarily keep the unity of their kind. For who would say that the aptitude for receiving learning, for laughing and for reasoning, which are proper to man, can be infused into a stone or a log? Much less can the divine property, which is infinite, be communicated to a finite and created nature, since it is agreed that a finite thing, enclosed within definite limits, cannot contain within itself an infinite and immeasurable thing.

units.la: 37 Adhæc cùm Dei potentia,sicut & scientia,& quęlibet eius perfectio, ipsissima & simplicissima eius sit essentia., vt etiam vltro aduersarius fatetur,euidenti& necessaria collectione efficitur , si diuina omnipotētia,&c. humanę naturę fuerit communicata,quemadmodū ille somniat, ipsisiipsissimā quoq.& simplicissimā Dei essen-tiā eidē naturę humanę fuisse cōmunica-tam:ita vt humanitas sit facta Deus sicut omnipotens.
units.tr: 37 Moreover, since the power of God, like his knowledge, and every one of his perfections, is his very and most simple essence, as the adversary himself even freely admits, it follows by a clear and necessary inference that if the divine omnipotence, and so on, had been communicated to the human nature, as he dreams, then the very and most simple essence of God would likewise have been communicated to that same human nature, so that the humanity became God just as it became omnipotent.

units.la: 38 Preterea cum idē hic οὐσία, potē-tia,gloria, & Maiestate,humanitatē diui-nitati exęquet, fateri vel inuitus debet, οὐσία quoq. essentia,natura atq. subsţātia humana Christi natura diuinitati æquale esse:cum hęc omnia in Deo sint vna ea-dēmque simplissima Deitatis natura.
units.tr: 38 Furthermore, since this man equates the humanity with the divinity in οὐσία, power, glory and majesty, he must admit, even against his will, that the οὐσία, essence, nature and substance of the human nature of Christ is equal to the divinity, since all these things are in God one and the same most simple nature of the Godhead.

units.la: 39 Hinc quoq.colligitur,idem prorsus esse,si dicas,diuinitatem realiter suas pro-prietates humanitati cōmunicasse, ita vt diuinę naturę ṗprietates de illa verè præ-dicētur,acsi dicas, diuinitatē semetipsam humanitati cōmunicasse, ita vt ipsa diui-na naturade humanaaffirmetur:&vnionē proinde duarum naturarū in Christo,nō in persona, sed etiam in natura factā esse.
units.tr: 39 From this it is also gathered that it is altogether the same thing whether you say that the divinity really communicated its properties to the humanity, so that the divine properties are truly predicated of it, or whether you say that the divinity communicated itself to the humanity, so that the divine nature itself is affirmed of the human. And so the union of the two natures in Christ has been made not only in the person but also in the nature.

units.la: 40 Nec aliud esse potest humanam na-turam omnipotenté euasisse,quàm crea-turam esse transmutatam in creatore ac Deum,quod nec fieri, nec intelligi vlla ratione potest, cùm neque Deitas in hu- manitatem, nec humanitas in Deitatem conuerti queat aut commutari.
units.tr: 40 Nor can it be otherwise than that the human nature has become omnipotent, that is, that a creature has been transmuted into the Creator and into God, which can be neither done nor understood by any reasoning, since neither can the Godhead be turned into the humanity, nor the humanity into the Godhead, or be changed.

units.la: 41 Quæ cùm ita sese habeant,nō po-
units.tr: 41 Since these things stand thus, this adversary cannot po-

units.la: Psal.102. Malach.3. Hebræ.4. test hic aduersarius, quicquid etiam gar-riat, à damnata Eutychianorum hæresi excusari, qui duas Christi naturas impiè iuxtà ac imperitè confundebant.nam, vt ostendimus, diuinas in Christo proprieta-tes, quas tamen prorsus idem cum ipsa di-uina essentia esse fatetur, cū humana na-tura manifestè confundit atq.permiscet.
units.tr: Psal. 102. Malach. 3. Hebr. 4. This opponent, whatever nonsense he may babble, cannot be excused from the condemned heresy of the Eutychians, who impiously and ignorantly confused the two natures of Christ. For, as we have shown, he openly confuses and mingles the divine properties in Christ with the human nature, although he admits that these properties are entirely the same as the divine essence itself.

units.la: 42 Quod cùm nouus hicEutyches quadantenus animaduertisset, & absur-dius ab se dictum nonnihil mitigare vel-let, hæc verba inseruit. Neque verò hac reali plenitudinis omnis diuinitatis commu-nicatione, natura humana cum diuina misce-tur, aut, sicut quibusdam videtur, plane abo-letur, sed quod diuinæ per essentiam est, id hu-manæ suo modo per accidens communicatur. Quibus quidem verbis non sanat hic ho-mo, sed aperit magis & pestilentiore red-dit morbum animi sui, nouásque euomit absurditates, tantum abest vt diluat obie-ctum argumentum.
units.tr: 42 When this new Eutyches had noticed this to some extent, and wished to soften somewhat what he had said too absurdly, he inserted these words: Neither, however, by this real communication of the whole fullness of divinity is the human nature mixed with the divine, or, as seems to some, plainly abolished; but what is of the divine by essence is communicated to the human in its own way by accident. With these words this man does not heal his error but reveals it, makes the disease of his mind more pestilent, and vomits forth new absurdities. So far is he from refuting the argument brought against him.

units.la: 43 Nam si illa plenitudinis diuinitatis communicatio per accidés est, vt loquitur, sequitur vnione hypostaticam, quæ secū-dum Eutychiani huius sententiam, in illa plenitudinis communicatione sita est, per accidens esse. Verum id falsò asseri, inde colligas licet, quòd hac ratione fie- ret,vt Christus Deus esset per accidens, & ipsa quoque diuinitatis plenitudo accidens quoddam esset, & reliquæ etiam diuinæ perfectiones, quæ cum plenitudine diuinitatis idem prorsus existunt, accidetia quædam haberentur. Sed hæc tam im pie quàm absurdè affirmari, nemo sanæ mentis dubitare potest.
units.tr: 43 For if that communication of the fullness of divinity is by accident, as he says, it follows that the hypostatic union, which according to this Eutychian's view consists in that communication of fullness, is accidental. That this is falsely asserted you may gather from the fact that by such reasoning Christ would be God only by accident, the fullness of divinity itself would be some accident, and the other divine perfections too, which are wholly the same as the fullness of divinity, would be held to be certain accidents. But that these things are affirmed as impiously as they are absurdly, no one of sound mind can doubt.

units.la: 44 Iam verò vt ad illud quoque pro grediamur, licet hæc Maiestatis, potestatis, autoritatis & gloriæ vnio fieri aliquo modo potuisset, aut etiam reipsa facta foret, ita vt in ea sola, non in essentia, duæ in Christo naturæ vnitæ fuissent, tamen hypostaticam vnionem non efficeret.
units.tr: 44 Now, to proceed also to that point: although this union of majesty, power, authority and glory could in some way have been effected, or even actually made, so that the two natures in Christ were united in it alone and not in essence, it still would not bring about the hypostatic union.

units.la: 45 Nam vt supra multis ostendimus, Patres omnes constanter asseuerant vnionem hypostaticam esse vnionē in sub sistentia, non in aliqua essentiali proprietate toti Trinitati communi: Idiomatum verò communicationem in persona, vnione illa personali naturæ ordine posteriorem esse, eámque iam factam necessario consequi. Ideo enim dicunt vtriusque naturæ idiomata de vna eademque persona Christi affirmari, quia illæ duæ naturæ in vna Christi persona sunt vnitæ: quod profecto constare non posset, si ipsamet idiomatum communicatio personalem efficeret vnionem.
units.tr: 45 For, as we have shown above with many arguments, all the Fathers constantly assert that the hypostatic union is a union in subsistence, not in some essential property common to the whole Trinity; and that the communication of idioms is in the person, that union being posterior in order to the personal union and necessarily following it once made. For they say that the idioms of each nature are predicated of one and the same person of Christ because those two natures are united in the one person of Christ. This could not hold if the communication of idioms itself effected the personal union.

units.la: 46 Quod autem sola illa potestatis & Maiestatis communicatio, qualé iste fingit, ad hypostaticam vnionem non sufficiat, docet Eph. Synodus in hęc verba, Nō potest vnire naturas (de vnione hypostatica loquitur) sola dignitatis aut potestatis æqualitas. Et rursus: Dicere Deum & hominem sibi inuicem velut dignitatis & autoritatis vnitate coiunctos, nouitas vocis est, & nihil aliud. Sic illa Synodus.
units.tr: 46 That the sole communication of power and majesty, of the kind this man invents, does not suffice for the hypostatic union, the Council of Ephesus teaches in these words: "Equality of dignity or power cannot unite natures" (it speaks of the hypostatic union). And again: "To say that God and man are joined to each other as by a unity of dignity and authority is a novelty of words and nothing else." So that Council.

units.la: 47 Quæ res vt per similitudinem illustretur, si forte Princeps aliquis, quocūque modo in Maiestate, potestate & auctoritate alteri sit æqualis, non inde consequitur, vtrunque Principe in eandē coaluisse personam, sicut nec ideo duo Apostoli, quod exemplum Synodus eadem in rem præsentem adducit, vna persona dici possunt, quòd paris fuerint potestatis, autoritatis, aut dignitatis.
units.tr: 47 To illustrate this by comparison: if some prince should be equal to another in majesty, power and authority in whatever way, it does not follow that the two princes have coalesced into one person. Nor, for that matter, can two apostles, an example which the Council also brings to the same point, be called one person because they were of equal power, authority or dignity.

units.la: 48 Quòd si Paulo credimus, Christus sua obedientia vsque ad mortem, humanitatis suæ exaltatione promeruit & Maiestatem. At si Maiestatis communicatio hypostaticam perficeret vnionem, fieret sanè vt sua passione suā quoq. cum diui-nitate promeruissetvnionem:quod ridi-culum est asserere.
units.tr: 48 And if we believe Paul, Christ by his obedience unto death merited majesty also through the exaltation of his humanity. But if the communication of majesty effected the hypostatic union, it would certainly follow that by his passion he merited union with the divinity too, which is ridiculous to assert.

units.la: 49 Imò cùm Christi corpus ante re-surrectionē non fuerit gloriosum, sed pa-tibile, & mortale:manifestè sequitur, an-tequam Christus resurgeret sacratissimū eius corpus diuinitati hypostaticè vnitū non fuisse,si quidem,vt hic homo vult,in gloriæ & Maiestatis communicatione v-nio hypostatica constistit.
units.tr: 49 Indeed, since the body of Christ before the resurrection was not glorious but passible and mortal, it clearly follows that before Christ rose his most sacred body was not hypostatically united to the divinity, if indeed, as this man wants, the hypostatic union consists in the communication of glory and majesty.

units.la: 50 Pręterea, si in illius potestatis & Maiestatis communicatione,hypostatica Christi vnio constituitur,non poterit vl-la ratione Deus naturam aliquam in per-sona sibi copulare, quin eiusccmodi pote statem,&c.ei impartiatur.Quod sanè ne-mo admittet,nisi qui diuinam omnipotē tiam ignoret,& quid hypostatica vnio sit plane nō intelligat. Constat enim corpus Christi etiam in triduo, cùm iam rationa li anima esset destitutum,hypostaticòs di uinitati coniunctum fuisse , quod tamen glorię,potestatis,Maiestatis, sapientię, & scientię diuinæ capax minimè fuisse, nul lus , nisi qua ratione caruerit, ambigere poterit.
units.tr: 50 Moreover, if the hypostatic union of Christ is constituted in that communication of power and majesty, God will in no way be able to join any nature to himself in one person without imparting such power, and so on, to it. No one will admit this except one who is ignorant of divine omnipotence and plainly does not understand what the hypostatic union is. For it is established that the body of Christ, even in the three days when it was deprived of a rational soul, was hypostatically joined to the divinity; yet that it was by no means capable of glory, power, majesty, wisdom and divine knowledge, no one will doubt, unless on the very ground that it lacked them.

units.la: 51 Iam si hic autor putat,corpus aliquod, praesertim animę rationalis expers, omnes aut aliquas diuinas perfectiones capere posse: insignis sane cuiusdam infci tiæ notam euadere nequit. Sin vero eas capere non posse censuerit, ut res ipsa habet, illud euitare non poterit, quin afferat corpus Christi, praesertim in triduo, Diuinitati vnitum haudquaquam remansisse, imo nec remanere potuisse. Sed id falsum esse & hereticum, Theologus nullus ignorat.
units.tr: 51 Now if this author thinks that some body, especially one lacking a rational soul, can receive all or some divine perfections, he certainly cannot escape being marked with a notable folly. But if he judges that it cannot receive them, as the matter itself stands, he will not be able to avoid asserting that the body of Christ, especially in the three days, by no means remained united to the divinity, indeed could not have remained so. But that this is false and heretical no theologian is ignorant.

units.la: 52 Ad hæc, cum Pater, & Filius, & Spiritus sanctus, no modo æqualis, sed vnius plane & eiusdem sint potestatis, Maiestatis, autoritatis & gloriæ, cum etiam eadem prorsus diuinitatis plenitudo in tribus illis personis reperiatur, si potestatis, &c. v-nitas, æqualitas, aut κοινωνία vnam personam constitueret, ut hic vane fingit, non iam tres, sed vnam tantum hypostasin in Deo esse, cum impio Sabellio, fateri prorsus cogeremur.
units.tr: 52 Besides, since the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are not only equal but plainly one and the same in power, majesty, authority and glory, and since the very same fullness of divinity is found in those three persons, if unity, equality or communion of power and so on constituted one person, as this man vainly imagines, we would be forced to confess, with the impious Sabellius, that there is not three but only one hypostasis in God.

units.la: 53 Praeterea cum potestas Diuina & reliqua attributa omnia, in tribus illis diuinis personis vnum & idem omnino exi-stant, ex eodem illo principio aperte deduceretur, Patrem & Spiritum sanctum æque incarnatos ac passos esse atque Filiũ si quidem vnio facta sit in re toti trinitati ex æquo communi.
units.tr: 53 Furthermore, since divine power and all the other attributes exist altogether one and the same in those three divine persons, it would be openly deduced from that same principle that the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate and suffered equally with the Son, if indeed the union were made in something common equally to the whole Trinity.

units.la: 54 Quam absurditatem cum Sabellius effugere non poterat, hoc sibi sectæ no men promeruit, vt ipsius sectatores omnes Patripassiani appellarentur. Quamobrem cum hic etiam Autor suo commento in Sabellij se heresin precipitet, non vi demus, quo pacto Patripassiani nomen ef fugere queat.
units.tr: 54 Since Sabellius could not escape this absurdity, his sect earned this name: all its followers were called Patripassians. Therefore, since this author too, by his invention, plunges headlong into the heresy of Sabellius, we do not see how he can escape the name of Patripassian.

units.la: 55 Postremò, vnionem illam potestatis, Maiestatis, &c. hypostaticam neutiquam esse, in ipso Trinitatis mysterio clare conspicitur. Etenim tres illæ diuinæ Personæ in potestate quidem, Maiestate, & reliquis perfectionibus quàm maximè sunt vnitæ, totámque Deitatis plenitudinem habent, cum nihilominus inter se verè & personaliter sint manéntque distinctæ.
units.tr: 55 Lastly, that union of power, majesty and so on is by no means hypostatic is clearly seen in the very mystery of the Trinity. For those three divine persons are indeed most closely united in power, majesty and the other perfections, and possess the whole fullness of the Godhead, yet are nevertheless truly and personally distinct among themselves and remain so.

units.la: 56 Igitur sola potestatis, virtutis, aut Maiestatis communicatio, quæcunque tandem illa fit, hypostaticam vnionem efficere nulla ratione potest. Quod ex eo etiam aperte deducitur, quòd potestatis, virtutis, aut Maiestatis, in genere consideratæ, communicatio, ad id non sufficiat: quum potestas, virtus & Maiestas nihil minus quàm hypostasin signi-ficent.
units.tr: 56 Therefore the sole communication of power, virtue or majesty, whatever it finally be, can in no way effect a hypostatic union. This is also clearly deduced from the fact that the communication of power, virtue or majesty, considered in general, does not suffice for it, since power, virtue and majesty signify nothing less than hypostasis.

units.la: 57 Vnde in Ephesina Synodo Nestorius condemnatus est, quòd hac sola Maiestatis, honoris & potestatis seu virtutis communicatione duas Christi naturas vniret, duásque proinde personas, ac totidem filios in Christo constitueret. Verba porro Synodi sic habent: Si quis in vno Christo diuidit subsistentias post vnitionem, sola societate coniungens ea, quæ secundùm dignitatem est, vel etiam auctoritatem aut potestatem, & non magis conuentu, qui per vnitatem factus est, naturalem, anathema sit. In quinta etiam Synodo generali hæc ipsa Nestorij hæresis hisce verbis damnatur. Si quis dicit secundùm gratiam vel secundùm operationem vel secundùm dignitatem, vel secundùm æqualitatem honoris, vel secundùm auctoritatem aut relationem aut effectum aut virtutem, vnitionem Dei Verbi ad hominem factam esse, &c. anathema sit.
units.tr: 57 Hence in the Council of Ephesus Nestorius was condemned because by this sole communication of majesty, honour and power or virtue he united the two natures of Christ, and thereby constituted two persons and as many sons in Christ. The words of the Council run thus: "If anyone divides the subsistences in the one Christ after the union, joining them only by a fellowship of dignity, or also of authority or power, and not rather by a meeting that is natural through unity, let him be anathema." In the Fifth General Council also this very heresy of Nestorius is condemned in these words: "If anyone says that the union of the Word of God with man was made according to grace, or according to operation, or according to dignity, or according to equality of honour, or according to authority, or relation, or effect, or virtue, and so on, let him be anathema."

units.la: 58 Dubium iam ex his nulli esse potest, Schmidelinum insigne esse Nestorianum, cùm nullam aliâ Dei & hominis in Christo vnionē agnoscat, quàm eam, quę Maiestatis, authoritatis, potestatis, virtutis seu energiae communicatione, aut effusione efficitur: ut his ipsis verbis diserte cõsitetur. Neque imaginanda (inquit) aut fingenda est alia Dei in Christo, quam in creaturis reliquis omnibus, quo ad οὐσίαν, diuinitatis praesentia. Quae ut in creaturis ἐνέργεια discernitur, quod alia in aliis agat, & operetur, ita in Christum tota effunditur, ut iam extra ipsum nihil, sed in homine & per hominem Christum omnia in omnibus operetur.
units.tr: 58 It can now be beyond doubt that Schmidelin is a notorious Nestorian, since he acknowledges no union of God and man in Christ other than that which is effected by the communication of majesty, authority, power, virtue or energy. He states this plainly in these very words: "Nor must we imagine or invent any other presence of God in Christ than the presence of the divinity in all other creatures, as regards [οὐσίαν] essence. This presence, which in creatures is distinguished as [ἐνέργεια] energy, so that one thing acts and works in one thing and another in another, is poured out wholly into Christ, so that now nothing works outside him, but in the man and through the man Christ all things work in all things."

units.la: Atque haec est communicatio plenitudinis omnis deitatis, de qua idem Apostolus loquitur. In quo, inquit, sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae Dei abscondit. Et iterum: In ipso inhabitat omnis plenitudo diuinitatis corporaliter.
units.tr: "And this is the communication of the fullness of all deity, of which the same Apostle speaks: 'In him, he says, are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom of God.' And again: 'In him dwells all the fullness of the divinity bodily.'"

units.la: Hactenus ille, apertissime Nestorianus, nisi qp in eo hebetior & Nestorio imperitior videri potest, quod nesciat eam solam coniunctionem, ad illam προσωπικὴν ἕνωσιν efficiendam, non sufficere, id quod neutiquam ignorabat Nestorius.
units.tr: Thus far he, a most clear Nestorian, unless he may seem in this respect duller and less skilled than Nestorius, in that he does not know that this conjunction alone is not sufficient to produce that personal union, which Nestorius by no means failed to understand.

units.la: 59 Iudicent ergo aequi & boni omnes de hoc Nestoriano, & animaduertant quaeso, qua fronte audeat Maiestatem hominis Christi, non solum obscurare, verumetiam utriusque Christi naturae, quamplurimum derogare: Humanae quidem, quia sola virtutis seu potestatis, & nescio qua Maiestatis vnione, quam ipse fingit, eā cum Verbo coniungit. Diuinæ verò naturæ non minus detrahit, quia humanitatem οὐσία, potentia, gloria atque Maiestate, diuinitati hic ineptus censor exęquat. Tum vtrique naturę simul in hoc maximam vim irrogat & iniuriam, quòd eas earúmq. proprietates insulse permiscet, atque confundit.
units.tr: 59 Let all fair and good people, then, judge this Nestorian, and let them consider, I beg, with what brazenness he dares not only to obscure the majesty of the man Christ, but also greatly to derogate from each nature of Christ. He diminishes the human nature, because he joins it to the Word only by a union of power or virtue and by some majesty I know not what, which he himself invents. He detracts no less from the divine nature, because this foolish critic makes the humanity equal to the divinity in [οὐσία] essence, power, glory and majesty. Moreover, he inflicts the greatest violence and injury on both natures together, in that he foolishly mixes and confuses their properties.

units.la: 60 Grauius adhuc peccat & à sacrile gij crimine defendi nō potest, qui ad hęc sua perniciosa tantáque impietate refer-ta aliáque plura insana dogmata confirmanda, non veretur sacrę legis verba furari. Sic ab initio, vt aliis veritatis & antiquitatis ignaris facilius imponeret, quædam Vincentij Lyrinensis verba, suis pręfixit Thesib. Tum non minùs impudenter quàm arroganter ausus est polliceri eam se doctrinam repetiturum, fincereq. declaraturū, quam nobis Prophetæ, Apostoli, primitiuæ Ecclesiæ Patres, Martyres & Confessores tradiderūt. At in progressu nullum ex his omnib. suorum dogmatum profert comprobatorem cuius se patrocinio tueatur. Hoc demum est sincerā veritatis & Euangelij doctrinā vindicare.
units.tr: 60 He sins still more gravely, and cannot be defended from the crime of sacrilege, who, in order to confirm these pernicious and so impious opinions, and many other insane dogmas, does not hesitate to steal the words of holy law. At the outset, so that he might more easily deceive others ignorant of truth and antiquity, he prefixed to his Theses certain words of Vincent of Lérins. Then, no less shamelessly than arrogantly, he dared to promise that he would set forth and sincerely declare the doctrine which the prophets, apostles, the Fathers of the primitive Church, the martyrs and confessors handed down to us. Yet in the course of the work he brings forward none of them as a witness of all his dogmas under whose protection he may shelter himself. This, at last, is what it means to vindicate the sincere doctrine of truth and the Gospel.

units.la: 61 Quid multa? Si volumus noua huius Veteratoris impiaq. sigmata inter se aliquo pacto cohærere, illud etiā admitta mus oportet, vt veteres & olim damnatę hæreses, quamuis inter se maximè disiun-ctæ atque dissectæ, in orbem veluti postli-minio reuocentur & veluti ab ipsius Or-ci faucibus iterum resuscitentur.
units.tr: 61 What more is there to say? If we wish the new and impious blasphemies of this old deceiver to cohere together in any way, we must also admit that the ancient heresies, long since condemned, however widely separated and divided from one another, are recalled as if by a return from exile, and are raised up again, as it were, from the very jaws of Orcus.

units.la: 62 Etenim, vt manifestè cōuicimus, hic sectarius in Christo cum Monothelitis proprietates confundit: cū Eutychete na turas in vna essentia coniungit: cū Nesto-rio personas distinguit ac separat: cū Sa-bellio Patripassiano Patrem & Filium & Spiritum sanctum in persona vnit, totám que, vt sic dicamus, incarnat Trinitatem.
units.tr: 62 For, as we have clearly shown, this sectarian in Christ confuses the properties with the Monothelites; with Eutyches he joins the natures in one essence; with Nestorius he divides and separates the persons; with Sabellius the Patripassian he unites the Father, Son and Holy Spirit in one person, and, so to speak, incarnates the whole Trinity.

units.la: 63 Nec opus est vlla hîc noua censura aut condēnatione. Iudicarunt de hac cau sa celeberrimæ Synodi, & pronuntiarunt anathema his omnibus, qui veterum im-pietatum essent cum Schmidelino propa gatores aut sectatores.
units.tr: 63 No new censure or condemnation is needed here. The most celebrated Synods have judged this cause and pronounced anathema on all those who were propagators or followers of the ancient impieties together with Schmidelin.

units.la: 64 Nec potest hic Autor, vt omniū ha rum hæresium notam euadat, ad illud per fugium se recipere, quòd initio dixerit, se duas naturas personaliter in Christo vni-tas agnoscere, cùm postea illud ipsum suo modo interpretatus, damnatis illorū hærefiarcharum opinionibus aperte suffragetur. Neque enim satis est (vt Ephesina Synodus testatur) fidem voce duntaxat confiteri, nisi recte quoque eam interpreteris.
units.tr: 64 Nor can this author, to escape the mark of all these heresies, take refuge in the claim he made at the start, that he acknowledges two natures united in Christ personally, since afterwards, interpreting that very statement in his own way, he openly supports the opinions of those heresiarchs which have been condemned. For, as the Synod of Ephesus bears witness, it is not enough to confess the faith in words alone, unless you also interpret it rightly.

units.la: 65 Sed quid tandem ad impias & ab surdas has opiniones revocandas impulit Schmidelinum? Nō id sane, vt Christi hominis Maiestatem extolleret, sicut Thematum illius titulus pollicetur, sed vt Sacrosanctæ Eucharistiæ dignitatem & excellentiam, quoad eius fieri posset, obscurarét, omnésque Sectarios plurimum inter sese differentes atque diuisos, cõtra Christum Christiq. sponsam Ecclesiā Catholicam hac ratione vniret ac coarmaret.
units.tr: 65 But what, finally, drove Schmidelin to revive these impious and absurd opinions? Certainly not to exalt the majesty of the man Christ, as the title of his Theses promises, but to obscure, as far as he could, the dignity and excellence of the most holy Eucharist, and in this way to unite and arm all the sectaries, who differ and are divided greatly among themselves, against Christ and his bride, the Catholic Church.

units.la: 66 Huc vt peruenireт, viam putauit expeditissimam sibi fore, si contra communem Ecclesiæ Apostolicæ sensum probare posset, Christi humanitatem corporaliter vbique præsentem adesse. Ex hoc enim principio mox sequebatur, nihil singulare aut admirabile in hoc Eucharistiæ Sacramento accidere, quantū ad præsentiam corporis & sanguinis Christi attinet, quod non in ceteris itidem rebus omnibus & creaturis vsu veniret. O artem verè Satanicam, quæ postea nobis apertius rius detegenda erit atque refellenda.
units.tr: 66 To reach this goal, he thought it would be a very easy path for himself if he could prove, against the common sense of the Apostolic Church, that the humanity of Christ is bodily present everywhere. For from this principle it followed at once that nothing singular or admirable happens in this sacrament of the Eucharist, so far as the presence of the body and blood of Christ is concerned, which does not also happen in all other things and creatures. O truly Satanic art, which will later have to be exposed more openly and refuted.

units.la: 67 Nunc ordo postulat vt demon-stremus Christi humanitatem non esse vbique corporaliter præsentem quem-admodum hic Theologus præcipue con-uincere studet. Et hac quidem sola ratio-ne ductus.Cùm diuinitas (inquit) in vnita-tem personæ assumpserit hominem, cuius ra-tio & definitio est plenitudinis Dei commu-nicatio,in quo omnis Deitas corporaliter in-habitat: sequitur, ipsam quoque humanita-tem Christi vbique præsentem esse. Et iterū: Restat tertia Maiestatis ratio, qua sine corpo-ris extensione & diffusione,humanitas Chri-sti à Verbo ita perficitur,vt eadem Maiestate res præsentes habeat rebúsque præsens sit,quà diuinitas.Hæc Schmidelinus.
units.tr: 67 Now the order of the argument requires that we show that the humanity of Christ is not bodily present everywhere, as this theologian especially strives to prove. And he is led to this by this one reason alone: "Since the divinity (he says) has assumed the man into unity of person, whose nature and definition is the communication of the fullness of God, in whom all deity dwells bodily, it follows that the humanity of Christ is also present everywhere. And again: There remains a third reason of majesty, by which, without extension and diffusion of body, the humanity of Christ is so perfected by the Word that it has present things and is present to things with the same majesty as the divinity." Thus Schmidelin.

units.la: 68 Vbi primùm obserua quòd Vbi-quitarius iste,vt alibi,sic nunc etiam nul-lam Scripturæ authoritatè, nullũ ex pro-batis Patribus aut Synodis testimonium in re tanta cõprobanda producit, imò cõ tta luculentas Scripturæ, & Patrum sen-tentias vnica solius Lutheri Magistri sui autoritate,nescio quàm fideliter recitata, contétus,&vnica ratione humana fultus, causam agit atq.cõcludit.Ita qui maximè
units.tr: 68 Here first observe that this Ubiquitarian, as elsewhere, so now also produces no authority of Scripture and no testimony of approved Fathers or Synods to prove so great a matter. Instead, content with the single authority of Luther, his master, quoted I know not how faithfully, and supported by a single human reasoning, he pleads and concludes his case, though he uses the clear sayings of Scripture and of the Fathers. Thus those who most like to boast of Scripture and demand it from everyone often peddle their own dreams without Scripture.

units.la: Thesi.34. Scripturis gloriari solent, & ab omnibus illas exposcunt, sine Scripturis sua sæpe somnia venditant.
units.tr: Thesis 34. Those who most like to boast of Scripture, and demand it from everyone, often peddle their dreams without Scripture.

units.la: 69 Quòd si rationem ipsam velimus expendere, falsum reperiemus antecedēs quod assumit, in eo nimirum sensu, quo ipsemet superiùs illud explicauit. Nomine enim vnionis personalis & plénitudinis diuinitatis inhabitationis, nihil aliud intelligit, quàm totius diuinæ ἐνεργείας in Christum effusionem, aut diuinę potestatis, autoritatis, &c. cōmunicatione. Quam quidem sententiam erroneam esse multis ante argumentis comprobauimus. Deinde, vt antecedēs illi maximè cōcedamus: non hinc conficitur, humanitatem perin de atque diuinitatem Christi vbique adesse præsentem. Quandoquidem ex eo, q; duo Principes paris sint omnino Maiestatis, autoritatis & potestatis malè colligitur, sicubi alter eorum fuerit, ibidem statim alterum quoque cōstituendū esse.
units.tr: 69 If we wish to weigh the reasoning itself, we shall find the antecedent he assumes false, in the very sense in which he himself explained it above. For by the name of personal union and the indwelling of the fullness of deity he understands nothing other than the pouring out of the whole divine [ἐνεργείας] energy into Christ, or the communication of divine power, authority, and so on. We have already proved by many earlier arguments that this opinion is erroneous. Next, let us grant him his antecedent entirely: it does not follow from this that the humanity and divinity of Christ are present everywhere. For it is poorly concluded from the fact that two principles are wholly equal in majesty, authority and power that, wherever one of them is, the other must immediately be present there too.

units.la: 70 Sed nec ideo aliquid aliquo in loco οὐσιωδῶς existere cōuincitur, quòd in eo vel operari possit, vel re vera operetur, quod est, potentia esse in loco, vt Philosophi vocāt. Nā & solē certa quadā parte orbis sui cōtentū ac circunscriptū esse constat, qui tamen in toto hoc subluna-ri orbe operatur,ac proinde potentia sua ibidem adest, vbi secundum suam essen-tiam non esse, certissimum est. Sic ambi-guum non est,quin quilibet Princeps to-ti suo regno Potestate adsit,qui tamen se cundùm essentiam totum regnum neque occupat,neque occupare potest.
units.tr: 70 Nor is it proved that anything exists [οὐσιωδῶς] essentially in a place because it can act there, or really does act there, which is to be in a place by power, as the philosophers call it. For it is established that the sun is contained and circumscribed in a certain part of its orbit, and yet it works throughout this whole sublunary world, and therefore is present by its power where, according to its essence, it is certainly not. So there is no doubt that any prince is present with his power throughout his whole kingdom, and yet he does not, and cannot, occupy the whole kingdom according to his essence.

units.la: 71 Iam si spectemus veram hyposta-ticamChristi vnionem,quę multò maior est,quàm fictitia illa solius energiæ & po-testatis communicatio, neque sic etiam colligitur,humanitatem Christi in omni bus rebus corporaliter esse, vt omnes ve-rè docti norunt.Satis nanque est ad hypo staticam naturarum vnionem, si diuina humanæ suam communicauerit subsi-stentiam,ex quo id tantùm conficitur, a-liquo in loco humanitatem esse, in quo ipsa etiam adest diuinitas.
units.tr: 71 Now if we consider the true hypostatic union of Christ, which is much greater than that fictitious communication of energy and power alone, not even then does it follow that the humanity of Christ is bodily in all things, as all truly learned people know. For it is enough for the hypostatic union of the natures that the divine nature has communicated its subsistence to the human, from which it follows only this: that the humanity is in some place in which the divinity itself is also present.

units.la: 72 Sicut etiam ad hoc vt anima ra-tionalis corpori sit vnita,necesse non est, vt vbicunque sit anima,ibidem &corpus existat.Nam sic fieret,vt caput esset in pe de, & pes in capite, & in quauis alia cor-poris parte,cùm anima ipsa tota sit in to-to corpore,& tota in quauis parte ipsius.
units.tr: 72 Just as, for the rational soul to be united with the body, it is not necessary that wherever the soul is, the body also exists there. For then the head would be in the foot, and the foot in the head, and so in every other part of the body, since the soul is wholly in the whole body and wholly in each part of it.

units.la: 73 Quòd si hoc argumentationis genus hîc nequaquam procedit, cùm tamē anima & corpus non in hypostasi solum, sed etiam in natura sint vnita, multò minus in vnione duarum naturarum in Christo proceder, vbi sola vnio hypostatica reperitur. Rectè ergo & prudenter Aug.de Christi humanitate loquens, dixit: Non est consequens quod in Deo est, ita sit ubique vt Deus.
units.tr: 73 But if this kind of argument does not hold here, since soul and body are united not only in hypostasis but also in nature, it will hold much less for the union of the two natures in Christ, where only the hypostatic union is found. Rightly and wisely, then, Augustine, speaking of the humanity of Christ, said: "What is in God does not follow in such a way that it is everywhere as God is everywhere."

units.la: 74 Hæc sufficere poterant, præsertim cordato lectori, ad plane refellēdam huius noui Vbiquitarij & sectarij argumentationem, siue assumptum, siue illationem expendas. Nam & antecedens aperte falsum, & consecutionem ineptam esse satis ostendimus. Vt tamen veritas magis elucescat, & omnis dubitandi occasio submoueatur, apertis Scripturæ sanctorumque Patrum testimoniis, perspicuis etiam rationibus, ex fidei fundamentis deductis, palàm faciemus, Christum secundum assumptam carnem non ubique præsentem adesse, eádem, qua Diuinitatem, Maiestate, neq. præsentem aliquando fuisse.
units.tr: 74 These points might have sufficed, especially for a discerning reader, to refute thoroughly the argument of this new Ubiquitarian and sectarian, whether one weighs its assumption or its inference. For we have already shown that the antecedent is plainly false and the consequence absurd. But so that the truth may shine more clearly and every occasion for doubt be removed, we will make it plain, by the clear testimonies of Scripture and the holy Fathers, and by plain arguments drawn from the foundations of faith, that Christ according to his assumed flesh is not present everywhere with the same majesty as his divinity, nor was he ever so present.

units.la: 75 Distinctionem tamen, ob varias quæ hîc se offerunt quæstiones, præmittemus, ne dum vnum errorem extremum mum confutamus, alterum illi oppositū confirmare videamur.Siquidem alia quę stio est, An ex eo quòd humanitas Verbo vnita est, vbique corporaliter sit præsens eadem Maiestate, qua ipsa diuinitas. Alia verò, An ea ipsa Christi natura per Dei omnipotentiam in pluribus locis, vel vbique locorum possit existere. Alia denique, An Christi humanitas talem ali quam potestatem sit sortita, qua se ipsam vel vbique, vel in pluribus locis valeat collocare.
units.tr: 75 We will, however, first set out a distinction, because of the various questions that arise here, lest while we refute one extreme error we seem to confirm the opposite one. For one question is whether, from the fact that the humanity is united to the Word, it is bodily present everywhere with the same majesty as the divinity itself. Another is whether that same nature of Christ can, by the omnipotence of God, exist in many places, or in all places. A third is whether the humanity of Christ has been endowed with such a power that it can place itself either everywhere or in many places.

units.la: 76 Hîc autē præcipuè contendimus, ex hypostatica illa naturarum vnione nequaquam consequi, Christi humanitatem aut vbique, aut in multis simul locis existere: Illud enim constanter tuemur atque defendimus, humanam Christi naturam nec semper fuisse, nec nunc quoq. corporaliter vllo pacto vbique esse præsentem, neque eiusmodi aliquam in ea facultatem esse, qua se vbiq.siitere valeat.
units.tr: 76 Here we chiefly contend that it does not at all follow from that hypostatic union of the natures that the humanity of Christ exists either everywhere or in many places at once. For we steadfastly maintain and defend this: that the human nature of Christ was neither always everywhere, nor is it now bodily present everywhere in any way, nor does it have any such faculty by which it could be everywhere.

units.la: 77 Atque rem ita habere, vel hinc facilè sit colligere: quòd caro assumpta, propter hypostaticam cum Verbo vnionē, naturales suas proprietates &affectiones neutiquā amiserit, nec proprietatem aliquā diuinam acquisiuerit, vt suprà latè commonstrauimus. Certo autem loco circumscribi ac definiri, inter naturales corporis affectiones recensetur: sicut & poteitas ad existendum vbique ad diuinas pertinet proprietates. Vnde Damascenus, post illam vnionem, incircumscriptum, id est, diuinitatem, mansisse incircumscriptum: & circumscriptum, id est, humanitatem, circumscriptum mansisse asserit. Non est enim, inquit, coextensa caro cum eius incircumscripta diuinitate. Idem ferè Gregorius Nazianzenus & alij Patres de eadem Christi humanitate docent.
units.tr: 77 That this is so may easily be gathered from the following. The assumed flesh, because of the hypostatic union with the Word, has by no means lost its natural properties and affections, nor has it acquired any divine property, as we have shown at length above. But to be circumscribed and confined to a certain place is counted among the natural affections of a body, just as the power of existing everywhere belongs to the divine properties. Hence Damascene asserts that after that union the uncircumscribed, that is the divinity, remained uncircumscribed, and the circumscribed, that is the humanity, remained circumscribed. For, he says, the flesh is not coextensive with its uncircumscribed divinity. Gregory Nazianzen and other Fathers teach much the same about the same humanity of Christ.

units.la: 78 Huc accedit, quòd potentia ad existendum, & re vera existere vbique, soli Deo ita est proprium, vt nulli alteri attribuatur. Sola namque diuinitas, vt Damasceni verbis vtamur, est infinita, incircumscripta, incomprehensibilis: cætera vero certo quodam loco definiuntur. Hinc Alcuinus dixit, Solius diuinitatis fuit loco non contineri. Et Fulgentius: Hæc est Trinitas vnus Deus, qui sicut potuit solus vniuersa condere, sic potest omnia solus implere.
units.tr: 78 Moreover, the power to exist everywhere, and actually to exist everywhere, is so proper to God alone that it is attributed to no other. For divinity alone, to use Damascene's words, is infinite, uncircumscribed and incomprehensible; all other things are defined by a certain place. Hence Alcuin said: "It belongs to divinity alone not to be contained in a place." And Fulgentius: "This is the Trinity, one God, who, as he alone could create all things, so he alone can fill all things."

units.la: 79 Hoc autem omnibus vsque adeo certum semper fuit atque persuasum, vt Ambro

units.la: Ambrosius, tanquam firmissimo argu-mento, Spiritus sancti diuinitatem contra Eunomium probare volens, in hæc verba loquatur: Cùm omnis creatura certis naturæ suæ sit circumscripta limitibus, quomodo quis audeat Spiritumsanctum creaturam appellare? qui non habet circumscriptam determinatámque virtutem, qui & in omnibus & vbique semper est: quod vtique diuinitatis & dominationis est proprium. Hæc ille. Et Cassiod. super illa verba: Quo ibo à Spiritu tuo, &c. Cùm tali prædicatione vbique Spiritum sanctum esse noscamus, dubium nō est, Spiritum sanctum coæternum & coæqualem Patri & Filio reperiri. Hieron. Ex quo intelligimus Deum esse, qui totus vbique sit. Si ergo Christi humanitas non est circumscripta, sed vbique semper omnibus rebus creatis adest, vt hic subiiquista docet, non est creatura sed Deus, vt colligunt Ambrosius, Hieron. & Cassiodorus, quia solus Deus vbique est.
units.tr: Ambrose, as a most firm argument, wishing to prove against Eunomius the divinity of the Holy Spirit, speaks in these words: "Since every creature is bounded by the fixed limits of its nature, how can anyone dare to call the Holy Spirit a creature? He does not have a bounded and determined power; he is in all things and everywhere always, which surely belongs to divinity and lordship." Thus he. And Cassiodorus, on the words "Whither shall I go from your Spirit?" etc.: since we know the Holy Spirit to be everywhere by such a predication, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit is found to be co-eternal and co-equal with the Father and the Son. Jerome: "From this we understand that God is he who is wholly everywhere." If therefore the humanity of Christ is not circumscribed, but is always everywhere present to all created things, as the opponent here teaches, it is not a creature but God, as Ambrose, Jerome and Cassiodorus infer, because only God is everywhere.

units.la: 8o Adhæc, si Christus Dominus secundum humanitatem, propter hypostaticam naturarum vnionem, in omnibus rebus exisseret, vt ipse Deus, fieret sanè vt primo conceptionis suæ momento, vbique fuisset,in cœlo, in terra, in mari,in inferno:si quidem ab eo tempore humanitas diuinitati personaliter vnita est.
units.tr: 80 Moreover, if Christ the Lord according to his humanity, because of the hypostatic union of the natures, existed in all things as God himself does, it would surely follow that from the first moment of his conception he was everywhere: in heaven, on earth, in the sea, in hell. For from that time the humanity has been personally united with the divinity.

units.la: 81 Sed aliter scriptura nos docet, dum affirmat,Christum super terram & mare ambulasse,totam Galilæam circumiuisse, ex vno loco in alium subinde commigrasse, & ianuis clausis ad discipulos introiisse, nec sallsum esse potest illud, Gaudete propter vos quia non eram ibi:item, sur-rexit,non est hîc.Non enim vere mouetur aut motu defatigari potest,aut ab aliquo loco abesse, quod omnem occupat locum quocunque demum id modo fiat. Vnde Athanasius sic ait: Eius est ire & venire qui aliquibus locorum terminis circumscribitur, & eum in quo erat deserens locum, vt ad eum vbi non erat veniat. Ambrosius quoque de eadem Christi humanitate loquens,in hæc verba docet: Nec enim Deus de loco ad locum transit, quia vbique semper est,vt homo est qui vadit, ipse est qui venit. Et Gregor. Nyssenus Qui dicit, Vado,localem discessum significat:& paucis interiectis: Quod autem per omnia graditur & in omnib. existit & omnia continet, non habet quò discedat eò quod à diuina plenitudine nihil est vacans. Et S. Maximus: In sanctis Euange. de Domino scriptum est: Postridie voluit Iesus ire in Galilæam. Ire nimirum voluit quatenus ibi non erat: Non erat autem humanitate, diuinitate enim vbique est. Quid ad dilucida hæc Scripturæ & Patrum testimonia respondebit Schmidelinus? nisi forte cum Manichæo dicat & sentiat omnes motus & operationes Christi non veras, sed phantasticas fuisse.
units.tr: 81 But Scripture teaches us otherwise, affirming that Christ walked upon the land and the sea, went round all Galilee, moved from one place to another from time to time, and entered to his disciples with the doors shut. Nor can that be false: "Rejoice, because I was not there," and "He is risen, he is not here." For what truly moves, or can be wearied by motion, or is absent from some place, does not fill every place, however that may be done. Hence Athanasius says: "It belongs to one who is circumscribed by certain limits of place to go and come, leaving the place where he was in order to come to where he was not." Ambrose also, speaking of the same humanity of Christ, teaches in these words: "For God does not pass from place to place, since he is always everywhere; but it is as man that he goes, and it is he who comes." And Gregory of Nyssa: "He who says 'I go' signifies a local departure." And a few lines later: "But what goes through all things, exists in all, and contains all, has nowhere to depart to, since nothing is empty of the divine fullness." And St. Maximus: "In the holy Gospels it is written of the Lord: 'On the next day Jesus wished to go into Galilee.' He wished to go, of course, insofar as he was not there. But he was not there in his humanity; for in his divinity he is everywhere." What will Schmidelin answer to these clear testimonies of Scripture and the Fathers? Unless perhaps, with the Manichaean, he says and thinks that all the motions and operations of Christ were not real but phantasms.

units.la: 82. Adde, quòd si ab eo tempore, quo Deus incarnatus est, eius humanitas vbique exisseret, aperte cõsequeretur, illum priusquam ex matre Virgine nasceretur, extra maternum vterum corporaliter fuisse: & postquam in lucem æditus fuit, in vtero nihilominus sicut ante erat remansisse, & ex vtero proinde materno exiuisse nunquam. Id autem constat absurdum esse, & veræ natiuitatis rationi planè contrarium.
units.tr: 82 Add that if from the time God was incarnate his humanity existed everywhere, it would clearly follow that before he was born of the Virgin Mother he was bodily outside the maternal womb; and after he was brought into the light he would nevertheless have remained in the womb as before, and never have come forth from the maternal womb. But this is agreed to be absurd and plainly contrary to the nature of true birth.

units.la: 83. Iam si Christus vbique præsens corpore aderat, ergo vbique loquebatur, vbique patiebatur, siquidé vnum & idem os, eadem lingua, idem corpus nō poterat in vno, nec in diuersis locis actiones illas exercere, & simul ab iisdem vacare.
units.tr: 83 Now if Christ was present everywhere in body, then he was everywhere speaking and everywhere suffering. For one and the same mouth, the same tongue and the same body could not exercise those actions in one place and in different places, and at the same time be free from the same things.

units.la: 84. Denique. Scriptura & omnia Fidei Symbola cõclamant, Christũ post mortẽ ad inferos descendisse, & post suam refur rectionem ad cœlos ascendisse, non qui- dem secundùm diuinitatem, sed secun- dùm humanitatem,secundùm quā Chri- stum tunc nondum in cœlis fuisse Patres omnes simpliciter & absque distinctione vlla contestantur. Vnde sic ait Cypria- nus: Ascendit ergo ad cœlos,non vbi Ver bum Dei antea non fuerat,quippe qui e- rat semper in cœlis,& manebat in Patre: sed vbi Verbum caro factum non sede- bat.Et Grego.Cùm Christus per humani tatem ascenderet in cœlum,per diuinita- tem terram pariter cōtinebat & cœlum.
units.tr: 84 Finally, Scripture and all the creeds proclaim that Christ descended to the dead after his death, and after his resurrection ascended into heaven, not indeed according to his divinity but according to his humanity. The Fathers all testify, simply and without any distinction, that according to this humanity Christ was not yet in heaven. Hence Cyprian says: "He ascended therefore to heaven, not where the Word of God had not been before, since he was always in heaven and remained in the Father, but where the Word made flesh had not sat." And Gregory: "When Christ ascended into heaven according to his humanity, by his divinity he equally held both earth and heaven."

units.la: 85 Quare vniuersus Patrum chorus, locum illum Ioan. 3. Nemo ascendit in cœlum,nisi qui descendit de cœlo, Filius hominis,qui est in cœlo:non aliter expo nit, quàm Filium hominis ratione deita- tis, propter idiomatum in persona com- municationem, tum temporis in cœlis fuisse,cùm adhuc in terris nobiscum ver- saretur: quemadmodum etiam propter eandem ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνίαν, Deus passus, mortuus & sepultus rectè dicitur. Hinc Augustinus:Secundùm hominem in ter- ra erat,non in cœlo vbi nunc est,quando dicebat:Nemo ascendit in cœlum:quam uis secundum quòd Filius Dei erat, esset in cœlo, secundum verò quòd Filius ho- minis erat,adhuc esset in terra,nondum- que ascendit in cælum.EtChrysostomus: Filium hominis hoc loco non carnem, sed à maiori substantia totum se ipsum, vt sic dicam,intelligit. Hic namq. ei mos est,vt nunc à diuinitate, nunc ab huma- nitate totum nuncupet. In eundem quo que sensum Beda loquitur: Non, inquit, caro Christi descendit de cœlo,neque an te tempus ascensionis erat in cœlo, nisi quia vna Christi persona est in duabus e- xistens naturis. Damascenus etiam eisdē consentit,dicens: Propter vnitatem per- sonæ Filius hominis ante passionem se in cœlis esse confessus est.Et Fulgentius: Vt immensitatem diuinitatis suæ in terra po situs demonstraret, & secundùm homi- nem, quem susceperat, in terra positus, secundùm Deum,quòd semper erat,pre- sentem se etiam cœlo doceret,ait:Nemo ascendit in cœlum,&c. Non quia huma- na Christi substantia vbique fuisset dissu- sa,sed quoniam vnus idémque Dei Filius atque hominis filius, verus Deus ex Pa- tre,sicut homo verus ex homine, licet se cundùm veram humanitatem suam localiter tunc esseт in terra, secundùm diuinitatem tamen (quæ loco nullatenus continetur) cœlum totus impleret & terram. Hæc ille. Idem Theophylactus & reliqui tam Græci quàm Latini interpretes sentiunt.
units.tr: 85 Therefore the whole company of the Fathers explains that passage in John 3, "No one has ascended into heaven, except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven," in no other way than this: the Son of man, in respect of his deity, by reason of the communication of properties in the one person, was in heaven at the time when he was still living with us on earth. In the same way, by that communication of properties (ἰδιωμάτων κοινωνίαν [idiōmatōn koinōnian]), God is rightly said to have suffered, died and been buried. Hence Augustine: "According to the man he was on earth, not in heaven where he now is, when he said, 'No one has ascended into heaven.' Although, in so far as he was the Son of God, he was in heaven, yet in so far as he was the Son of man he was still on earth, and had not yet ascended into heaven." And Chrysostom: "By the Son of man in this place he understands not the flesh but the whole person from the greater substance, so to speak. For it is his custom to name the whole now from the divinity, now from the humanity." Bede speaks to the same sense: "The flesh of Christ, he says, did not descend from heaven, nor at the time of the ascension was it then in heaven, except that the one person of Christ exists in two natures." Damascene also agrees, saying: "On account of the unity of the person, the Son of man confessed that before the passion he was in heaven." And Fulgentius: "That he might show the immensity of his divinity while placed on earth, and teach that, according to the man he had taken, placed on earth, but according to God, which he always was, he is present also in heaven, he says, 'No one has ascended into heaven,' etc. Not because the human substance of Christ was spread everywhere, but because one and the same Son of God and son of man, true God of the Father and true man of man, although according to his true humanity he was then locally on earth, nevertheless according to his divinity (which is in no way contained by place) wholly filled heaven and earth." Thus he. Theophylact and the rest, both Greek and Latin interpreters, hold the same view.

units.la: 86 Hìc iam est operæ precium memi-nisse lectorem, quòd Schmidelinus ipse recte & verè, Lyrinensis personam induens, præfatur, horrendum peccatum esse, si quis noui dogmatis autor existat vel propagator, cuius Christum, Apostolos & Prophetas non habet autores. Quanto igitur est hoc crimen & piaculum execrabilius ô Schmideline censendum? quòd tu cum paucis nouum & tot seculis inauditum dogma contra Christum, Prophetas, Apostolos & omnes Doctores inuenis atque propagas? nempe Christum non solùm ratione diuinitatis, sed etiam ratione humanæ naturæ corporaliter vbique præsentem adesse: cùm hactenus Orthodoxi omnes vnanimi consensu, vnum hoc ratione solius diuinitatis Christo attribuendum esse docuerint, expresseque dixerint eum secundum humanitatem non esse vbique præsentem.
units.tr: 86 Here it is worth reminding the reader that Schmidelin himself rightly and truly, putting on the character of the Lerinensian, declares that it is a horrible sin if anyone should become the author or propagator of a new doctrine whose authors are not Christ, the Apostles and the Prophets. How much more execrable and sinful, then, must this crime be judged, O Schmidelin, when you, with a few others, devise and propagate a new doctrine, unheard of for so many centuries, against Christ, the Prophets, the Apostles and all the teachers? For you hold that Christ is present everywhere bodily, not only in respect of his divinity but also in respect of his human nature; whereas hitherto all the Orthodox, with unanimous consent, have taught that this is to be attributed to Christ by reason of the divinity alone, and have expressly said that he is not present everywhere according to his humanity.

units.la: 87 Verùm vt nonnulla Scripturæ loea à nobis allata, & iuxta sanctorum Patrum sensum explicata, peruertat, forsan ad illam triplicis distinctionis, quam construxit, arcem, cōfugiet. Vult enim vnius eiusdémque corporis Christi triplicem esse considerationem, vnam Physicam, qua ipsum naturalibus proprietatibus & affectionibus subiectum fuit, quod pati- bile, inquit, appellamus, & eo modo non vbique præsens esse fatetur. Alteram, qua corpus Christi iam est & dicitur impati- bile, ratione gloriæ, sed ne hoc quidem modo vbique illud existere asseuerat, sed in cœlo duntaxat. Tertiam Maiestatis, qua corpus in diuinitatis consortium assumptum, in pari gloria est, & Maiestate cum Verbo, à quo in vnitatem personæ assumptum est, & hac ratione omnibus rebus eadem Maiestate, qua diuinitatem, corpus Christi præsens adesse decernit.
units.tr: 87 But if he should pervert some of the passages of Scripture we have cited and explained according to the sense of the holy Fathers, perhaps he will flee to that citadel of the threefold distinction which he has built. For he wants there to be a threefold consideration of the one and the same body of Christ: first, the physical, by which it was subject to natural properties and affections, which we call passible, and in this way he admits that it is not present everywhere; second, that by which the body of Christ now is, and is called, impassible by reason of its glory, but not even in this way does he assert that it exists everywhere, only in heaven; third, that of majesty, by which the body, taken up into fellowship with the divinity, is in equal glory and majesty with the Word, by which it was assumed into unity of person, and in this way he decrees that the body of Christ is present to all things with the same majesty by which the divinity is present.

units.la: 88 At incassum laborat noster Vbiquitarius, in hac noua distinctione fabricanda, siquidem ea cōsistere non potest, cùm illam Maiestatis vnionem, vnde suam illam tertiã cōsiderationem deducere conatur, quò aperta sacrę Scripturæ testimonia facilius deprauet atq. eludat, satis perspicuè iam ante ostenderimus, falsam & ineptam esse: Patribus verò tam recentioribus, quàm vetustioribus hactenus incognitam prorsus & inauditam esse. Atqui in rebus tanti momenti maximèque ad fidem pertinentibus, nulli fas sit novas pro arbitratu suo distinctiones fingere, aut sacram Scripturam, ut beati Clementis verbis utamur, secundum proprij ingenij intelligentiam legere aut docere, sed ex Patrum traditione. Etenim non pauca verba passim in Scripturis occurrunt, quæ trahi possunt ad eum sensum, quem sibi unusquisque sponte præsumpsit. Sic Clemens. Imò, ut ait Cyrillus & experientia ipsa aperte commonstrat, Hæretici omnes de Scripturis diuinitus inspiratis, erroris sui colligunt occasiones, & ea, quæ à Spiritu sancto dicta sunt, sua malitia corrumpunt.
units.tr: 88 But our Ubiquitarian labours in vain in fashioning this new distinction, since it cannot stand. For the union of majesty from which he tries to derive that third consideration, so that he may more easily distort and mock the clear testimonies of holy Scripture, we have already shown sufficiently clearly to be false and absurd, and entirely unknown and unheard of to the Fathers, both more recent and more ancient. But in matters of such great moment, and especially those pertaining to faith, it is not right for anyone to invent new distinctions at his own pleasure, or to read or teach Holy Scripture, to use the words of blessed Clement, "according to the understanding of his own wit," but according to the tradition of the Fathers. For not a few words occur here and there in the Scriptures which can be drawn to that sense which each person has presumed of his own accord. Thus Clement. Indeed, as Cyril says, and experience itself openly shows, all heretics gather occasions of their error from the Scriptures inspired by God, and by their malice corrupt what the Holy Spirit has said.

units.la: 89 Ad rem redeamus. Si ex vnione illa hypostatica Christus Dominus hoc est consecutus, ut rebus omnibus secundum humanitatem præsens adesset, ergo priusquam in vltima illa cœna Eucharistiam confecisset, corpus & sanguis ipsius in pane & vino præsentia continebantur, ut nunc in Sacramento Eucharistiæ conticontinentur: cùm panis & vinum ante verba cœnæ prolata, res quædam essent. Quocirca secundum huius Vbiquistæ sententiam, qui corpus & sanguinē Christi in Sacramento Eucharistiæ cum substantia panis & vini simul esse confingit; corpus & sanguis Christi, non aliter nūc in Eucharistia essent, quàm fuissent, etiāsi verba cœnæ Dominicæ nunquam à Christo essent pronunciata.
units.tr: 89 Let us return to the matter. If Christ the Lord obtained, from that hypostatic union, this, that he should be present to all things according to his humanity, then before he instituted the Eucharist at that last supper, his body and blood would already have been present and contained in the bread and wine, as they are now contained in the sacrament of the Eucharist, since the bread and wine, before the words of the supper were spoken, were already something. Wherefore, according to the opinion of this Ubiquitist, who fancies that the body and blood of Christ are present in the sacrament of the Eucharist together with the substance of bread and wine, the body and blood of Christ would be in the Eucharist now no differently than they were, even if the words of the Lord's Supper had never been pronounced by Christ.

units.la: 90 Id autem quis vnquam dicere vel cogitare ausus fuit præter hunc Vbiquistam? qui Lutherum tot sectarum Antistitem & Magistrum secutus, vt ipse testatur, veritus non est, tantam & tam inusitatam blasphemiam, contra vniuersam Ecclesiæ Catholicæ traditionem effutire. Et gloriatur adhuc, in illo suo Vbiquitatis commeto Lutherum non parui pendendum robur sententiæ suæ posuisse, eundemque constanter affirmasse, vel ea sola Vbiquitate, veram corporis & sanguinis Christi præsentiam asseri & confirmari posse, si maximè verba cœnæ nunquam à Christo dicta essent.
units.tr: 90 But who has ever dared to say or think this, except this Ubiquitist? He, following Luther, the chief and teacher of so many sects, as he himself testifies, has not been afraid to utter so great and so unusual a blasphemy against the whole tradition of the Catholic Church. And he still boasts that in his Ubiquity commentary Luther placed no small strength for his opinion, and that Luther constantly affirmed that by this Ubiquity alone the true presence of the body and blood of Christ can be asserted and confirmed, even if the words of the supper had never been spoken by Christ.

units.la: 91 Quid mirum verò si nouator iste nihil ibi absurditatis animaduerterit, qui non modò in pane & vino, verumetiam in hordeo & fœno & quibuslibet rebus, licet vilissimis (quod pudor est referre) eodem modo corpus & sanguinem Christi adesse, sicut in Sacramento Eucharistiæ comminiscitur. Verùm facessat impictas, non vt fœnum vel hordeum, iumentorum pabulum, pij omnes habent Eucharistiam, quam vt panem viuum, qui de cœlo descendit, Angelorum cibū, diuinis honoribus cum sancta Ecclesia summo iure prosequuntur.
units.tr: 91 What wonder, then, if this innovator noticed no absurdity there, he who imagines that the body and blood of Christ are present in the same way not only in bread and wine, but also in barley and hay and whatever things, however worthless (it is shameful to report it), as he devises for the sacrament of the Eucharist. But let such impieties go away. Not as hay or barley, the fodder of beasts, do all the godly regard the Eucharist, but as the living bread which came down from heaven, the food of angels, which all the pious, with holy Church, rightly honour with divine worship in the highest degree.

units.la: 92 Tandem vtcunque imaginetur, & somniando sensa sua interpretetur, tueri tamen nulla ratione potest, corpus Christi, & vbique corporaliter præsens adesse, & vero Physicóque ac corporeo motu moueri, cùm id tantùm corporeo motu ferri agitarique dicatur, quod ex vno loco transit in alium, vbi prius non erat corporaliter.
units.tr: 92 Finally, however he imagines it, and interprets his own feelings by dreaming, he can by no reasoning defend that the body of Christ is bodily present everywhere and is moved by a true, physical and corporeal motion. For only that is said to be carried and moved by corporeal motion which passes from one place to another, where previously it was not bodily.

units.la: 93 Sed nec vllo etiam modo fieri potest, vt idem Christi corpus in vno eodémque loco circumscriptum fit & incir cumscriptum, definitū & indefinitū, visibile & inuisibile, patibile & impatibile, quod tamen iste Neotheologus, modò sibi constet, fateri cogitur.
units.tr: 93 But it cannot by any means come about that the same body of Christ should be both circumscribed and uncircumscribed in one and the same place, both defined and undefined, visible and invisible, passible and impassible; yet this New Theologian, if he is to be consistent with himself, is compelled to confess it.

units.la: 94 Adhæc ne fingi quidem, animóve conciconcipi potest, corpus Dominicum ante Christum passum in pari gloria & Maiestate cum Verbo vbique fuisse, & nihilominus pati & mori potuisse. Quomodo enim id, quod dolori, passioni, morti, caeterisque humanis miseriis obnoxium est, eadem cum Verbo, gloria & Maiestate præditum esse, aut dici queat?
units.tr: 94 Moreover, it cannot even be imagined or conceived in the mind that the Lord's body, before Christ suffered, was everywhere in the same glory and majesty as the Word, and yet could suffer and die. For how can that which is subject to pain, suffering, death and the other human miseries be said to be endowed with the same glory and majesty as the Word?

units.la: 95 Quòd si dixeris, ante resurrectionem corpus Christi non fuisse in omnibus rebus eadem Maiestate & gloria, qua Verbum; consequens est, ante resurrectionem corpus Christi, non fuisse cum diuinitate hypostaticôs vnitû, si quidem, vt tu somnias, in gloriæ & Maiestatis communicatione vnio hypostatica cósistit. Alterum itaque Schmideline ex duobus asseras oportet; aut corpus Christi ante passionem æquali gloria & Maiestate cum Verbo præditum fuisse, quod alicubi haud obscurè doces, aut ipsum ante resurrectionem cum Verbo non fuisse vnitum hypostaticôs: vtrumque autem impium est & hæreticum.
units.tr: 95 But if you say that before the resurrection the body of Christ did not have the same majesty and glory in all things as the Word, it follows that before the resurrection the body of Christ was not hypostatically united with the divinity, since, as you dream, the hypostatic union consists in the communication of glory and majesty. So, Schmidelin, you must assert one of two things: either that the body of Christ before the passion had the same glory and majesty as the Word, which you teach quite openly in places, or that before the resurrection it was not hypostatically united with the Word. Both are impious and heretical.

units.la: 96 Quocirca qui asserit cum isto Vbiquitario ac pertinaciter defendit, corpus Christi à conceptionis suæ tempore; vbique, hoc est, in cœlis, in terra, & in inferioribus terræ partibus, eadem Maiestate & gloria, qua diuinitatem, corporaliter vbique semper præsens fuisse, is reuera negat Christum secundùm humanam naturam nouem mensibus in materno vtero fuisse conclusum, & ex eodem in hanc lucem editum, negat eum passum, in crucem sublatum, mortuum, sepultum iterúmque ex sepulchro suscitatum, negat eundem ipsum ad inferos descendisse, & inde reuersum ad cœlos ascendisse, negat demum ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos tandem aliquando rediturum.
units.tr: 96 Therefore whoever asserts with this Ubiquitarian, and stubbornly defends, that the body of Christ, from the time of its conception, has been everywhere present bodily, that is, in the heavens, on the earth, and in the lower parts of the earth, with the same majesty and glory as the divinity, in fact denies that Christ according to his human nature was enclosed in the mother's womb for nine months and born into this light from it; denies that he suffered, was lifted up on the cross, died, was buried, and was raised again from the tomb; denies that he himself descended to the dead and, returning from there, ascended to the heavens; and finally denies that he will at last return to judge the living and the dead.

units.la: 97 Nos igitur cum Ephesino Concilio Christum, vt Deum, omnia replere & repleuisse dicimus, etiam cum adhuc paruulus esset. Nam quod diuinum est, sine quantitate & mole esse agnoscitur. At secundùm humanitatem Christum vbique esse vel fuisse, cum toto sanctorum Patrum ordine pernegamus.
units.tr: 97 We, then, with the Council of Ephesus, say that Christ, as God, fills and has filled all things, even when he was still a little child. For what is divine is recognised to be without quantity and bulk. But we deny, along with the whole order of the holy Fathers, that Christ is or was everywhere according to his humanity.

units.la: 98 Nec ideo tamen quòd Christum secundùm corpus vbique esse inficiamur consequens est, eum facta nostra, nostrásque cogitationes ignorare, aut secundùm humanitatem assumptam apud Deum & Patrem pro nobis nō intercedere, aut nullam rerum nostrarum curam gerere. Quin imò licet absens corpore sit, ita tamen perfectè in sua diuinitate, quę nusquā deest nostra omnia nouit ac perscrutatur, vt nihil eum latere queat, nec secus a pro nobis interpellat, nostràqueguber-nat & b quæ ad salutem nostram faciunt, procurat & operatur, ac si corpore præ-sens adesset.
units.tr: 98 Yet it does not follow, because we deny that Christ is everywhere according to his body, that he is ignorant of our deeds and our thoughts, or that he does not intercede for us with God the Father according to the humanity he assumed, or that he takes no care of our affairs. Indeed, although he is absent in body, he nevertheless knows and searches out all our affairs so perfectly in his divinity, which is nowhere absent, that nothing can escape him; and a he intercedes for us, and b governs our affairs, and brings about and effects what pertains to our salvation, just as if he were present in body.

units.la: 99 c Sed nec ipse solus rerum huma-narum, tametsi absens corpore sit, cura tangitur, verumetiam Sanéti & Beati omnes ad paternam hæreditatem iam admissi, pro nobis intercedunt, quicquid veteres & noui Vigilantiani obstrepant, résq. nostras multo melius ac fœlicius procurant, quàm si corpore eos præsentes habe-remus.
units.tr: 99 c But it is not only he himself, although absent in body, who is concerned with human affairs; all the saints and the blessed, already admitted to the paternal inheritance, also intercede for us, whatever the old and new Vigilantians may clamour, and they look after our affairs far better and more happily than if we had them present in body.

units.la: 100 Vbi nobis prætereundum nō est quod alicubi Schmidelinus ita loquitur. Humanitas Christi eadem Maiestate res præsentes habet; rebúsque præsens est, qua Diuinitas, et si alio modo fiat in Diuinita-te, quàm in humanitate, quia humani-tas manet creatura. Hæc ille. Qui cauto silentio tegit, quisnam ille modus esset, videbat enim Deum non aliter vbique præsentem existe re, quàm illimitatum,
units.tr: 100 Here we must not pass over what Schmidelin says somewhere: "The humanity of Christ has present things under the same majesty, and is present to things as the divinity is, although in a different way in the divinity than in the humanity, because the humanity remains a creature." So he says. He conceals with a cautious silence what that mode would be. For he saw that God is present everywhere in no other way than as unlimited, without circumscription, whole in the whole world and whole in each of its parts; and by this same mode he had earlier asserted that the humanity is present everywhere. From his principles it is therefore rightly concluded that the humanity is present to all things in no other way than the divinity is.

units.la: a Epist.ad Celi. Grego.1.Hō. Mar.16. Maxim.difp. cum Pyrrho. Beda Ioan.3. Theoph.Ioa. Cassio.Psa. 138. Euth.Rup. Ioan.3. Alcuin.lib.3 de Trini.c.13. Ansel.Ephe. 4. Damasc.li.1 c.17.&3.e.3. Russi.in suo Symbolo. Bern.Ser.18. 19. Fulgenti.lib. de immensita te Filii Dei &c. Pet.Lombar. 3.libro d.22 a Rom.8, b Hebr.7. c Cōc.Turō. 1.c.13.in rescri pro Ioan. Hic rof.Epis.&E-pis.quisub il lo sunt,recita to Syno.Cōst. a act.1.&Ma rian. ibidem Cōc.Cabilo-nen.c.1. 6.Synodo.a-ction 13.in Litu rgia Sā-ti Iacobi, Ba filii.Chryso-stomi &c. Thesi.38.39 & incircumscriptum, totum in toto mun do, & totum in singulis eius partibus, quo omnino modo humanitatem vbi- que præsentem esse prius astruxerat. Qua re non alio modo humanitatem omni- bus rebus adesse, quàm diuinitatem, ex e- ius principiis recte concluditur.
units.tr: 101 That, however, can be seen to have happened by a certain divine providence: that, to explain his notion of the ubiquity of Christ's humanity, he brought forward the opinion or example of no Father except Augustine alone, who professedly attacks and refutes this very error. Hence this man cites no particular passage in which Augustine teaches what he falsely attributes to him, but merely appeals to Luther as asserting it thus.

units.la: 101 Illud autem diuina quadam pro- uidentia effectum videri potest, vt ad ex- plicandam suam illam humanitatis Christi Vbiqueitatem, nullius Patris sententia aut exemplum attulerit, præterquam v- nius Augustini, qui istum ex professo er-rorem impugnat atque refellit. Vnde & nullum iste citat locum peculiarem, vbi Augustinus hoc doceat, quod ipse illi sal- so tribuit, sed tantùm allegat Lutherum sic asserentem.
units.tr: 101 It may seem, by some divine providence, that in explaining his doctrine of the ubiquity of Christ's humanity he cites no saying or example from any Father except Augustine, who expressly attacks and refutes this error. Hence he cites no particular passage where Augustine teaches what he falsely attributes to him, but merely alleges Luther as asserting it.

units.la: 102 Ostendimus hactenus ex sacris literis, Concilijs, Patribúsque & totius Ec clesiæ Catholicæ consensu, quid sit hypo- statica naturarum in Christo vnio, quan- tâque Christi Maiestas & eminentia, vn- de manifestè deduximus, Christum secū- dùm corporalem humanitatis præsentiâ non esse omni in loco, eadem Maiestate, quia Deus: id quod Schmidelinus Vbique tarius, tanquam accómodatissimù omnis erroris & absurditatis operculû, ex falsa hypostaticę vnionis intelligentia imperi-tissimè colligebat. Illud vnû superest explicandum, vbinam locorû Christus Saluator noster secundùm præsentiam corporalem contineatur.
units.tr: 102 We have shown so far, from Holy Scripture, the Councils, the Fathers and the consensus of the whole Catholic Church, what the hypostatic union of natures in Christ is and how great is Christ's majesty and eminence. From this we have clearly deduced that Christ, according to his bodily presence, is not in every place with the same majesty as God. This is what Schmidelin, the Ubiquitarian, most unskilfully inferred from a false understanding of the hypostatic union, as the most convenient cover for every error and absurdity. One thing remains to be explained: in which place of the world Christ our Saviour is contained according to his bodily presence.
