units.la: 103 Si igitur consideramus Christi corpus vt visibilę & circûscriptum est, ea nimirum forma, qua Christus in hoc mûdo conuersatus & in cœlum assumptus est, vt omnino ita considerari oportet verum corpus humanum. neq. enim diuer sa, aut plura numero corpora habuit Dominus.
units.tr: 103 If therefore we consider Christ's body as visible and circumscribed, in that very form in which Christ lived in this world and was taken up into heaven, then it must be considered in this way, as a true human body. For the Lord did not have different bodies, or more than one body in number.

units.la: 104 Hoc inquam modo in cœli tantûm Christus Dominus modò habitat, nô quidê tôtius cœli ambitû suo corpore implens. non enim dilatatur neq. in immensum diffunditur, aut multiplicatur. huius modi enim humani corporis veritati omnino aduersantur, vt etiâ hic Autor asseuerat, sed certam quandā cœli partê secû dùm quantitatis suæ modum occupans, quemadmodum & cætera Beatorum corpora olim occupabant.
units.tr: 105 To this point is also what Augustine says somewhere: "Christ, he says, took the visible form of a man, not only born in it, but also ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father in it." And elsewhere: "Do not doubt that the Lord Christ is everywhere present as God, but in some place of heaven on account of the mode of his true body." And in this same way Scripture and all the saints speak when they affirm that Christ exists only in heaven, or is circumscribed.

units.la: 105 Hucspectat, q; alicubi dicit Augu-stinus, Christus (inquit) visibilê hominis formam accepit, non solùm natus in ea, sed etiam ascendit in cœlum & sedet ad dexteram Patris in ea. Et alibi: Chri-
units.tr: 105 To this pertains what Augustine says elsewhere: Christ, he says, took on the visible form of man, not only being born in it, but also ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father in it. And elsewhere: Chri-

units.la: Thesi.37. (marginal reference, beside paragraph 104) stum Dominum vbique præsentem esse non dubites, tanquam Deum, & in loco aliquo cœli propter sveri corporis modum. Atque hoc eodem modo Scripturę & Sancti omnes loquuntur cùm Christū in cœli tátùm existere, aut circunscriptū esse asseuerant.
units.tr: Thesis 37. Christ the Lord, you should not doubt, is present everywhere as God, but in some place of heaven on account of the mode of his true body. And in this same way Scripture and all the saints speak when they affirm that Christ exists only in heaven, or is circumscribed.

units.la: 106 Constat mediocriter eruditis cœ-lum illud Beatorùm domicilium, locum esse corporeum, & sicut cætera corpora quantitate effectum, quamuis qualitati-bus illis destituatur, quæ locum Physieū constituunt atque naturalem. Quapro-pter vel inuitus aduersarius fateatur ne-cessum est, in cœlo locum esse, non qui-dem Physicum seu naturalem, sed Mathe-maticum & cælestem, nisi dicere malue-rit, Beatos omnes nusquam esse, qui non alibi quàm in cœlo illo continentur.
units.tr: 106 It is generally agreed among moderately learned people that that heaven, the dwelling of the blessed, is a corporeal place, and, like other bodies, is endowed with quantity, although it lacks those qualities which make up a physical and natural place. Therefore, even if the opponent is unwilling, he must admit that there is a place in heaven, not indeed physical or natural, but mathematical and heavenly, unless he prefers to say that the blessed are nowhere, since they are contained in no place other than that heaven.

units.la: 107 Nec tamen Christum cæterŏs-que beatos vni cœli parti, veluti conchas marinas, scopulis affixos, aut veluti stipiti alligatos teneri existimabimus. hæc enim conditio miserrima foret, & cum glorifi-catorum corporum fœlicitate plane re-pugnans, tantum abest vt hoc illis pro-prium sit & necessarium, vt noster Vbi-quista somniat. Sed pro liberrima volun-tate tate sua coelites moueri posse, & interdum etiam moueri intrepide profitemur. Cuius modi autem motus talium corporum sint futuri, temere definire (inquit Augustinus) non audeo, quod excogitare non valeo: tamen & motus, & status sicut & species ipsa decens erit. Certe vbi volet spiritus, ibi protinus erit corpus, nec volet aliquid spiritus, quod nec spiritu possit decere nec corpus. Haec Augustinus.
units.tr: 107 Nor, however, shall we suppose that Christ and the other blessed are held fixed to one part of heaven, like sea shells clinging to rocks, or bound like a man tied to a post. For this condition would be most wretched and plainly repugnant to the happiness of glorified bodies. So far is it from being proper and necessary to them, as our Ubiquitarian dreams, that we freely profess that the heavenly ones can be moved by their most free will, and sometimes are indeed moved. But what kind of motions such bodies will have, I dare not rashly define, as Augustine says, because I cannot conceive it; yet both motion and rest, and also the very appearance, will be fitting. Certainly where the spirit wills, there at once will be the body, nor will the spirit will anything that could be unbecoming either to spirit or to body. Thus Augustine.

units.la: 108 Sanctorum porro foelicitati non repugnare quod in loco sint aut de loco in locum moueantur, ex eo liquet, quod quocunque tandem ferantur, priuari non possunt summo aeternoque bono, Deo scilicet, quem intra se posident foelicissime.
units.tr: 108 That the saints' happiness is not inconsistent with their being in a place, or with their being moved from place to place, is clear from this: wherever they are carried, they cannot be deprived of the supreme and eternal good, namely God, whom they possess most happily within themselves.

units.la: 109 Hinc est quod scriptura sacra te statur, administratorios illos spiritus, in ministerium aliquod missos, ad nos saepe descedere, & nobiscum manere eos, qui nostrae custodiae sunt addicti, Christum praeterea Salvatorem nostrum, post resurrectionem suam, cum iam perfecta simul animi & corporis beatitudine potiretur, toto quadraginta dierum spatio in hoc mundo haesit se, variisque in locis apparuisse, & tandem ad coelos ascendisse. Tum multa corpora sanctorum cum Christo resuscitata in sanctam Ierusalem introgressa esse legimus, quos tamen, ideo beatitudinem aut non habuisse, aut habitam, vel ex toto, vel ex parte amisisse, nemo unquam recte putabit. Et haec satis de veri corporis Christi consideratione & loco dicta sint.
units.tr: 109 Hence it is that Holy Scripture testifies that those ministering spirits, sent out for some service, often come down to us and remain with those who are committed to our keeping. Moreover, Christ our Saviour, after his resurrection, when he already enjoyed the perfect blessedness of soul and body together, stayed in this world for the whole space of forty days, appeared in various places, and at last ascended into heaven. Then we read that many bodies of the saints, raised with Christ, entered the holy Jerusalem; yet no one will ever rightly think that they therefore either did not have blessedness, or, having had it, lost it wholly or in part. And let this be enough said concerning the consideration of the true body of Christ and its place.

units.la: Praeterimus cōsultò, nec nimis longiores, reliquas Schmidelini tam absurdas quàm impias opiniones, quas ex praeclaro illo Vbiquitatis fundamento colligit atque deducit. Nobis enim propositum fuit ea, quae ad Christi Maiestatem asserendam pertinet, & à Schmidelino perquam inique traduntur, ad normam Catholicae veritatis revocare & breviter explicare.
units.tr: We have deliberately passed over the rest of Schmidelin's opinions, which are as absurd as they are impious, and which he gathers and deduces from that famous foundation of ubiquity; we are not going to go on at too great a length. Our purpose has been to recall to the standard of Catholic truth, and briefly to explain, those things which pertain to asserting the majesty of Christ and which Schmidelin hands down most unfairly.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIONES IN NOVVM ILlud Doctrinæ Corpus, quod Repetitio seu Expositio confessionis Augustanæ inscribitur.
units.tr: Observations on that new body of doctrine, which is entitled the Repetition or Exposition of the Augsburg Confession.

units.la: ANIMADVERSIONES IN NOVVM CORPVS DOCTRINÆ quorundam Theologorum Germanorum, quòd Repetitione, seu expositionem,&c. vocant.
units.tr: ANIMADVERSIONS ON THE NEW BODY OF DOCTRINE of certain German theologians, which they call a Repetition, or exposition, etc.

units.la: I
units.tr: I

units.la: ERIA sunt præcipuè,de quibus iudicium nostrum expetere videmini.Primùm: An hoc scriptum (quod vocant Repetitionem,sed expositionem vnanimem, perspicuam, rectam ac postremam,quorundam articulorum confessionis Augustanæ, de quibus inter ipsorum Theologos mota est ante aliquot annos,controuersia,&c.)contineat vlla noua dogmata,quæ doctrinæChristianæ in Ecclesiis Helueticis, & Allobrogicis(cum quibus vos hactenus in doctrina semper consensistis)iamdudum constanter receptæ & prædicatæ,aduersentur.
units.tr: There are chiefly three questions on which you seem to want our judgment. (1) Whether this writing, which they call a Repetition but describe as an exposition, unanimous, perspicuous, correct and final, of certain articles of the Augsburg Confession, over which a controversy arose some years ago among their own theologians, etc., contains any new doctrines that conflict with the Christian doctrine long since constantly received and preached in the Helvetic and Allobrogian churches, with which you have always agreed in doctrine until now. (2) Whether this book condemns any part of the doctrine that we profess. (3) Finally, whether this writing agrees thoroughly in all respects with the Augsburg Confession and rests on the same foundations as it does.

units.la: II Deinde, An damnetur hoc libro vlla pars eius doctrinæ,quam nos profitemur.
units.tr: Second, whether this book condemns any part of the doctrine that we profess.

units.la: III Postremo, An hoc scriptum probe bè in omnibus cum confessione Augu- stana conueniat, & iisdem cum illa fun- damentis nitatur.
units.tr: Third, finally, whether this writing agrees thoroughly in all respects with the Augsburg Confession and rests on the same foundations as it does.

units.la: Cùm vero inuocato ante omnia diui- no Numine totum hoc scriptum perle- gissemus, atq. diligenter singula cum ver- bo Dei conferentes, expédissemus: Com- perimus annotauimúsque bona fide, ea quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: When, after first invoking the divine Power, we had read through this whole writing and, comparing each point carefully with the Word of God, had examined it, we found and in good faith noted the following.

units.la: De auctoritate & inscriptione huius libri.
units.tr: On the authority and title of this book.

units.la: PRimùm: Cùm polliceantur libri hu- ius auctores summam, integrámque omnium dogmatum, quæ inter Augusta- næ confessionis professores, ac Theolo- gos controuersa esse cœperunt, decisio- nem ac consensum: non explicare tamen eos vllibi qua auctoritate, aut à quibus, aut quomodo fuerit liber hic composi- tus: Et tamen magistraliter ( vt scholasti- co verbo vtamur) in eo tũ decisiones suas tum aliorum condemnationes, concipe- re & pronuntiare: Hæc autem agendi ra- tio prorsus est intolerabilis in Ecclesia Dei, in qua si quæ vnquam dissidia de re- bus alicuius momenti orta sunt, in liberis legitimísque semper Synodis solita sunt decidi: & componi: auditis prius liberè, & pię examinatis vtriusque partis rationibus & argumentis: iísque vel receptis, si cum sincero verbo Dei conuenirent, vel repudiatis si cum illo pugnare conuincerentur. Hoc verò ipsum est, quod & Lutherus, & Ecclesiæ omnes Christianæ à Regibus, & Principibus, aduersus Papam eiúsque asseclas, semper expetiue-runt.
units.tr: First: although the authors of this book promise a complete and full decision and agreement on all the doctrines that have begun to be disputed among the professors and theologians of the Augsburg Confession, they nowhere explain by what authority, by whom, or how this book was composed. Yet in it they conceive and pronounce, in a magisterial manner (to use a scholastic word), both their own decisions and their condemnations of others. This way of acting is utterly intolerable in the Church of God. In the Church, whenever disputes over matters of some importance have arisen, they have always been settled and composed in free and lawful synods, after the arguments of each side had first been heard freely and examined piously, and then accepted if they agreed with the sincere Word of God, or rejected if they were shown to conflict with it. This is precisely what both Luther and all Christian churches have always demanded of kings and princes against the Pope and his followers.

units.la: Quod si aliquando certis quibusdam viris, eiusmodi controuersiarum com-positio commissa est, electos illos prius communi Synodi alicuiius conscnsu suis-se oportuit, ad quam postea omnia refer-rentur. Quum igitur contraria omnino ratione, hoc scriptum conceptum fue-rit, nec debet nec iure potest a quoquam propter incommoda quæ inde consequc-rentur, aut recipi aut probari, multoque minus temere subscribi: nè si quidem do-ctrinam omnino puram cótineret: quod quidem de hoc scripto (quantum nos ex verbo Dei iudicare potuimus) dici non potest.
units.tr: But if at some time the settling of controversies of this kind was entrusted to certain men, those men ought first to have been chosen by the common consent of some synod, to which everything would afterwards be referred. Since this writing was therefore conceived by an entirely contrary method, it neither ought nor can rightly be accepted or approved by anyone, because of the inconveniences that would follow, much less rashly subscribed, even if it contained wholly pure doctrine. That, at least, cannot be said of this writing, so far as we could judge it by the Word of God.

units.la: Quòd si fortasse prætexere Principum quorundam autoritatem audeant, quorū iussu aliquot Theologi conuenerint, vt de componendis controuersiis in Religionis negotio rationes inirent: hoc tamē tantam autoritatem huic scripto conciliare non potuit, vt pro vnanimi, & ab omnibus Germanicis ecclesiis recepta cō trouersorum dogmatum decisione statim agnosci debeat, atque omnib. obtrudi, vt sine publici & generalis Synodi examine & approbatione syngraphis omnium obsignetur. Neque hic dissimulare possumus peruenisse ad nos exemplar responsionis, seu potius c ōsilij, q sex illi Theologi (qui huius libri authores, aut compilares fuisse ab omnibus perhibentur) Bergæ apud Magdeburgum ad 5 Calend. Quintileis nuper congregati illustrissimo Principi Duxi Saxoniæ obtulerunt: Quo responso apparet ipsos mandati fines non solùm transiliisse sed planè peruertisse. Nam quum scriptum quoddam duntaxat examinandum sibi à Principe fuisse propositum ipsimet fateantur, vt ad Celsitudinem ipsius suum de eo iudicium referrent: ac simul de publica & generali Synodo (siue conuentu omnium ordinum Imperij qui Augustanam confessionem profitentur) cogenda cogitarent, in qua liber ille offerri, propo-nique (cum aliis, quæ ad concordiam Ec-clesiarum necessaria viderentur) commo-dè posset: Illi côtra statuunt non expedi-re vt vlla Synodus, de doctrina hoc scri-pto contenta (quam sciunt, agnoscunt & fatentur, plerísque tũ Principibus atq.or-dinib^ imperij Augustanæ confessionis tũ quamplurimis eorum Theologis, & pasto-ribus non probari) cognoscat & iudicet. Sed tutius fore si pri^ subscriptiones à sin-gulis Theologis eorum ordinum (quos i-sti certò statuunt, secum sentire) caute ex torqueantur ad eius approbationem. Ita-que piam Principis mentem isti sic elu-dunt, & consilium fraudulentum & peni-tus iniquũ ac verè tyrannicũ suggerunt.
units.tr: But if they perhaps dare to put forward the authority of certain princes, at whose command some theologians met to consider how controversies in religious matters might be settled, this still could not lend such authority to this writing that it should at once be acknowledged as a unanimous decision on the disputed doctrines, received by all German churches, and forced upon everyone, to be sealed by the signatures of all without the examination and approval of a public and general synod. Nor can we conceal that a copy has reached us of the response, or rather the advice, which those six theologians (who are said by everyone to be the authors or compilers of this book) recently presented to the most illustrious Prince, the Duke of Saxony, after assembling at Bergen near Magdeburg on the fifth day before the Calends of July. By that response it appears that they have not only overstepped the limits of their commission but utterly perverted it. For although they themselves admit that the Prince had proposed to them a single writing to examine, so that they might report their judgment of it to his Highness, and although they at the same time considered convening a public and general synod (or assembly of all the orders of the Empire who profess the Augsburg Confession), in which that book could conveniently be offered and proposed along with other matters seen as necessary for the concord of the churches, they instead decide that no synod should learn of or judge the doctrine contained in this writing. They know, acknowledge and confess that most of the princes and orders of the Empire who hold the Augsburg Confession, and very many of their theologians and ministers, do not approve it. Rather, they say, it would be safer if subscriptions to its approval were first cautiously extracted from individual theologians of those orders whom they are certain think as they do. Thus they mock the pious mind of the Prince, and suggest a fraudulent, wholly unjust and truly tyrannical plan.

units.la: Qua fronte igitur aut Principis auctori-tatem prætexere, vt huic scripto publi-cam auctoritatem acquirant, quia ipsius inspectio à Principe committa est: aut vnanimè in doctrina consensum hoc scriptum inscribere ac tanquã publicè ab omnibus approbatum venditare audent? quod à pauculis tantum: sex nimirum, vt aiunt, scriptũ, probatum, & qua voluerũt forma compactum est. An non hoc est alienæ fidei dominari, ac tyrannidem in EccleEcclesiam vsurpare. si paucorum hominū placitis reliqui omnes sine disquisitione quoquo iure, quáque iniuria subscribere vel iubeantur, vel cogantur? Hæc ergo primum intolerabilis est arrogatia, quæ olim à D. Luthero, hodie tum à nobis, tū ab istis merito in Pontificiis reprehenditur, & damnatur: quòd scilicet priuatorum hominū scripta Dei verbo exæquare fas non sit. Quid autem aliud faciunt isti, dum clandestinis suis consiliis hoc agunt apud Principes, vt nemini liceat in hoc suum scriptum inquirere, sed cogantur omnes illi assensū præbere & subscribere, tanquam certissimæ fidei Regulæ? Audiat quæso, quomodo D. Lutherus in eiusmodi usurpatam auctoritatem (qua sibi vnis Pontificij de aliorum scriptis iudicium arrogant, cum à nemine tamen sua decreta iudicari patiantur) inuehatur, Vbi manet (inquit ille contra Erasmum de seruo arbitrio) libertas & potestas iudicandi Decretores illos? vt Paulus 1. Cor. 14. docet, dicens, Ceteri diiudicent. Non placet tibi esse iudicem in Decretis Ecclesiæ (quod Paulus tamen præcipit) Quæ ista noua religio, & humilitas? vt nobis tuo exemplo potestatē adimas iudicandi decreta hominum. & subiicias nos sine iudi cio hominibus? Vbi nobis hoc mandat scriptura Dei? Hactenus Lutherus, cuius verba, ali non merito in istos Theologos vsurpari possunt qui aliis omnibus sua placita praescribere audent: & interim mi ris artibus libertatem diiudicandi Eccle- siis adimere conantur: ac tantundem au- ctoritatis humanis suis scriptis arrogant, quantum solis scripturis sanctis deberi om- nes orthodoxi semper confessi sunt? Quid hic pontificij? Annon iure conque- rentur ad priuatum istos Doctores collo- quium accitos, plus sibi iuris & authoritatis vsurpare in Ecclesias, quàm ipsi toti pa- stico Clero in vnum publicè conuoca- to concedere velint? En quomodo non se duntaxat, sed Ecclesias omnes Germa- niæ, aduersariorum sannis, atque expro- brationibus exponant: & pios simul om- nes hoc suo saftu & arrogantia offendat & irritent. Taceo de Dei excandescentia in eiusmodi arrogantes iuris sui vsurpa- tores. Non est ergo quod de auctoritate huius libri magnopere vel ipsi gloriētur, vel pij homines sint de eius subscriptione deneganda solliciti. Ea enim plane nul la est, cum nec Ecclesiasticum eiusmodi scriptum dici, nec Theologicum merea-tur, vtpote contra morem veteris Eccle-siæ,& nō à Theologis,sed potiusà factio-sis hominibus conscriptum: qui nihili fa-ciunt Ecclesiarum iudicium,sed omnibus semel os obstruere hac sua finali seu po-strema vt vocat determinatione satagūt: damnatis omnibus qui illis assentiri recu-sabunt.
units.tr: With what face, then, do they dare to plead the Prince's authority in order to win public authority for this writing, on the ground that its examination was committed by the Prince? Or with what face do they dare to entitle this writing a unanimous consensus in doctrine and to peddle it as if it had been publicly approved by all? It was written, approved and put together in whatever form they wished by only a few, six as they say. Is this not to lord it over another's faith and to usurp tyranny over the Church, when all the rest are ordered or compelled, without any inquiry, by whatever right or wrong, to subscribe at the pleasure of a few men? This, then, is first an intolerable arrogance, which Dr Luther rightly reproached and condemned in the Papists, and which we and they condemn today: namely, that it is not lawful to equate the writings of private men with the Word of God. What else do these men do when, by their secret counsels with the princes, they bring it about that no one may examine their writing, but all are compelled to give assent and subscribe, as if it were the most certain rule of faith? Let us hear how Luther inveighs against such an arrogated authority, by which the Papists alone claim for themselves the judgment of others' writings, while they suffer no one to judge their own decrees. Where, he says (against Erasmus, on the bondage of the will), does the liberty and power of judging those decretalists remain? As Paul teaches in 1. Cor. 14, saying, "Let the others judge." You do not wish to be a judge of the decrees of the Church, though Paul commands it. What new religion and humility is this? Do you, by your example, take away from us the power of judging human decrees and subject us without judgment to men? Where does the Scripture of God command us this? Thus far Luther, whose words can rightly be turned against those theologians who dare to prescribe their own opinions to all others, while by clever arts they try to take the liberty of judging away from the churches, and claim for their human writings as much authority as all orthodox men have always confessed is due to the holy Scriptures alone. What do the Papists say to this? Will they not rightly complain that these private doctors, summoned to a private conference, have usurped more right and authority over the churches than they themselves would be willing to grant to the whole pastoral clergy publicly gathered in one place? See how they expose not only themselves but all the churches of Germany to the jeers and reproaches of their adversaries, and at the same time offend and provoke all the pious by this their pride and arrogance. I say nothing of the wrath of God against such arrogant usurpers of his right. There is therefore no reason for them to boast greatly of the authority of this book, nor for pious men to be anxious about refusing its subscription. For it has plainly no authority, since it deserves to be called neither an ecclesiastical nor a theological writing: it is against the custom of the ancient Church, and was written not by theologians but rather by factious men, who care nothing for the judgment of the churches and strive to stop everyone's mouth at once by this so-called final or ultimate determination, condemning all who refuse to assent to them.

units.la: De Præfatione.
units.tr: On the Preface.

units.la: Secundò assumunt quidem huius scri-pti autores in sua præfatione pro ba-si & fundamento suarū decisionum, Ver-bum Domini:quod certissimam regulam esse statuunt,ad quam omnes tum docto-res,tum doctrinæ sint examinandæ: Qua in re facile cum illis consentimus. Dein-de addunt tanquā testes omni exceptio-ne maiores,tria Symbola, nempe Apostolicum,Nicenum,& Athanasij,quæ & nos probamus.In eo tamen ab istis dissentien-tes,quòd Ephesinum ,& Chalcedonense omiserint, quorum non minor fuit sem-per in Ecclesia,quàm reliquorum, auctoritas,& quæ idcirco videri possunt ab istis præterita, quòd eorum dogmati ex dia-metro repugnent.
units.tr: Secondly, the authors of this writing rest their preface on the Word of the Lord as the basis and foundation of their decisions, which they declare to be the most certain rule by which all teachers and all doctrine must be examined. In this matter we readily agree with them. Next, they add, as witnesses beyond all exception, three creeds: the Apostles', the Nicene, and the Athanasian, which we too approve. In this they differ from us, however, in that they have left out the Ephesine and the Chalcedonian, whose authority in the Church has never been less than that of the others. These may seem to have been passed over by them because they flatly contradict their doctrine.

units.la: Quod autem tertio loco isti adiiciunt Confessionem Augustanam Caesari anno, M. D. XXX. oblatam, eiúsq. Apologiam. Item Articulos Smalcaldicos. Et postremò Magnam & paruam Lutheri Catechesin.
units.tr: As for the third item they add, namely the Augsburg Confession presented to the Emperor in the year 1530, together with its Apology; likewise the Smalcald Articles; and finally Luther's Larger and Smaller Catechisms.

units.la: Id vero nō ita simpliciter & sine exceptione recipiendum esse in Ecclesia Dei, existimamus: in qua semper discrimè constitutum est, & obseruatum inter sacram verbi Dei scripturam, symbolaq. illa, quae vocant, & priuatorum doctorum scripta quantavis doctrina & sanctitate illi excellerent. Verbum enim Dei à seipso auctoritatè habet inexpugnabilem. Symbola vero pro authenticis testimoniis ideo habita & recepta fuerunt, quòd decreta & decisiones ex puro Dei verbo communi vniuersæ Ecclesiæ consensu, decerptas continerent. Non fuit tamen eorum tam certa & illibata auctoritas, quin liceret semel in eis constituta iterum atque iterum ad examen & regulam verbi Dei in aliis æquè legitimis Synodis, reuocare & exigere, quoties id necessitas requireret.
units.tr: We do not think that these should be received in the Church of God so simply and without exception. In the Church a distinction has always been maintained and observed between the sacred Scripture of God's Word and those creeds, as they call them, and the writings of private teachers, however much they excel in learning and holiness. For the Word of God has unassailable authority in itself. The creeds, however, were held and received as authentic testimonies only because they contained decrees and decisions drawn from the pure Word of God by the common consent of the whole Church. Yet their authority was never so certain and unimpaired that, once established in them, the same things could not be called back and demanded again and again for examination and for the rule of God's Word in other equally lawful synods, whenever necessity required it.

units.la: Id quod D. Lutherus sonorè & grauiter in primis illis heroicárum actionum suarum defensionibus palam & voce & scripti est testatus, cui magnam iniuriam faciunt isti qui hæc audent pro irrefragabili diuinæ scripturæ interpretatione omnibus obtrudere. Id verò, apparet vel ex eo quòd primum illud œcumenicum Concilium (cuius præcipua semper fuit autoritas) Nicenum videlicet, sæpissimè fuit discussum & examinatum, atque toties probatum ac confirmatum, quoties impugnare, & arguere illud quidam ausi sunt.
units.tr: This is what Dr. Luther openly and emphatically testified, both by voice and in writing, in those first defences of his heroic actions; and those who dare to force these creeds on everyone as an irrefutable interpretation of divine Scripture do him great wrong. That this is so appears even from the fact that the first ecumenical council, the Nicene (whose authority has always been the chief), was frequently discussed and examined, and was approved and confirmed as often as certain men dared to attack and challenge it.

units.la: Quod verò ad Augustanam confessionem attinet, notum est omnibus (quod tamen sine præiudicio veritatis in ea contentæ dictum sit) neque fuisse primùm conscriptam generali omnium principum, ordinúmque Germaniæ (qui Tyrannidē Papæ Romani eiurarant) nomine & consensu, sed septem duntaxat Principum, & duarum ciuitatum: neque postea nisi paulatim modò ab his, modò ab illis approbatam, idq. sine Ecclesiastica vlla dis-quisitione & examine. Denique, quod non leuioris est momenti, non fuisse vnquam ab aliis Ecclesiis vel Heluetiorum, vel eorum qui illis fœdere iunguntur receptam. Vnde duo consequuntur. Pri·mùm, etsi minimè sit eleuanda eius scripti auctoritas, tamen nulla ratione habendam illam esse sine exceptione pro symbolo Ecclesiarum, quas reformatas vocant, vti in huius voluminis praefatione appellatur. Deinde etiamsi symboli nomen illi competeret, tamen subiacere adhuc Ecclesiae vniuersalis examini, & iudicio per verbum Dei: in quo audiantur libere quivel illi contradicere, vel de eius germana interpretatione disputare contendunt: maximè cum constet ab eo ipso quitam confessionem, quàm Apologiam eius, conscripsit, aliter intellecta & expo-sita pleraque fuisse, quàm à Luthero atq. huius libri autoribus exponantur.
units.tr: As for the Augsburg Confession, it is known to everyone (though this is said without prejudice to the truth contained in it) that it was not first drawn up in the name and with the consent of all the princes and estates of Germany who had renounced the tyranny of the Roman Pope, but only of seven princes and two cities. Afterwards it was approved only gradually, now by one, now by another, and that without any ecclesiastical inquiry or examination. Finally, and this is of no small weight, it was never received by the other Churches of the Swiss, or by those who are joined to them in covenant. Two consequences follow. First, although the authority of this writing is by no means to be disparaged, yet it must in no way be regarded as an unqualified creed of the Churches which are called reformed, as this volume's preface calls them. Second, even if the name of creed were fitting for it, it would still be subject to examination and judgement by the universal Church through the Word of God, where those who wish either to contradict it or to dispute its genuine interpretation may be heard freely. This is especially so since it is established that the author himself, both in the Confession and in its Apology, has been understood and expounded in many places otherwise than Luther and the authors of this book expound it.

units.la: Porrò Apologiam, confessioni adiectam, (vnde illi volunt peti veram & germanam confessionis interpretationem) nusquam apparet publicè fuisse vel ab vllis Principibus, atque ordinibus Imperij: vel ab vllis ipsorum Theologis subscriptâ, & sigillis authenticis approbatam. Et extant alia scripta magis authentica, vt confessio Saxonicarum Ecclesiarum (quae & Repetitio Augustanae confessionis inscribitur) non solum à triginta vno Saxoni-cis cis Theologis, tam pastoribus, quàm doctoribus sollenniter subscripta: sed etiam à legatis quatuor Illustrissimorum Principum: Item ab omnibus pastoribus Ecclesiæ Argentinensis, & denique à tota Ecclesia, atque academia citerioris Pomeraniæ, sollennibus scriptis & testimoniis in Ecclesiastico conuentu witteberգæ, x. Iulij Anno 1551. approbata, tanquam certa, solida, ac (vt quidā ex illis loquuntur) consummata, magísque clara & perspicua Augustanæ confessionis expositio, quæ nullis cauillis sophisticis labefactari possit. Ea verò cùm pro legitima confessionis repetitione & expositione publicè tot annis à tōt tantisque viris & Ecclesiis probata, edita, atque recepta hactenus fuerit: mirum cur ab istis profsus silentio prætereatur, aut cur dissimulent consensum publicum huic potius repetitioni (quamuis multò explicatius, & ad nostram de hoc sacramento sententiā accommodatius interpretetur articulū de Cœna Domini, quàm vel Apologia, vel Articuli illi Smalcaldici, de quib. isti tantum in hoc scripto meminerunt) præbitum fuisse: quàm vllis aliis scriptis ab istis sex viris in hoc suo libro citatis & pro
units.tr: Moreover, the Apology appended to the Confession, from which these men wish the true and genuine interpretation of the Confession to be sought, nowhere appears to have been publicly subscribed and approved with authentic seals either by any princes and estates of the Empire, or by any of their own theologians. There are other writings of far greater authority, such as the Confession of the Saxon Churches (which is also entitled the Repetition of the Augsburg Confession), which was not only solemnly subscribed by thirty-one Saxon theologians, both ministers and teachers, but also by the envoys of four most illustrious princes; likewise by all the ministers of the Church of Strasbourg; and finally by the whole Church and academy of Further Pomerania, approved by solemn writings and testimonies in an ecclesiastical assembly at Wittenberg on 10 July 1551, as a certain, solid and (as some of them put it) consummate and clearer and more perspicuous exposition of the Augsburg Confession, which no sophistical quibbles could overturn. Since this has been publicly approved, published and received for so many years as a lawful repetition and exposition of the Confession by so many and such great men and Churches, it is strange why these men pass over it in complete silence, or why they dissemble that public consent has been given to this Repetition rather than to any other writings cited in their book by these six men and approved as an authentic exposition of their confession. (Although the Repetition explains the article on the Lord's Supper far more fully, and more suitably to our view of this sacrament, than either the Apology or those Smalcald Articles, of which these men make mention only in this writing.)

units.la: authentica suæ confessionis expositione probatis. Oportuit enim sex istos Theologos (qui hoc suum scriptū Vnanimem Augustanæ Confessionis Repetitionem, & rectam ac postremam expositionem (ad hanc Apologiam & Smalcaldicos articulos referendam) inscribere & omnibus Ecclesiis subscribendam, obtrudere audent) prius vel fidem facere, quomodo & quando omnes tam Ecclesiæ quàm Principes ac Theologi (qui priorem illam sol lemni ritu approbarant & subscripserât) eandem autoritatem in hanc contulerint quam priori illi tribuerant: vel si hoc non possunt, illos aperte ex albo sociorum Augustanæ confessionis eximere: vel denique agnoscere falsò se hunc titulum huic libro præfixisse, vt hoc fuco facilius ab incautis subscriptionem extorqueret. Hinc ergo & ipsi Apologiæ, & huic scripto omnis autoritas adimitur.
units.tr: by the authentic exposition of its own confession. For these six theologians, who dare to entitle their work "A Unanimous Repetition of the Augsburg Confession, and its right and final exposition" (to be read alongside this Apology and the Smalcald Articles), and to press it on all the Churches for subscription, ought first to show how and when all the Churches, princes and theologians who approved and subscribed that earlier confession with solemn rite have conferred the same authority on this work as they gave to the earlier one. Or, if they cannot do this, they must openly remove those men from the roll of allies of the Augsburg Confession. Or finally, they must admit that they falsely prefixed this title to the book, so that by this pretext they might more easily extract subscriptions from the unwary. In this way all authority is taken away both from the Apology and from this writing.

units.la: Reliqui autem tractatus, quibus suam doctrinam miti affirmant, vt est Catechesis, tam parua quàm magna D. Lutheri, priuati hominis scripta sunt, quem nos certe pro eximio viro, & præ ceteris excellentibus donis ornato, hominem tamen agnoscimus: Cuius vnius sententia tia omnibus reliquis,fidei normam ac regulam sine controuersia prescribere nec potest,nec debet.Nec ille ipse D. Luthe-rus se eo loco vult haberi,quasi nusquam aut errarit aut errare potuerit, sed sepe contrarium restatur: vt in prefatione ad Genesin de suis operibus loquens hec liberè profitetur: Mallem (inquit) pias operas & bonas horas in meliorem autorem collocatas esse : Neque enim ego is sum,de quo dici possit, fecit: neque is de quo dicere possis,faciebat: In vltimo ordine consisto qui vix dicere audet, Volui facere: Et vtinam essem dignus in hoc ordine vltimo vltimus esse. Et paulo post. Denique non ille est optimus qui omnia comprehendit,aut nusquam defecit. nullus enim talis fuit,aut erit. Hæc ille non ficta & hypocritica modestia: sed suam (vt reliquorum omnium hominum) renuitatem,& ad ignoranda multa,imo ad errandum quoque procliuitatem ex animo agnoscens.Et sane negari non potest D. Lutherum in quibusdam aliquando hallucinatum fuisse. Veluti cum alicubi scribit:Liberum cuique esse citra periculum salutis,alterutrum imaginari,opinari, aut credere: Videlicet vel panem re-
units.tr: The remaining treatises, in which they affirm their doctrine with mild language, such as the Catechism of Dr. Luther, both the small and the large, were written by a private man. We certainly acknowledge him as an outstanding man, adorned with gifts above others, yet still a man. His single opinion can and ought not, without controversy, prescribe to all the others the norm and rule of faith. Nor does Luther himself wish to be regarded in that way, as though he had nowhere erred or could never have erred. Rather he often testifies to the contrary. Speaking of his own works in the preface to Genesis, he freely confesses: "I would rather that pious labours and good hours had been devoted to a better author. For I am not the one of whom it can be said, 'he did,' nor the one of whom you can say, 'he was doing.' I stand in the last rank, who hardly dares to say, 'I wished to do.' And would that I were worthy to be the last in that last rank." And shortly after: "Finally, he is not the best who comprehends all things, or who has never failed. For no such man was, or will be." Luther says this not in a feigned and hypocritical modesty, but acknowledging from his heart his own weakness, like that of all other men, and his proneness to ignorance, indeed even to error. And certainly it cannot be denied that Luther sometimes went astray in certain matters. For example, when he writes somewhere: "It is free to each person, without danger to salvation, to imagine, to hold an opinion, or to believe either the one or the other: namely, either that the bread remains in the sacrament (as all of us, taught from the Scriptures, rightly and truly believe and teach), or that the bread is changed into the body and only its accidents remain (which the scholastic sophists have falsely handed down, and the whole Papacy wrongly holds), since here, says Luther, there is no necessity of faith."

units.la: manere in sacramento (vt nos omnes à scripturis edocti recte ac vere credimus, & docemus) vel pane mutato in corpus, sola eius accidentia restare (quod scholastici sophistæ falsò tradiderunt, & totus Papatus perperam opinatur) cùm hîc nulla sit, inquit Lutherus, fidei necessitas. Itáne verò ex Lutheri sententia, impunè scripturam sacram corrumpere cuiq. liberum erit? Nec transsubstantiatio & quæ eam consequuntur absurda, contra articulos fidei esse censebitur? Ergòne quiduis de sacramentis sentire & imaginari cuilibet citra piaculum licebit? Sed hæc forte Lutherus adhuc nouitius scripsisse dicetur. Illud verò quàm durum & ambiguum quod longo post tempore de virgine Maria scriptum reliquit. Tom.7. f.402. Nos in Deum fiduciam nostram ponimus, qui à Maria corporaliter & spiritualiter in hanc lucem edi, nec tamen corporaliter nec spiritualiter ab eadem manducari & bibi, voluit. Unde verò id habet Lutherus? quod si omnimodo verum esset, de Mariæ fide ac proinde de eius salute (vt cætera absurda non attinga mus) merito dubitari posset: cùm de spiritali carnis suæ manducatione & sanguinis nis bibitione quæ fit per fidem dixerit Dominus Ioan.6. Nisi ederitis carnem filij hominis & biberitis eius sanguinem, non habebitis vitā in vobis.Hîc certè nemo fidelium excipitur. Et quod pagina sequenti addit, falsi etiam argui posset. Quocunque,inquit,in scripturæ loco, sibi inuicem opponuntur Caro & spiritus ibi caro non potest de corpore Christi intelligi sed semper de veteri carne quæ de carne nata est. Hæc ille. Atqui in fine 3 cap.1.ad Tim.Caro & sanguis ita opponuntur,vt caro non de veteri carne, quæ de carne nata est : sed de corpore Christi quod ex spiritu sancto in Maria conceptum & sine labe veteris hominis ex Maria natum est, manifestè intelligatur. Sic Deus(inquit Paulus)manifestatus in carne,iustificatus in spiritu,&c. Item Rom. 1. De filio suo facto ex semine Dauid secundum carnem:& declarato filio Dei secundum spiritum sanctificationis. Et 1. Pet.3.Christus mortificatus carne, viuificatus autem spiritu. Quibus omnibus locis caro pro tota natura humana Christi incorrupta:Spiritus autem pro natura Diuina vsurpatur. Possent & alia exempla proferri ex quib. apparet Lutherum
units.tr: Is it then, by Luther's judgment, free for anyone to corrupt Holy Scripture with impunity? Will the transubstantiation and the absurdities that follow from it not be judged contrary to the articles of faith? Will it then be permitted to anyone to think and imagine whatever he likes about the sacraments without sin? But perhaps it will be said that Luther wrote these things while still a novice. What of his harsh and ambiguous statement, left by him long afterwards, about the Virgin Mary? (Vol. 7, fol. 402.) "We place our trust in God, who wished to be born into this light from Mary both bodily and spiritually, yet who wished to be eaten and drunk neither bodily nor spiritually by her." Where does Luther get this? If it were true in every respect, one could rightly doubt Mary's faith and therefore her salvation (not to mention the other absurdities), since the Lord spoke of the spiritual eating of his flesh and drinking of his blood, which is done through faith: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you" (John 6). Here certainly no believer is excluded. And what he adds on the following page could also be proved false: "In whatever place of Scripture flesh and spirit are set against each other, the flesh cannot there be understood of the body of Christ, but always of the old flesh which is born of flesh." So he says. Yet at the end of 1 Tim. 3, flesh and spirit are so set against each other that flesh is clearly understood not of the old flesh which is born of flesh, but of the body of Christ, which was conceived in Mary by the Holy Spirit and born of Mary without the stain of the old man. Thus Paul says: "God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit," etc. Likewise Rom. 1: "concerning his Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, and declared to be the Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification." And 1 Pet. 3: "Christ, put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit." In all these places, "flesh" is used for the whole uncorrupted human nature of Christ, and "Spirit" for the divine nature. Other examples could also be brought forward, from which it appears that Luther

units.la: non solùm vt hominem errare potuisse, sed etiam manifestè erraffe. Vt merito optarit in præfatione suorum operum sua scripta cũ summa miseratione & iudicio legi :vt infra citabimus. Ergo firmũ fundamentum fidei esse non possunt D.Lutheri (quantumuis excellentis ferui Dei) scripta,vt isti volunt.
units.tr: not only that he could err as a man, but that he manifestly erred. Hence he rightly wished, in the preface to his works, that his writings be read with the greatest charity and judgment, as we shall cite below. So the writings of Dr Luther, however excellent a servant of God he was, cannot be a firm foundation of faith, as these men claim.

units.la: His omnibus addunt,probari &recipi abs fe tanquam authentica testimonia suæ doctrinæ, aliorum etiam doctorum scripta, quæ ante controuersias de vera Auguftanæ confessionis interpretatione inter ipsorum Theologos ortas, edita & recepta fuerunt.Hoc vero vti ab ipsis dicitur nullo pacto admitti debet, cùm neque scriptorum nomina, neque tempus vllum certum exprimant, quo scripta illa in lucem prodierunt. Tanta enim reperitur scriptorum varietas vt nemini constare certò possit, quæ probanda, quæve improbanda sint.
units.tr: To all this they add that they accept and approve, as authentic testimonies of their doctrine, the writings of other teachers too, which were published and received before the controversies over the true interpretation of the Augsburg Confession arose among their theologians. But this appeal to them must in no way be admitted, since they name neither the authors nor any definite time at which those writings appeared. Such is the variety of writings that no one can know for certain which of them should be approved and which rejected.

units.la: Habuerunt certè & nostræ Ecclesiæ iampridem communem confessionem Basileæ primum ab Heluetiis compositã. Habent & aliam generalem, Tiguri postea conscriptam: quæ non solum ab omnibus Ecclesiis Christianis, quę sunt in Heluetia, Rhetia, & confœderatis prouin ciis, vt Geneua &c. sed etiam ab iis quæ sunt in Belgio, in Gallia, Scotia, & maxima parte Poloniæ, Hungariæ atq. Transfyluaniæ diligenter examinata, approbata, & tandem etiam subscripta fuit. Neq. vlla est in doctrina controuersia inter Anglicanas Ecclesias, & eas omnes quæ hanc confessionem sunt amplexæ. Pleræque etiam ex suprà nominatis Ecclesiis receperunt & vtuntur formula Catechismi, quam Caluinus pro Geneuensi Ecclesia conscripserat. Absit tamen vt vel vlla prædictarum confessionum, vel illa Catechesis, aliáve huiusmodi scripta, à quoquâ nostrûm obtrudantur cuiquam, pro Symbolo aut fidei regula. Sed summis semper votis hoc vnum optauimus, optamúsque adhuc, vt liceat omnia eiusmodi scripta in œcumenica omnium Ecclesiarum Christianarum synodo, liberè discutere (auditis omnibus qui contradicere cupiant) & tandem ex puro puto verbo Dei omnes controuersias dirimere, & ab omnibus receptam veritatis doctrinam communi omnium consensu stabilire.
units.tr: Our own Church, too, has long had a common confession, first drawn up at Basel by the Swiss, and it has another general one, written later at Zurich. These have been carefully examined and approved, and at last subscribed, not only by all the Christian churches in Switzerland, Rhaetia and the allied provinces, such as Geneva, but also by those in the Netherlands, France, Scotland, and most of Poland, Hungary and Transylvania. Nor is there any controversy in doctrine between the English churches and all those that have embraced this confession. Most of the churches just named have also received and use the catechism form which Calvin drew up for the church of Geneva. Yet far be it from any of us to impose on anyone any of the aforesaid confessions, or that catechism, or other writings of this kind, as a creed or rule of faith. Our constant prayer has been, and still is, this one thing: that all such writings may be freely discussed in an ecumenical synod of all the Christian churches (with a hearing for everyone who wishes to object), and that at last all controversies be settled by the pure Word of God alone, and the doctrine of the truth, received by all, be established by the common consent of all.

units.la: Hæc igitur de auctoritate, inscriptione & præfatione huius libri dicenda & notanda visa sunt: Nunc ad tres illas propositas quæstiones accedimus.
units.tr: These, then, are the points about the authority, title and preface of this book that seemed to need saying and noting. Now we come to the three questions proposed.

units.la: Ac primùm quod ad noua dogmata, & veræ doctrinæ, quæ in nostris Ecclesiis inde ab initio prædicata est, còtraria spectat: hæc potissimum deprehendimus.
units.tr: First, as regards the new doctrines which run contrary to the true doctrine preached in our churches from the beginning, we have found the following to be the chief ones.

units.la: In tractatu seu cap. 1. De peccato originis, sectione seu art. 21. qui incipit in Gallica versione, Item quemadmodum Diuus Augustinus &c. scribunt (vti sonat Gallica versio) hominem naturaliter à patre & matre secundum corpus & secundum animam genitum in sua natura vniuersa, omnibusque facultatibus, ad summum esse corruptum.
units.tr: In the treatise, or chapter 1, On original sin, section or article 21, which begins in the French version, "Likewise, as the divine Augustine etc. write", they say (as the French version has it) that man, begotten naturally of father and mother according to body and soul, is in his whole nature and all his faculties corrupted to the highest degree.

units.la: Quibus verbis dogma de Traduce animæ inuehunt in Ecclesiam: quod tamen hactenus communiter à nulla receptum est, & quod nos minimè recipiendum esse existimamus.
units.tr: By these words they introduce into the Church the doctrine of the traducianism of the soul; yet this has hitherto been accepted by no one in common, and we think it must by no means be accepted.

units.la: Item in tractatu seu cap. 3. De iustitia fidei coram Deo (in 6. errore ab ipsis dam nato sub finem ferè capitis) statuunt non solum Dei dona, sed & Deum ipsum in credentibus habitare: At nos cum vni-uersa uersa Ecclesia docemus, Deum quidem sua effentia vbique esse, nusquam autem habitare perfonaliter nisi in vnica Iesu Christi persona: fecundum virtutem vero & efficaciam bonitatis suæ, quæ illi propria est, habitare duntaxat in sanctis.
units.tr: Likewise, in the treatise, or chapter 3, On the righteousness of faith before God (in the sixth error, which they themselves have set out, near the end of the chapter), they hold that not only God's gifts but God himself dwells in believers. But we teach, with the whole Church, that God indeed is everywhere by his essence, yet dwells personally nowhere except in the one person of Jesus Christ; and that by the power and efficacy of his goodness, which is proper to him, he dwells in the saints alone.

units.la: Item in tit. seu cap. 4. De bonis operibus. fect. 17. & 19. volunt fidem & Spiritum sanctum prorsus amitti à fidelibus, quoties scienter ac voluntarie peccant. Nos vero docemus cum Apostolo veram fidem atque perseuerantiā, quemadmodum & electionem, dona esse Dei ἀμετα-μέλητα in iis qui vere credunt, & ideo penitus amitti non posse, quamuis interrumpantur eorum effecta, illius vitio qui à tentatione vincitur.
units.tr: Likewise, in the title, or chapter 4, On good works, sections 17 and 19, they hold that faith and the Holy Spirit are altogether lost by the faithful whenever they sin knowingly and wilfully. But we teach, with the Apostle, that true faith and perseverance, like election, are gifts of God that are irrevocable [ἀμεταμέλητα] in those who truly believe; and therefore they cannot be wholly lost, although their effects may be interrupted through the fault of one who is overcome by temptation.

units.la: In tract. 5. de Lege & Euangelio confundunt fere vbique terrorem conscientiæ qui à lege proficiscitur, cum refipifcētia quæ cordis est conuersio, & à Spiritu Iesu Christi procedit, per Euangelij prædicationem.
units.tr: In the fifth treatise, On Law and Gospel, they confuse almost everywhere the terror of conscience that comes from the law with repentance, which is a conversion of the heart and proceeds from the Spirit of Jesus Christ through the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: Sic etiam eiusdem cap. fect. 6. vbi de pœnitentiæ significatione agitur, ita tribuunt spiritualem Legis expositionem, prædicationi Euangelij à Christo factæ, vt eam prorsus à Mosis ministerio exclu-
units.tr: So too in the same chapter, section 6, where the signification of repentance is discussed, they ascribe the spiritual exposition of the Law to the preaching of the Gospel made by Christ, so as to exclude it entirely from the ministry of Moses,

units.la: L.ij. dant: Cùm constet eam legis explicatio- nem, quæ à Domino Iesu Christo est tra- dita, eandem esse cum ea, quam & Moses ipse & prophetę docuerunt. Neq. enim proprie expositio illa ad ministerium E- uangelij pertinet: quanuis qui Euangeliū annuntiat, idem & legem prædicare de- beat.
units.tr: since it is agreed that the explanation of the law which the Lord Jesus Christ has delivered is the same as that which Moses himself and the prophets taught. For that exposition does not properly belong to the ministry of the Gospel, although the one who announces the Gospel must also preach the law.

units.la: In tract.de Cœna Domini cap. 7. sect. 22. affirmant, in nullo neque veteris neq. noui testamenti sacramento Dominum vsum fuisse verbis figuratis: sed semper propriis & simplicibus. Hanc autem sal- sam propositionem, dum adCœnæ verba accommodant, & simplicem ac naturalem singulorum verborum significationem retineri debere contendunt, ipsi si- bi aliis in locis contradicunt. Alibi enim fateri coguntur, Prædicationem sacra- mentalem esse inusitatam, neque tamen figuratam. Quid hoc aliud est quàm pu- gnantia scribere? An enim propriæ enun- tiationes inusitatæ sunt? An verò figura- tæ passim vsitatæ?
units.tr: In the treatise On the Lord's Supper, chapter 7, section 22, they affirm that the Lord never used figurative words in any sacrament of either the Old or the New Testament, but always proper and plain ones. Yet while they adapt this false proposition to the words of the Supper, and contend that the plain and natural meaning of each word must be retained, they contradict themselves elsewhere. For in another place they are forced to confess that the sacramental predication is unusual, yet not figurative. What is this but writing contradictory things? For are proper statements unusual? Or are figurative ones commonly used everywhere?

units.la: Item quamuis nullum tropum, nullam horumverborum aliam quàm simplicem expositionem agnoscant, aut ab aliis af- ferri patiantur: sibi tamen scribunt licet afe aliis enunciatis Christi verba exponente, exemplo scripturæ quæ hanc propositionem Verbum caro factum est, aliter alibi enuntiat, vt Deum manifestatum fuisse in carne, item Assumpsisse carnem. Sic ergo sibi licere pro Hoc est corpus meum, dicere In hoc vel cum hoc vel sub hoc (scilicet pane) est corpus meum. Quid hoc vero est si non est scripturæ auctoritate abuti, & id ipsum agere quod in aliis ferre non possunt? Si tam clara sunt verba Christi, quid hac expositione indigent? Si naturalis est verborum significatio retinenda, cur à verbi substantiui naturali significatione recedunt? Esse enim aliquid, nonne aliud est quàm esse cum aliquo, aut in aliquo, aut sub aliquo? Est ergo & hæc noua doctrina veteri Ecclesiæ incognita, & secum pugnans ac diffidens.
units.tr: Again, although they acknowledge no trope, and allow no other exposition of these words than the simple one, and do not suffer it to be put forward by others, yet they write for themselves that it is permitted to explain the words of Christ by other sayings, on the example of Scripture, which expresses the proposition "The Word was made flesh" differently elsewhere, as that God was manifested in the flesh, and likewise that he assumed flesh. So, they say, it is lawful for them to say, instead of "This is my body", "In this, or with this, or under this (namely, the bread), is my body." What is this but misusing the authority of Scripture, and doing the very thing which they cannot tolerate in others? If the words of Christ are so clear, why do they need this exposition? If the natural meaning of the words must be retained, why do they depart from the natural meaning of the substantive verb? For to be something is surely other than to be with something, or in something, or under something. So this new doctrine too is unknown to the ancient Church, and at odds with itself and unsound.

units.la: Et sect. 23. eiusdem cap. afferere audet tam tres Euangelistas quàm Paulum in historia institutionis & distributionis Cœnæ iisdem verbis & syllabis vsos fuisse absque vlla vel expositione, vel mutatione. Quod ex contextus collatione falsi convincitur. Vbi enim Matthæus simpliciter de corpore loquitur, vt & Marcus: Lucas
units.tr: And in section 23 of the same chapter they dare to assert that the three Evangelists as well as Paul, in the account of the institution and distribution of the Supper, used the same words and syllables without any exposition or alteration. This is shown to be false by comparing the context. For where Matthew speaks simply of the body, as Mark does, Luke

units.la: addit ad maiorem expressionem Quod pro vobis traditur & Paulus pro traditur habet frangitur. In porrećtione itemcalicis vtuntur aliis & quidem diuersissimis verbis, Lucas & Paulus, quàm Matheus & Marcus. Vbi igitur illa verborū & syl labarum identitas ? In eodé cap.seu tract. sępe affirmant verum corpus Christi in sua naturali substantia, recipi & mandu- cari ore corporis. Item & ipsammet sub- stantiam ipsius sanguinis ore sumi & bi- bi. Vnde aliud absurdissimum colligunt, nempe hypocritas & indignos veré fie- ri participes veri corporis & sanguinis Christi, qua ratione Christi corpus à spi- ritu ipsius separant & contradicunt ver- bis Christi qui ait, Qui comedit meam carnem & bibit meum sanguinem habet vitam æternam. Caro enim mea veré est cibus, &c.
units.tr: adds, for fuller expression, "which is given for you", and Paul has "broken" for "is given". In the giving of the cup they use other words, and quite different ones, Luke and Paul than Matthew and Mark. Where, then, is that identity of words and syllables? In the same chapter, or treatise, they often affirm that the true body of Christ in its natural substance is received and eaten with the mouth of the body; and likewise that the very substance of the blood itself is taken and drunk with the mouth. From this they draw another most absurd conclusion, namely that hypocrites and the unworthy really become partakers of the true body and blood of Christ. By this reasoning they separate the body of Christ from his Spirit, and contradict the words of Christ, who says: "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. For my flesh is truly food, etc."

units.la: Item alibi volunt verba institutionis Cœnę Domini cantari in Ecclesia.
units.tr: They also elsewhere want the words of the institution of the Lord's Supper to be sung in the Church.

units.la: Item eodem tract.sect.41. quæ incipit An Deus plures modos, &c. affirmare aut dent, Deum efficere posse vt vnum idém quecorpus, vno eodémque sit momento pluribus simul in locis : modo etiam cor- porali & sensibili. At nos fatemur quidem Deum facere posse, ut corpus, defi-nat corpus esse & statim in nihilum abeat: Ut vero corpus (quod ex Dei decreto fi-nitum est) dum corpus revera est, & manet, pluribus locis simul esse possit, hoc est sit infinitum, Id certe negamus Deum aut velle aut facere. Cum enim finitum esse,& infinitum, sint ex diametro opposita, alterutrum falsò de eodem corpore dici necesse est: Deum autem falsa & pugnantia velle aut facere, non potest sine blasphemia affirmari.
units.tr: Likewise in the same treatise, section 41, which begins "Whether God has more modes, etc.", they affirm or grant that God can make one and the same body, in one and the same moment, to be in several places at once, and in a bodily and sensible way. We indeed acknowledge that God can make a body cease to be a body and at once pass into nothing. But that a body, which by God's decree is finite, while it truly is and remains a body, should be able to be in several places at once, that is, to be infinite, this we deny that God either wills or does. For since to be finite and to be infinite are diametrically opposed, one of the two must necessarily be falsely predicated of the same body; and to affirm that God wills or does things false and contradictory cannot be done without blasphemy. ## On the personal union.

units.la: De Personali unione.

TOto porro tractatu, seu capite 8: de Persona Christi, novum dogma confingunt De hypostatica seu personali duarum naturarum in Christo unione, atq. (ut nos quidem certò existimamus) plane contrarium, tum sacrae scripturae, tum doctrinae à Christiana Ecclesia iam inde ab initio ad haec usque tempora receptae.
units.tr: Throughout their whole treatise, or chapter 8, on the Person of Christ, they devise a new doctrine concerning the hypostatic, or personal, union of the two natures in Christ, which (as we indeed firmly hold) is plainly contrary both to Holy Scripture and to the doctrine received by the Christian Church from the beginning until these times.

units.la: I Primùm enim nomine personae IESV CHRISTI duas quidem naturas (nempe deitatem filij Dei, & humanitatem) in Christo unitas intelligunt: sed ita vt nusquam exprimant hoc nomen hypostaseos, seu personæ ad naturam diuinam proprie referendum, & in ea sola considerandum esse, quia humanitas nō in sese sed in Diuinitate subsistat.
units.tr: 1. For first, under the name of the person of Jesus Christ, they understand indeed the two natures (namely, the deity of the Son of God and the humanity) as united in Christ. But they nowhere express that this name of hypostasis, or person, is to be referred properly to the divine nature and considered in it alone, because the humanity subsists not in itself but in the Deity.

units.la: 2 Secundò non distinguunt inter proprietates essentiales nature diuinæ in communicabiles (quales sunt æternum esse, infinitum esse, ac proinde vbique esse) & illas quarum effectus creaturis communicantur (quales sunt esse, viuere, bonum esse, fortem esse & similes) Quanuis enim proprie loquendo omnes Dei proprietates per se sint incommunicabiles, effecta tamen illarum (quæ in nobis qualitates creatæ dicuntur) incommunicabilia non sunt.
units.tr: 2. Secondly, they do not distinguish between the essential properties of the divine nature that cannot be communicated (such as eternal existence, infinite existence, and therefore being everywhere) and those whose effects are communicated to creatures (such as being, living, being good, being strong, and the like). For although, strictly speaking, all God's properties are in themselves incommunicable, their effects (which in us are called created qualities) are not incommunicable.

units.la: 3 Tertiò abutuntur vocabulo communionis seu communicationis duarum naturarum: Cum eius loco potius coiunctionis seu vnionis nomine vti debuerint propter harum locutionum abusum.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, they abuse the word "communion," or "communication," of the two natures; they ought rather to use the term "conjunction," or "union," because of the abuse of these expressions.

units.la: 4 Quartò confundunt pariter proprietates essentiales nature humanæ (quales sunt finitum, corporeum, circumscriptum, & proinde vno duntaxat loco esse) cum illis quæ sunt accidentariæ, vt sunt samere, sitire, pati, mori, &c.
units.tr: 4. Fourthly, they likewise confuse the essential properties of the human nature (such as being finite, corporeal, circumscribed, and therefore being in only one place) with those that are accidental, such as to be hungry, to thirst, to suffer, to die, and so on.

units.la: § Quintò nullam adhibent distinctione inter hæc nomina, Deus & diuinitas: Homo & humanitas: Quæ tamen necessariò distinguenda sunt vt vitetur hæreses Nestorij & Eutychetis. Istæ.n. propositiones Filius Dei est homo : item, Hic homo est Filius Dei: verissimæ sunt aduersus Neftorium: Sicut & hæ Diuinitas non est huma nitas, & contra Humanitas non est Diuinitas, veræ sunt aduersus Eutychen.
units.tr: Fifthly, they make no distinction between these names, God and divinity, man and humanity, which nevertheless must necessarily be distinguished in order to avoid the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches. For the propositions "the Son of God is man" and "this man is the Son of God" are most true against Nestorius; and likewise these: "the divinity is not the humanity," and conversely "the humanity is not the divinity," are true against Eutyches.

units.la: Sextò inducunt realem communicationem proprietatum essentialium diuinitatis in humanitatem: verbi gratia, esse eodem temporis momento pluribus in locis: Item implere omnia: Et hanc vocant Maiestatem hominis Christi: qua volunt humanitate Christi realiter (vt vocant) esse præsentem vbicunque vult.
units.tr: Sixthly, they introduce a real communication of the essential properties of the divinity into the humanity: for example, being in several places at the same moment of time, and likewise filling all things. And they call this the majesty of the man Christ, by which they want the humanity of Christ to be really (as they say) present wherever he wills.

units.la: Postremo etsi fateantur proprietates humanitatis, non communicari realiter (vt loquuntur) ipsi Diuinitati (qua in re illis assentimur) fateri tamen nolunt solâ Iesu Christi humanitatem passam esse: Quæ tamen sunt ex diametro pugnantia. Ex hac autem personali seu hypostatica vnione male intellecta, isti errores consequuntur:
units.tr: Lastly, although they admit that the properties of the humanity are not really (as they put it) communicated to the Deity itself (in which matter we agree with them), they nevertheless refuse to confess that the humanity of Jesus Christ alone suffered; yet these things are diametrically contradictory. From this personal or hypostatic union, wrongly understood, the following errors follow:

units.la: r D.Iesum Christum non solùm secundum Diuinitatem, sed & secundum suam humanitatem (quæ realiter sit omnium Diuinarum proprietatū particeps) esse vbique seu vbicunque vult, maximè verò in pane & vino Cœnæ Domini.
units.tr: 1. That the Lord Jesus Christ is present, or wherever he wills, not only according to his Deity but also according to his humanity (which is really a partaker of all the divine properties), and above all in the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper.

units.la: 2 Et ex consequenti, Corpus & sanguinem D. Iesu Christi, sumi, manducari, ac bibi ore corporis, ab iis omnibus qui panem & vinum participant siue digni sint, siue indigni.
units.tr: 2. And consequently, that the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ are taken, eaten, and drunk with the mouth of the body by all who partake of the bread and wine, whether they are worthy or unworthy.

units.la: 3 Item, eos qui Dominum Iesum esse tialiter negant in Cœna, tam secundum ipsius humanitatem, quàm secundum Diuinitatem præsentem vbique esse, separare duas naturas. Quasi quicquid de persona dicitur in concreto, etiam & quidem necessariò, de vtraque natura dici debeat in abstracto.
units.tr: 3. Likewise, that those who deny that the Lord Jesus is really present in the Supper separate the two natures, since he is present everywhere according to his humanity as well as according to his Deity. As if whatever is said of the person in the concrete must necessarily also be said of each nature in the abstract.

units.la: 4 Vnionem sacramentalem Corporis & sanguinis Christi cum pane & vino Cœnæ non pendere à sola Institutione, & mandato Domini, sed præcipuè ab hac personali vnione.
units.tr: 4. That the sacramental union of the body and blood of Christ with the bread and wine of the Supper does not depend on the institution and command of the Lord alone, but chiefly on this personal union.

units.la: 5 Glorificatione Humanitatis Christi cœpisse iam inde ab ipso conceptionis momento.
units.tr: 5. That the glorification of the humanity of Christ began from the very moment of conception.

units.la: 6 Omnia miracula à Christo facta, manasse ab hac maiestate quæ humanitati ipsius communicata est: atque vnicam esse in Christo potentiam seu virtutem.
units.tr: 6. That all the miracles done by Christ flowed from this majesty communicated to his humanity, and that there is in Christ one single power or virtue.

units.la: 7 Articulum sessionis ad dextera Patris, intelligendum de hac communicatione Maiestatis quæ a momento conceptionis coepit.
units.tr: 7. That the article of the session at the right hand of the Father is to be understood of this communication of majesty, which began from the moment of conception.

units.la: Item sub finem fere huius tractatus, videntur afferere ipsam diuinitatem secundum suam essentiam, habitare vel habitasse in Petro quemadmodum & in Christo. In expositione autem articuli de Descensu Christi ad Inferos affirmant totam personam Dei & hominis Christi post sepulturam corporis, descendisse ad Inferos. quę doctrina adeo noua est, vt hactenus in Ecclesia Dei nunquam fuerit audita.
units.tr: Likewise, near the end of this treatise, they seem to assert that the Deity itself, according to its essence, dwells, or has dwelt, in Peter just as it does in Christ. In their exposition of the article concerning the descent of Christ into hell, moreover, they affirm that the whole person of God and man, Christ, after the burial of his body, descended into hell. This doctrine is so new that until now it has never been heard in the Church of God.

units.la: In tractatu x. de Ceremoniis, &c. Ordinationem Pastorum & Ministrorum Ecclesiæ ponunt inter res indifferentes: quam tamen constat legitimam non esse nisi ex verbo Dei reformata & restituta obseruetur, & Pastores iuxta præscriptum à Deo ordinem eligantur.
units.tr: In the tenth treatise, on ceremonies, etc., they place the ordination of pastors and ministers of the Church among things indifferent; yet it is certain that it is not lawful unless it is observed as reformed and restored according to the Word of God, and the ministers are chosen in the order prescribed by God.

units.la: Ibidem ordinationem vel confirmationem Pastorum & Ministrorum verbi ab Episcopis Papisticis (qui Euangelij doctrinam amplecti volent) factam, legitimam esse,illíque ius ordinationis competere, etiam in Ecclesiis reformatis concedunt: quod certè nos probare non possumus, quum ij ipsi Episcopi, & plerique ab eis ordinati, sint ex veteribus ipsis canonib. purioribus,imò & à recentibus multis, in ordinatè ordinati: adeò vt ne Papistica quidé ecclesia fuerit eos receptura si qua illic supereßet vera ordinationū species.
units.tr: In the same place they also concede that the ordination or confirmation of pastors and ministers of the Word, performed by Papist bishops (who wish to embrace the doctrine of the Gospel), is lawful, and that the right of ordination belongs to those bishops even in the reformed Churches. This we certainly cannot approve, since those very bishops, and most of those ordained by them, have been ordained irregularly, both according to the older and purer canons themselves and according to many recent ones. So much so that not even the Papist Church would receive them, if any true form of ordination survived there.

units.la: De Prædestinatione.
units.tr: On Predestination.

units.la: IN tractatu de Prædestinatione confundunt vocabulum præscientiæ Dei, qua scilicet Deus scit nouítque omnia, cū nomine prouidentiæ, qua rectè iustéque decernit de omnibus.
units.tr: In their treatise on Predestination they confuse the word foreknowledge of God, by which God knows and has known all things, with the word providence, by which he rightly and justly decrees concerning all things.

units.la: Sic etiam eandem prouidentiam Dei qua cuncta administrat cofundunt cum ipsius prædestinatione, quæ proprie pertinet tum ad salutē Electorū, per Dei misericordiam, tum ad reliquorum condemnationem, ex iusto ipsius iudicio.
units.tr: Likewise they confuse that providence of God, by which he governs all things, with his predestination, which properly concerns both the salvation of the elect, through God's mercy, and the condemnation of the rest, through his just judgment.

units.la: Non agnoscunt Deum (etsi malum, seu peccatum ex sola peccantis malitia oriatur, ob quam iustas pœnas luat) nihilominus iustè decernere quæcunq. & Diabolus & homo male agunt: Neque propterea rea mali authorem vllo pacto existere.
units.tr: They do not acknowledge that God, although evil or sin arises from the sole malice of the sinner, who suffers just punishment for it, nevertheless justly decrees whatever the devil and man do wickedly. Yet for that reason he is in no way the author of evil.

units.la: Nec distingunt inter ꝯeternum Dei co-silium(quod semper iustum est tam respe ƈtu Electorum', quàm reproborum) eius- que executionem, quæ à causis secundis pendet.
units.tr: Nor do they distinguish between God's eternal counsel, which is always just with respect both to the elect and to the reprobate, and its execution, which depends on secondary causes.

units.la: Vocationem,quæ fit per Euãgelij pre- dicationem ita generale costituunt vt ad singulos quosq. homines pertinere eam existiment:Cùm potius indefinita cēsen- da dicendáque sit, hoc est pertinere ad quoduis genus hominum duntaxat, non ad singula indiuidua. Quæ ipsorū doctri- na manifestè pugnat cum iis quę ipsimet scripserunt & docuerunt hoc ipso libro in tractatione de peccato originis, & li- bero arbitrio.
units.tr: They so generalise the calling that comes through the preaching of the Gospel that they think it pertains to each and every person, whereas it ought rather to be regarded and described as indefinite, that is, as pertaining only to some kind of people and not to individuals one by one. Their teaching clearly contradicts what they themselves have written and taught in this same book, in the treatment of original sin and free will.

units.la: Licet autem fateantur electionem nō ad omnes pertinere,suspensum tamen le ƈtorem retinent de Dei consilio circa re- probationem,de qua ne verbo quidē me- minerunt.
units.tr: Although they admit that election does not pertain to all, they nonetheless keep the reader in suspense about God's counsel concerning reprobation, of which they do not say so much as a word.

units.la: In summa toto hoc capite multa ab i- stis dicuntur præter modum ab Augusta na confessione præscriptum:multa à seip- sis admiscét:& à Lutheri doctrina de pre- destinatione longissimē recedunt. Deni- que locis sacrarum literarum sepissimē abutuntur & in alienùm sensum detor-quent:Errores omnino paucos accumu-lant,à nullis adhuc proditos:vt merito di ci possit, hanc tractationem minimè om-nium esse Theologicam & cum sana Do ctrina conuenientem, cuius ipsos auêto-res pudere necesse fuerit, si coram legi-timo cœtu rationem scriptorum suo-rum edere,sicuti in Ecclesia fieri cõsueuit, tenerentur, vt minimè profecto mirum sit,eos examen istud refugisse.
units.tr: In sum, throughout this whole chapter they say many things beyond the measure prescribed by the Augsburg Confession; they add many things of their own; and they depart very far from Luther's doctrine of predestination. Finally, they very often abuse the passages of Holy Scripture and twist them to a foreign sense. They pile up errors, very few of which have been brought forward by anyone before. So it may fairly be said that this treatment is by no means theological or in keeping with sound doctrine. The authors themselves would have had to be ashamed of it, if they had been obliged to give an account of their writings before a lawful assembly, as is customary in the Church. It is therefore hardly surprising that they have shrunk from such an examination.

units.la: Atque hæc hactenus de noua boctrina toto hoc libro sparsa. Nunc de Con-demnationibus huic scripto aduer-sus nos insertis.
units.tr: So much for the new doctrine scattered throughout this whole book. Now let us turn to the condemnations inserted in this writing against us.

units.la: Quamuis nemo nisi legitimè vocatus Iudicis officio fungi,iúsque tum absoluen di tum damnandi vsurpare aut possit aut debeat,nec authores huius scripti quicun que tandem illi sint, appareat vsquam le gitimè ad hoc munus vocatos: Quamuis item nulli iudici iure liceat quèquam dã-nare nisi prius legitimè vocatum, auditû atque conuictum, toto tamen hoc libro, doctrina quæ inde ab initio in aliis Eccle siis recepta atque prędicata fuit, & cui o-stendimus longè plurimas Nationes sub-scripsisse,magistrali supercilio,& summa quaquadam potestate atque autoritate damnantur: idque non sine atrocibus iniuriis atque contumeliis. Quinetiam sub finem præfationis, non solum aperte dicunt, non esse recipiendam illam aliarum Ecclesiarū doctrinam, sed addunt nominatim partem errantem (id est, eos omnes qui huic aliarum Ecclesiarum doctrinæ assentiuntur) nec posse, nec debere in Ecclesia ferri, ac ne excusatione quidem, aut vllo patrocinio dignam esse. Et alibi inter sectas & hereses explosas atque damnatas à veteri Ecclesia nostram doctrinam ideo duntaxat recensent, quia cum ipsorum confessione non conueniat. Vt merito in eos idipsum quod D. Luthe-rus in Pontificiorum condemnationes aduersus Vvicleuum & Ioanne Hus, cordatissime exclamat, torqueri possit. Nolo eos audire (inquit Lutherus in Captiuitate Babylonica) nec tantilli facere, qui clamaturi sunt, Hoc est Vviclephisticum, Hussiticum, hæreticum & contra Ecclesiæ determinationem: & qui suas sententias non alia re probare, nec contrarias a- lia ratione improbare possunt, quàm dicē do, Hoc est Vviclephisticū, Hussiticū, hære-ticū. Hoc.n.elumbe in summa semper natat faliua.atque aliud nihil. Vbi fi petas fcripturam,dicut,Nos fic fentimus,& Ec-clefia(id eft nos ipfi)fic determinauit: A-deo homines reprobi circa fidem,&incre dibiles,nobis fua phantafmata authorita te Ecclefiæ pro articulis fidei audent ob-trudere.Hęc Lutherus in pontificios per uerfos innocentium piorumque hominū cenfores,ac iniquos de doctrina ipforum fuáque iudices,quales certè ifti fex in nos uoftrámq.;doctrinā fe effe,fatis fupérq.tū aliâs femper tū in hoc fcripto prodiderūt, Quidenim frequentius ab iftis auditur, quàm hoc eft Caluinicum, Zvvingliani-cum , Sacramentarium,hereticū . At ve-rò fatis ex fuperioribus conftat quibus quantífque ipfi hærefibus fint contamina ti,& non folùm à noftris ( quos tanquam facramentarios odiofè , fibíque aduerfan tes plenis buccis damnant , fine vlla iufta caufæ cognitione, fed authoritate plus quàm pontificia,ne dicam Pharifaica)de multis,errorib . admoniti:fed & à fuis ho-minib.qui Augustanā confessionē ample-ctuntur & quos de Caluinifmo, vt ipfi vo cant, fufpectos habere non poffunt . Te-ftis eft inter alia,Epiftola ipfa Heshufij ad D.Chemnizium in qua ille desiderat fe-riam riam tum in Iacobo Andrea, tum in Selneccero, tum in Crellio refipiscentiam & recantationem priusquam pro fratribus eos agnoscat. De Andrea Musculo, quæ sit omnium piorum in Germania opinio, testantur aliorum scripta. En igitur quales habeantur isti censores & iudices inter suos. Taceo enim aliorum de his iudicia à quibus merito, vt nouatores & hereticî taxantur. Habeant ergo ipsi D. ipsum Lutherum iudicem huius temeritatis, & audaciæ, qua non secus in nos feruntur quàm olim Pontificij in Vviclephum, & Hussium. Quomodo enim nõ solùm suos calamos, sed etiam Principum gladios & seueritatem in nostros acuere studeant, tum ex Brentij testamento, tum aliunde quoque constat.
