Et hunc librum omnes norunt fuisse ab ipsis scriptum non alio fine quàm vt optimorum Principum (qui nostra nunquam cognouerunt) autoritate ad eos omnes proscribendos abutantur, qui non fuerint sexvirorum istorum tyrannidi assensi.
units.tr: Although no one may or should exercise the office of judge, or claim the right to absolve or to condemn, unless he has been lawfully called; and although it nowhere appears that the authors of this writing, whoever they may be, have been lawfully called to this task; and although likewise no judge may by right condemn anyone unless he has first been lawfully summoned, heard and convicted: nevertheless, throughout this whole book, the doctrine that has been received and preached from the beginning in other Churches, and which we have shown to have been subscribed by by far the greater part of the nations, is condemned with a schoolmasterly arrogance and with a certain supreme power and authority, and that not without savage insults and abuse. Moreover, at the end of the preface they not only openly say that the teaching of the other Churches is not to be received, but they add by name that the erring part (that is, all those who assent to the teaching of the other Churches) cannot and should not be tolerated in the Church, and is not worthy of excuse or any defence whatever. Elsewhere, among the sects and heresies cast out and condemned by the ancient Church, they list our doctrine merely because it does not agree with their own confession. So it may rightly be turned against them what Dr. Luther, in the condemnations of the Papists, cried out so wisely against Wycliffe and John Hus. "I do not want to hear them," says Luther in the Babylonian Captivity, "nor to make so little of those who will cry out, 'This is Wycliffite, Hussite, heretical, and contrary to the determination of the Church'; and who cannot prove their opinions by any other means, nor refute opposing ones by any other argument, than by saying, 'This is Wycliffite, Hussite, heretical.' For this slobbering fool always swims in saliva and nothing else. If you ask for Scripture, he says: 'We think so, and the Church (that is, we ourselves) has so determined.' Thus reprobate men, unbelieving in matters of faith, dare to force their fantasies upon us as articles of faith, under the authority of the Church." These are Luther's words against the Papists, who turned their censure against innocent and pious men, and who were unjust judges of their doctrine. Such are certainly those six men, who have made it sufficiently and more than sufficiently plain, both on other occasions and in this writing, what they are toward us and our doctrine. For what is heard more often from them than this: "It is Calvinistic, Zwinglian, sacramentarian, heretical"? Yet it is sufficiently clear from what has been said above with what heresies they themselves are defiled. They have been admonished about many errors not only by ours (whom they damn with full cheeks as sacramentarians, hateful to them and opposed to them, without any just examination of the cause, and with an authority more than papal, not to say Pharisaical), but also by their own people, who embrace the Augsburg Confession and whom they cannot suspect of Calvinism, as they call it. A witness among others is the letter of Heshusius himself to Dr. Chemnitz, in which he desires a serious repentance and recantation from Jacob Andreae, from Selnecker and from Crell before he will acknowledge them as brothers. About Andreas Musculus, what the opinion of all the godly in Germany is, the writings of others bear witness. Behold, then, what sort of censors and judges they are considered among their own people. For I say nothing of the judgments of others about them, by whom they are rightly branded as innovators and heretics. Let them therefore have Dr. Luther himself as judge of this rashness and audacity, with which they assail us no less than the Papists once assailed Wycliffe and Hus. For it is also clear, both from Brenz's testament and from elsewhere, how eagerly they sharpen not only their pens but also the swords and severity of princes against ours. And all know that this book was written by them for no other purpose than to abuse the authority of the best princes (who have never known our teaching) to proscribe all those who have not assented to the tyranny of these six men.

units.la: At si iustus hic esset defensionis locus, aduersus ipsorum criminationes, quibus nos vt hereticos & sectarios apud omnes ordines traducunt: possemus merito de innocentia nostra non solùm verbis glo- riari : sed re ipsa ( Deo sit omnis hæc glo- ria)palàm facere, quanta nobis fiat ab ip- sis iniuria.Hoc certè ne ipsis quidem Pon- tificiis ignotũ est, in nostris Ecclesiis quã- tumuis latè pateant & per varias Euro- pẹ regiones diffusẹ sint, nullas hucvsque sectas fuisse , nullum peregrinum dog- ma aut à præcipuis Cõfessionis nostræ ca- pitibus dissidens, adhuc repertũ summo Dei beneficio,qui puras illas sub tot cru- cibus hucvsque seruauit . Vt de illis om- nibus quæ in Anglia,Scotia,Belgio, Ger- mania,Heluetia,Polonia,Bohemia, Vnga ria,Gallia denique, eandem atq . nos do- ctrinam variis confessionib.professę sunt, verè illud vsurpari possit, quod de Zvin- glio & Oecolàpadio D.Lutherus aliquã do dixit. Hoc certũ est(inquitLutherus) bis dissonent, tamen de re idem sentire. Non posse autem istos de suarum Eccle- siarum tali concordia & puritate gloria- ri,hoc ipsum eorum scriptum manifestè testatur.In quo incautè sanè,& intempe- stiuè proferunt & veluti velitant omnes cõtrouersias,&diuersissima dogmáta,quę in omnibus fere doctrinæ capitib . in suis EccleEcclesiis adhuc reperiuntur. Hoccine est Pontificiis os obstruere? quos nō ignorāt ipsis iamdudū exprobrasse (utinam non tam verè, quàm inuidiosè) Nullas vsquam Ecclesias magis nūc de fidei doctrina dissentientes reperiri quàm eas quæ ab vno architecto Luthero fundatæ, in tot sectas dissectæ, se mutuo conficiunt miserèque proscindunt. Satius foret igitur istas controuersias silentio consopitas, quàm hoc libro vulgatas, vt solis Sacramentariis maior conflaretur inuidia, quos præcipuè in hoc libro exagitant, & temerè multa illis falsò impingunt.
units.tr: But if there were a just occasion for defence against their accusations, by which they disparage us as heretics and sectaries before all orders, we could rightly boast of our innocence not only in words but in fact, and show plainly (to God be all this glory) how great the injury is that they do to us. This is certainly not unknown even to the Papists themselves: that in our Churches, however widely they extend and however far they are spread through the various regions of Europe, no sects have so far arisen, and no foreign doctrine dissenting from the principal heads of our Confession has yet been discovered, by the highest blessing of God, who has preserved those pure doctrines through so many crosses until now. And as for all those in England, Scotland, the Low Countries, Germany, Switzerland, Poland, Bohemia, Hungary and finally France, who have professed the same doctrine as we do in various confessions, what Dr. Luther once said of Zwingli and Oecolampadius may truly be applied to them: "This is certain, they differ in words, yet agree in substance." That they cannot glory in such concord and purity of their own Churches is clearly attested by this very writing of theirs. In it, rashly and untimely indeed, they bring forward and as it were skirmish over all the controversies and very diverse opinions that are still found in their own Churches on almost all the heads of doctrine. Is this how to stop the mouths of the Papists, who, as they know, have long reproached them (would it were not as truly as it is hatefully) that nowhere are Churches found more divided about the doctrine of faith than those founded by one architect, Luther, and cut into so many sects, which consume and miserably tear one another apart. It would therefore have been better to let these controversies lie buried in silence, rather than to publish them in this book, so that greater hatred might be stirred up against the Sacramentarians alone, whom they chiefly harass in this book, and against whom they rashly hurl many false charges.

units.la: Nam (vt tandem præcipuas ipsorū calumnias toto hoc libro sparsas recensea- mus) præter illas generales condemnationes quas supra attigimus: initio fere capitis de Cœna Domini, nostram de ea confessionem & sententiam, petniciosissimū errorem & verbo Dei penitus repugnantem, ac sæpe damnatum pronuntiare audent: quamuis nulla vnquam ad eam examinandam aut conuincendam, legitima cognitio habita, aut Ecclesiastica Synodus coacta adhuc fuerit.
units.tr: For, to list at last the chief calumnies scattered through this whole book, besides those general condemnations which I mentioned above, they dare, almost at the beginning of the chapter on the Lord's Supper, to pronounce our confession and opinion on it a most pernicious error, utterly repugnant to the Word of God and often condemned, although no lawful inquiry has ever been held to examine or refute it, nor has any ecclesiastical synod yet been convened for that purpose.

units.la: Eandem alibi sæpe condemnationem repetunt, & quidem verbis multò atrocioribus vt fect.31. quæ incipit Quamobrem omnes orthodoxi &c. & fect.228, 230, & 232. Vbi nos quidē hisce iniuriis proscin- dunt, vt nos vocent Sacramentarios, hę- reticos, phreneticos, venenosos, pernicio sos, stupidos, verucces, fantasticos, Doctri nam autem nostram errore perniciosum falsum, erroneum, decipiens,&c.
units.tr: They repeat the same condemnation elsewhere, and in far harsher words, as in section 31, which begins "Wherefore all the orthodox," etc., and in sections 228, 230 and 232. There they tear us apart with these insults, calling us Sacramentarians, heretics, frantics, poisonous, pernicious, stupid, warty, fanatics, and calling our doctrine pernicious, false, erroneous, deceptive, and so on.

units.la: Vt autem constet de fundamēto, quo istiusmodi Magistrales condemnationes niuntur, prēterquam quod omnes quib. ipsorum opiniones non probantur, pro hæreticis habēt: istas insuper calumnias nobis imponunt.
units.tr: But to show what foundation such magisterial condemnations rest on: apart from the fact that they count as heretics all those whose opinions they do not approve, they also impose these calumnies upon us.

units.la: Primū initio tractatus de Cœna Domi ni.fect. 1. & 4.dicūt Nostras ecclesias sta- tim ab initio secessisse ac sese segregasse à Theologis Confessionis Augustanæ,non secus acsi separatam ab illis Religionem colere instituissemus, nihilque eorū pro- baremus, quę Confessione illorum conti nerentur. Quod certe tam est à vero alie- num, vt pauca sint in ea confessione quæ ad amussim verbi Dei examinata nostri non facilē omni tempore recipere & pro bare parati fuissent: si ad illam non ac- cessissent tot variæ ac dissidentes ipsorū interpretationes.
units.tr: First, at the beginning of the treatise on the Lord's Supper, in sections 1 and 4, they say that our churches broke away and separated themselves from the theologians of the Confession of Augsburg from the very beginning, as if we had set about cultivating a religion apart from them and approved nothing of what their confession contains. This is certainly so far from the truth that there are few statements in that confession which, when weighed exactly against the Word of God, our people would not have been ready at all times to accept and approve, had not so many different and conflicting interpretations of theirs stood in the way.

units.la: Deinde sect.2. & 49, eiusdem tractatus falsò nos accusant, quasi Corpus Domini nostri Iesu Christi à sacra ipsius Coena prorsus secludamus, quia dicimus illud iā nō in terris esse corporaliter, sed in cælo.
units.tr: Then, in sections 2 and 49 of the same treatise, they falsely accuse us of wholly excluding the body of our Lord Jesus Christ from his holy Supper, because we say that it is no longer on earth bodily, but in heaven.

units.la: Eadem item sect.2, & 6.calumniosè dicunt nos non plus tribuere communicationi Christi, quæ fit per sacramentorum distributionem, quàm illi quæ fit sola nudáque verbi prædicatione.
units.tr: Likewise, in sections 2 and 6 of the same, they say slanderously that we attribute no more to the communion of Christ which takes place through the distribution of the sacraments than to that which takes place by the bare preaching of the Word alone.

units.la: Item sect. eadem & sect.43 & 50. Arguunt nos (sed perperā) quod doceamus in Coena Domini ore nihil aliud recipi quàm panem & vinum: quasi nullum constituamus discrimen inter panem & vinum quæ sacramenta sunt; & panem ac vinum commune.
units.tr: Likewise, in the same section and in sections 43 and 50, they charge us (but wrongly) with teaching that in the Lord's Supper only bread and wine are received by the mouth, as if we made no distinction between bread and wine, which are sacraments, and common bread and wine.

units.la: Ibidem & sect.44. ac 45. Causantur nos (perinde ac Anabaptistas) docere sacramenta nihil esse aliud quàm externas notas, & tesseras, quibus Christiani ab infidelibus distinguuntur: quod millies à nobis refutatum est.
units.tr: In the same place and in sections 44 and 45, they accuse us (just like the Anabaptists) of teaching that the sacraments are nothing but external marks and tokens by which Christians are distinguished from unbelievers; a charge we have refuted a thousand times.

units.la: Item nos statuere Christū in sacra Coena secundum diuinā tantùm natura præsentem esse: & per communicationem (vt aiunt) Idiomatum: de quo dogmate nunquam cogitauimus. Item sect.24. & 44. falsò afferunt, Nos docere, quòd in sacra Cœna non fiamus participes veri corporis Christi, sed tantum ac simpliciter virtutis ipsius, energiæ, meriti, & efficaciæ: Quasi verò idcirco separemus virtutem atque meritum Christi ab ipso Christo, ita vt alterius sine alte ro dicamus nos fieri participes, quòd sub stantiam Christi negemus nostræ aggluti nari, aut Christū aliter quā fide percipi.
units.tr: Also, that we hold that Christ is present in the holy Supper according to his divine nature only, and by the communication (as they call it) of properties; a doctrine we have never even thought of. Also, in sections 24 and 44, they falsely assert that we teach that in the holy Supper we do not become partakers of the true body of Christ, but only of his power, energy, merit and efficacy simply. As if we separated the power and merit of Christ from Christ himself, so that we said we become partakers of the one without the other, because we deny that the substance of Christ is joined to ours, or that Christ is received otherwise than by faith.

units.la: Item, sect. 3. quòd doceamus, Nos non communicare in Cœna, nisi symbolo cor poris Christi.
units.tr: Also, in section 3, that we teach that we do not communicate in the Supper except by the symbol of the body of Christ.

units.la: Item, alibi sect.22. imponūt nobis quasi dicamus Panem ipsum Cœnæ metonymi cè sumi pro cibo spirituali animarum, nō pro vero pane naturali.
units.tr: Also, elsewhere, in section 22, they impute to us that we say the bread of the Supper is taken metonymically for the spiritual food of souls, not for true natural bread.

units.la: Item sect.37. Quod panis & vinū Cœ-næ sint sacramenta virtute fidei nostræ, non autem virtute institutionis IesuChri sti, aut omnipotentiæ ipsius.
units.tr: Also, in section 37, that the bread and wine of the Supper are sacraments by virtue of our faith, and not by virtue of the institution of Jesus Christ or his omnipotence.

units.la: Item sect.43.& 44. Quod panis & & vi nū sint signa absentis Christi àCœna sua, quādoquidē dicimus corp9 IesuChristi in cœlo esse, panē vero &vinū in terra. Quę consecutio tam est valida, ac si quis dice-ret, Caput à pedibus separatum esse, quia non sit caput eodem loco quo pedes.
units.tr: Also, in sections 43 and 44, that the bread and wine are signs of Christ's absence from his Supper, since we say that the body of Jesus Christ is in heaven and the bread and wine on earth. This inference is as valid as if someone said that the head is separated from the feet because it is not in the same place as the feet.

units.la: Item eadem sectione fingunt nos asserere, fidem discedere à Coena, quia dicimus eam à signis sese in cœlos attollere: quamuis & ipsi canant Sursum corda.
units.tr: Also, in the same section they pretend that we assert that faith departs from the Supper, because we say that it lifts itself up to heaven from the signs; although they too sing "Lift up your hearts."

units.la: Item sect.45.accusant nos falsi, quòd perfidè & malitiosè locum illum, Act.3. (Oportet Christum cœlo capi vsque ad tempora restitutionis omnium) corrupe-rimus, quum ipsi inficiari non possint, verum esse Christi corpus ac proinde in cœlis capi, id est, secundum veri corporis modum ibi contineri.
units.tr: In section 45 they accuse us of falsehood, saying that we have treacherously and maliciously corrupted that passage in Acts 3 ("Christ must be received into heaven until the times of the restoration of all things"), since they cannot deny that Christ's body is true and therefore contained in heaven, that is, held there according to the manner of a true body.

units.la: Item sect.47.dicunt nos omittere verba institutionis in celebratione Coenæ: Quod putidissimum mendacium & nostris liturgiis, & hominum myriadibus convinci potest.
units.tr: Also, in section 47, they say we omit the words of institution in the celebration of the Supper. This is a most putrid lie, which can be refuted by our liturgies and by myriads of men.

units.la: Atque vt hanc doctrinam impiam, & in sacramentum corporis Christi blasphemam, esse probent, subinde Lutheri auctoritatem proferunt qui eam pro tali habuit, & ad ipsius scripta nos relegant. Quasi nobis non perinde liceret à Luthe-ri scriptis ad nostrorum Doctorum scripta eos revocare, si humana auctoritate fi-dem nostram stabilire & confirmare suf-ficeret. Cæterum etsi de Luthero (vt su-prà dictum est) id sentimus, quod de ex-cellente Dei organo, hominem tamen eū fuisse & aliorũ quoque Doctorum Eccle‐fiæ iudiciis subiectum, ipsemet, fi super‐stes effet, non negaret. Sed & illud res ipsa clamat eum æstu & ardore difputationũ extra metas nonnũquam fuisse abreptũ. Verumtamen istis condemnationibus & criminationibus Lutheri opponi etiam possunt multę aliæ præclaræ ipsius sententiæ, à nostra doctrina non ita alienę. Nam quod isti in nobis reprehendunt dum di‐cimus cum Augustino, modo loquendi facramentali, nomen rei significatę signo tribui: Vt panis dicatur corpus Christi quia fit sacramentum, id est sacrum fignũ corporis Chriftı. Hoc ipsum Lutherus quoq; fatetur in suis ad cap. 6. Efaiæ com‐mentariis: Vbi dicit Propheta fe vidisse Dominum, cum tamẽ (inquit Lutherus) non nisi in visione viderit: Et tamen ap‐pellat id quod in visione vidit Dominũ. Et vt species Domini, & Dominus, figu‐ ra sermonis, recte pro eodem accipiũtur: sic corpus Domini, & panis Domini, pro vno accipiuntur. Quid potuit dici ma‐gis perspicuè, ad confirmandam no‐ftram sententiam, qua dicimus figura‐tam esse locutionem in verbis Domini? Simile est & illud quod isti Theologi tan‐topere exagitant, dum dicimus ita diftinguendum esse signum a re sacramenti, vt non statim consequatur, quòd quicunq. sumit signum, fiat etiam particeps rei signatæ. Infideles enim tantùm sumere panem non corpus. Hoc etiam fatetur & Lutherus dum scribit Tom 2. pag.31. b. Turpissimũ fœdissimúmque est opprobrium, vel vnum inueniri Episcopum, qui nesciat sacramentum a corpore Christi sti distinguere, quæ sic differúnt, vt nec oriens nec occidens tato distinguantur. Item Tom.7.f.4.12. Vtile est, inquit, & bonum superbos & impios conuitiatores ita separari, vt à participatione sacrosanctæ Cœnæ arceantur, & seiungantur: Nam sanctum non est dandum canibus, neque margaritæ porcis proiiciendæ. Et paulò post (quod tamen immerito in nos detorquet.) Quare cùm sacramentarij credant tantùm panem, & vinum ibi adesse, certum est rem, fidei suæ respondere, nihilque amplius adesse quàm quod credunt. Merum igitur panem & vinum sumunt, & corpore Domini neque spiritualiter, neque carnaliter fruuntur. Et hoc quidem vtile bonúmque censeri debet, quòd nostèr ille thesaurus ad indignos non dispergatur: sed integer, & san ëtus in Cœna reconditus conseruetur. Hæc Lutherus, quibus manifestè comprobat nostram de indignorum manducatione sententiam, sicut etiam ab initio in lib.de captiuitate Babylonica scripsit rectissimè, Dominum Cœnam instituendo, hæredes eos instituisse corporis & sanguinis sui, qui acceptant, & credunt promissioni testatoris. fides enim hîc hæredes facit: Et postea addit: Si promissio est (vt dictum est) nullis operibus, nullis viribus, nullis meritis ad eam acceditur, sed sola fide. Vbi enim est verbum promittentis, ibi necessaria est fides acceptantis &c. Quid potuit clarius dici in nostræ causæ (quam censores isti condemnant) patrocinium? Quod si isti repudient, & ex aliis locis Lutheri agere in nos non desinant, concilient prius istas Lutheri antinomias: desinant denique se eius vnius authoritate tueri, & nos damnare. Sed vt ad reliquos errores redeamus quos isti nobis immeritò ascribunt: Eadem fide initio capitis de PersonaChristi culpam controuersiæ & disputationis de Vbiquitate sua monstrosa, in Zvvingliũ & doctores nostræ confessionis transferre conantur. Neque enim nostra doctrina de na de Humana natura & veri ac naturalis corporis Christi in cœlum ascensu: (quę sacris literis consentanea est) caussa fuit, vt isti inuehere monstrum illud Vbiquitatis cogerentur, sed potius falsa ipso rum thesis de præsentia corporali & orali sumptione corporis Christi realis in, sub & cum pane, quam mordicus retinere ac tueri quo iure quáve iniuria constituerunt, in causa fuit cur desciuerint non solùm ab omnibus aliis Augustanæ confessionis sociis, verùm etiam ab omnibus Ecclesiis quotquot vnquam in toto terrarum orbe Christianissimum sunt professæ. In quibus nemo repertus est (istis vnis exceptis) qui errorem istum Vbiquitatis impiissimum, & toti primitiuæ Ecclesiæ ignotum, non sit detestatus. Adeò vt hæc sit prima ipsorū valde impudens calumnia, qua nos in hoc capite doctrinæ de Persona Christi eiúsque maiestate, graue niτuntur.
units.tr: And to prove that this doctrine is impious and blasphemous against the sacrament of Christ's body, they repeatedly bring forward the authority of Luther, who held it to be such, and refer us to his writings. As if it were not equally open to us to call them back from Luther's writings to the writings of our own teachers, if it were enough to establish and confirm our faith by human authority. Yet although we think of Luther (as has been said above) as an excellent instrument of God, he was nonetheless a man, subject also to the judgments of other teachers of the Church, as he himself, if he were still alive, would not deny. And the thing itself cries out that in the heat and ardour of disputation he was sometimes carried beyond bounds. Moreover, against these condemnations and accusations of Luther many other excellent sayings of his can also be set, not far removed from our doctrine. For what they find fault with in us, when we say with Augustine, in the sacramental manner of speaking, that the name of the thing signified is given to the sign, so that bread is called the body of Christ because it is made a sacrament, that is, a holy sign of the body of Christ, Luther himself admits this in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 6, where the prophet says he saw the Lord, though (says Luther) he saw him only in a vision; and yet he calls what he saw in the vision the Lord. And just as "the appearance of the Lord" and "the Lord" are rightly taken for the same thing by a figure of speech, so "the body of the Lord" and "the bread of the Lord" are taken as one. What could have been said more plainly to confirm our view, that the expression in the Lord's words is figurative? Similar is what those theologians so greatly harass, when we say that the sign must be so distinguished from the thing of the sacrament that it does not follow at once that whoever takes the sign is also made a partaker of the thing signified. For unbelievers take only the bread, not the body. Luther too admits this when he writes (vol. 2, p. 31b): "It is a most base and foul disgrace if even one bishop is found who does not know how to distinguish the sacrament from the body of Christ; they differ so much that East and West are not so far apart." Likewise (vol. 7, f. 4.12): "It is useful and good," he says, "that proud and impious revilers be so separated that they are kept back and cut off from participation in the most holy Supper; for what is holy must not be given to dogs, nor pearls cast before swine." And a little later (though he wrongly twists this against us): "Therefore, since the sacramentarians believe that only bread and wine are there, it is certain that the thing corresponds to their faith, and nothing more is present than what they believe. So they take mere bread and wine, and enjoy the body of the Lord neither spiritually nor carnally. And this indeed ought to be judged useful and good, that our treasure is not scattered among the unworthy, but is kept whole and holy, laid up in the Supper." Thus Luther; by which he clearly confirms our view about the eating of the unworthy, just as he also wrote most rightly at the beginning of his book On the Babylonian Captivity, that in instituting the Supper the Lord made heirs of his body and blood those who accept and believe the promise of the testator: "for faith here makes heirs." And afterwards he adds: "If it is a promise (as has been said), it is approached by no works, no powers, no merits, but by faith alone. For where the word of the one promising is, there the faith of the one accepting is necessary," etc. What could have been said more clearly in defence of our cause, which these censors condemn? But if they reject this, and do not cease to bring Luther's other passages against us, let them first reconcile these contradictions of Luther's; and finally let them stop defending themselves by his authority alone and condemning us. But to return to the remaining errors which they wrongly ascribe to us: with the same boldness, at the beginning of the chapter on the Person of Christ, they try to transfer the blame for the controversy and dispute about his monstrous ubiquity onto Zwingli and the teachers of our confession. For our doctrine about the human nature of Christ and the ascension of his true and natural body into heaven (which agrees with the sacred letters) was not the cause for which they were forced to bring forward that monster of ubiquity; rather, the cause was their own false thesis about the bodily presence and oral reception of the body of Christ, really in, under and with the bread, which they stubbornly hold and defend, whether by right or by wrong. This is why they departed not only from all the other allies of the Confession of Augsburg, but also from all the churches, however many have ever professed Christianity throughout the whole world. In those churches no one has been found (apart from these men alone) who has not detested that most impious error of ubiquity, unknown to the whole primitive Church. So this is their first, very shameless calumny, by which they weigh heavily upon us in this chapter of doctrine concerning the Person of Christ and his majesty.

units.la: Addunt autem postea etiam alias, non minus falsas: Vt quum initio eiusdem tractatus dicere & inferre audent: Nos, quia ex verbo Dei docemus proprietates essentiales Diuinitatis (quarum nulla Creatura capax esse potest) non posse tribui Humanitati Christi, quòd alioqui Natura eius humana esse desineret: propterea inquâ dicunt nos negare Maiestatem humanæ ipsius naturæ à Diuinitate acceptam, cùm Humanitati ad omnem plenitudinem (longè alio modo, & supra quàm cum aliis vllis creaturis) Diuinitas vnita fit.
units.tr: They also add other charges, no less false. At the start of the same treatise they dare to say and infer that we, because from the Word of God we teach that the essential properties of the Godhead (of which no creature can be capable) cannot be attributed to the humanity of Christ, since otherwise his human nature would cease to be human, therefore, they say, we deny that the majesty received by the human nature itself from the Godhead is attributed to it, although the Godhead is united to the humanity in all its fullness (in a manner far different from, and above, that of any other creature).

units.la: Itė, quia dicimus ea quæ propria sunt, & essentialia humanitatis, humanitati esse tribuenda, vt & illa quæ propria sunt & essētialia Diuinitatis Diuinitati (quâuis modo illo loquendi qui vocatur àTheol. κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων, vel Alloeosis in concreto (at non in abstracto) fiat vt vel ea quę sunt propria Dei, tribuantur homini, veluti quum dicitur filius hominis fuisse in cœlo, etsi Nicodemum alloqueretur interius, vel quę sunt hominis Deo, vt quū dicitur Deus glorię fuisse crucifixus) dicunt nos non toti personę Christi tribuere, ea quę vnius tantum sunt naturę propria, & ita diuidere personam.
units.tr: Again, because we say that the properties that are proper and essential to the humanity are to be attributed to the humanity, and likewise that the properties proper and essential to the Godhead are to be attributed to the Godhead (although, by that mode of speaking which theologians call communication of properties [κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων], or alloeosis in the concrete (but not in the abstract), it happens that either what is proper to God is attributed to man, as when it is said that the Son of Man was in heaven while he was speaking inwardly with Nicodemus, or what belongs to man is attributed to God, as when it is said that the Lord of glory was crucified), they say that we do not attribute these things to the whole person of Christ, and so that we divide the person.

units.la: Hęc sunt præcipua argumenta quibus putant nos iam de hisce erroribus conuictos, merito pro hereticis esse damnandos. At prius iusto iudicio cio & examine discutiendum fuit, An ita vt ipsi putât setiamus, quod longissimè à nobis abesse, Deum & homines testamur : Deinde an errores , aut hereses sint quę ipsi pro heresibus & erroribus nobis imputant. Nec fuit ςam temere falsis tot piarum & celebrium Ecclesiarum condemnationib.indulgedū.
units.tr: These are the main arguments by which they think we have already been convicted of these errors and rightly deserve to be condemned as heretics. But it first ought to have been discussed and examined with a just judgement, whether we hold what they think we hold, which is very far from us, since we testify that God and men are one. Then, whether the errors or heresies they impute to us are really errors or heresies. Nor should so many condemnations of pious and famous Churches have been rashly indulged on false grounds.

units.la: NVnc vero ad tertium & vltimū caput veniendum est, quo queritur: An hoc scriptum probè cum Augustana confessione conueniat,& iisdem (vt eius authores iactant)fundamentis nitatur.
units.tr: Now we must come to the third and last point, in which it is asked whether this writing agrees properly with the Augsburg Confession, and rests on the same foundations (as its authors boast).

units.la: Est autem luce meridiana clarius,& sa tis ex nouis dogmatibus quæ supra à nobis commemorata, & ex hoc libro colle- ta sunt, probatum, abuti istos sex Theologos non solùm authoritatę, & nomine Augustanæ confessionis atque Apologiæ,sed & scriptis ipsius D.Lutheri, quę toties citant tanquam authorem omnium suorum dogmatum: cuiq. plus tribuunt, quàm ipse sibi vnquā arrogare ausus sit, idq.vt audacius aliis omnib.Ecclesiis quę cunque volent præscribant, & veluti ex Tripode aliqua pronuntient.
units.tr: It is clearer than the noonday sun, and has been sufficiently proved from the new doctrines recounted above by us and collected from this book, that these six theologians abuse not only the authority and name of the Augsburg Confession and its Apology, but also the writings of Dr Luther himself, whom they cite so often as the author of all their doctrines, and to whom they attribute more than he ever dared to claim for himself; and they do this so that they may prescribe more boldly to all other Churches whatever they wish, and pronounce as if from a tripod.

units.la: Id vero à nobis non fingi aut falsò illis imponi,ex ipsius D. Lutheri testimonio, patebit & ex collatione sincera aliquot capitum doctrinæ ipsorum cum Augusta na confessione.
units.tr: That we are not inventing this or falsely imposing it on them will be shown both from the testimony of Dr Luther himself and from a sincere comparison of some heads of their doctrine with the Augsburg Confession.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem neque Confessio Augustana neque eius Apologia, de orali corporis Christi manducatione vllam mentionem continent : sed loquuntur tantùm de vera ipsius corporis in Cœna Domini præsentia, distributione & perceptione. Quæ nos(modò sincerè & iuxta fidei analogiam,& sacramentales locutiones, intelligantur ) nunquam negaiimus,ac ne nunc quidem negamus. Quan uis autem D. Lutherus de ea orali manducatione, multa in polemicis suis scriptis odiosè satis & vehementius certè quàm tantum virum decuit, in nostros scripserit : tamen eam doctrinam ex Augustana confessione , aut eius Apologia probare isti non possunt:Et scimus quan tum D. Lutherus ipse suo huic dogmati authoritatis tribuedum sentiat. Sic enim ille de se scribit sub finem libri de captiui tate Babylonica,in quo multa certè modestius de hoc dogma te tradidit, quàm postea vbi contentionibus exacerbatus bilem continere non potuit: Fine, inquit, hic faciam huius præludij, quod piis omnibus qui sinceram scripturæ intelligentiam germanúmque sacramentorum vsum desiderant nosse, libens & gaudens offero. Est enim non parui momenti donum, nosse ea quæ nobis data sunt, vt 1. Cor. 2. dicitur, & qua ratione donatis vti oporteat. Hoc enim spiritus iudicio instructi non fallaciter innitemur iis quæ se cus habent. Has duas res cū nobis Theologi nostri nusquam dederint, quin velut data opera obscurarint, ego si non de di, certe id feci ne obscurarem, & aliis occasionem præbui MELIORA COGITANDI. Conatus meus saltem fuit vt exhiberem vtrumque; non tamen omnia possumus omnes. Ex quibus rursus apparet non solum suam conditionem, & mediocritate modeste D. Lutherum agnouisse, sed nul lis etiam præscribere in doctrina Cœnæ Domini voluisse, vt suam opinione mordicus retinerent: meliora enim fatetur posse ab aliis afferri, quæ ipse videre aut præstare non potuerit. Idem de se suisq. aliis & quidem postremis scriptis iudicium fieri cupit in præfatione suorum operum. hæc enim sunt ipsius verba: Ante „ omnia oro pium leſtore, & oro propter „ Dominum noſtrum Iesum Christum, vt „ ista legat cum iudicio,imo cum multa mi „ feratione, & sciat me aliquando fuisse „ monachum,&c. Quae est igitur haec mo- deftiae ipsius inusta nota, cum vel omnes Ecclesias ad huius vnius scripta isti alliga re contendunt, vel quicquid iste sensit, pro oraculo haberi volunt,adeo vt ne hi- fcere quidem contra liceat: omniaque aliorum scripta ad huius sententiam re- uocare, etsi nihil eiusmodi contineant? Inde igitur apparet primum, hoc dogma de orali manducatione, nullum habere in Confessione, aut eius Apologia funda mentum,ac proinde condemnationes in nos hoc scripto effusas, horum scriptorum authoritate minime niti.
units.tr: And first, neither the Augsburg Confession nor its Apology contains any mention of the oral eating of the body of Christ, but they speak only of the true presence, distribution and reception of his body in the Lord's Supper. We have never denied these things, provided they are understood sincerely and according to the analogy of faith and sacramental modes of speech, and we do not deny them even now. Although Dr Luther, in his polemical writings, wrote much against our side about that oral eating, with enough bitterness and certainly more vehemence than became so great a man, yet these men cannot prove that doctrine from the Augsburg Confession or its Apology. And we know how much weight Dr Luther himself thought should be given to his own authority in this dogma. For he writes thus of himself at the end of the book On the Babylonian Captivity, in which he taught many things about this dogma far more modestly than he later did, when, exasperated by controversies, he could not restrain his bile: "I will end here this prelude," he says, "which I offer gladly and willingly to all the pious who desire to know the true understanding of Scripture and the genuine use of the sacraments. For it is no small gift to know what has been given to us, as it is said in 1 Cor. 2, and in what way those gifts ought to be used. For instructed by the judgement of the Spirit, we shall not fallaciously rely on things that are otherwise. Since our theologians have never granted us these two things, but have always, as if deliberately, obscured them, I, if I have not taught them, have at least taken care not to obscure them, and have given occasion to others for THINKING BETTER THINGS. My endeavour has at least been to set forth both; yet we cannot all do everything." From these words it appears again that Dr Luther not only acknowledged his own condition and modestly his mediocrity, but also did not wish to prescribe to anyone in the doctrine of the Lord's Supper that they should cling stubbornly to his opinion: for he confesses that better things can be brought forward by others, which he himself could not see or achieve. He wishes the same judgement to be made of himself and of his other writings, even the last ones, in the preface to his works. For these are his own words: "Above all I beg the pious reader, and I beg it for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he read these things with judgement, indeed with much forbearance, and know that I was once a monk, etc." What, then, is this mark of his modesty branded with, when these men contend that all the Churches must be bound to the writings of this one man alone, or wish whatever he thought to be held as an oracle, so that it is not even lawful to dissent from it, and all the writings of others must be called back to his opinion, even though they contain nothing of the kind? From this, therefore, it appears first that this dogma of the oral eating has no foundation in the Confession or its Apology, and consequently that the condemnations poured out against us in this writing do not rest at all on the authority of these writings.

units.la: Idem & de dogmate de MaieftateCor poris Christi (qualem isti vt suam illam monftrofam Vbiquitatem stabiliant, to- to hoc libro astruunt contra veteris Ec- clefiae, & omnium piorum & Orthodo- xorum sententias)dici merito potest. Na de his duobus capitibus neque Augusta- na Confessio,neque eius Apologia vsquam meminit. Et testis est ipse Lutherus in articulis Smalcaldicis ,nullam fuisse tum temtemporis inter Euangelicas Ecclesias, & Pontificios de his capitibus (scilicet de Deo & de persona Christi) controuersia, quia ab utraque parte idem sentirent & confiterentur omnes. Qualis autem fuerit semper Ecclesiæ Romanæ (quamuis in plerisque aliis doctrinæ Christianæ capitibus, corruptissimi mæ) in hoc dogmate sententia, non est difficile ex ipsorum scriptis colligere. Et maxime ex thesibus olim aduersus Iacobi Andreæ Theses con scriptis de Maiestate hominis Christi, quæ sane Orthodoxam resipiunt omnino, & puram veterum Patrum doctrinam, de duabus in Christo naturis, ut ipsos appareat sententiam hac in parte numquam mutasse & ab Vbiquitatis doctrina (quam nunc inuehunt) semper fuisse alienissimos. Adeo ut hinc manifeste constet, vel D. Lutheri ipsius testimonio, nouam & confessioni Augustanæ prorsus aduersam esse hanc istorum opinionem. Si enim cum hæc confessio exhiberetur, Pontificij olfecissent istud monstrum à Theologis Augustanis ali, non utique dissimulassent: Nec Lutherus Ecclesiarum nomine scripsisset, doctrinam de persona Christi nihil habere apud utrosque contro-
units.tr: The same can rightly be said of the dogma concerning the majesty of the body of Christ (which these men, to establish their monstrous ubiquity, argue for throughout this whole book, against the opinions of the ancient Church and of all the pious and orthodox). For neither the Augsburg Confession nor its Apology ever mentions these two heads. And Luther himself bears witness in the Smalcald Articles that at that time there was no controversy between the evangelical Churches and the Papists about these heads (namely concerning God and the person of Christ), because on both sides all men held and confessed the same thing. What the opinion of the Roman Church has always been on this dogma (although it is very corrupt in most other heads of Christian doctrine) is not difficult to gather from their writings, especially from the theses once written against the Theses of Jacob Andreae concerning the majesty of the man Christ, which indeed savour entirely of orthodoxy and of the pure doctrine of the ancient Fathers concerning the two natures in Christ, so that it is clear that they never changed their opinion on this point, and have always been most alien to the doctrine of ubiquity which they now advance. So that from this it is plainly established, even by the testimony of Dr Luther himself, that this new opinion of theirs is wholly contrary to the Augsburg Confession. For if this Confession had been presented, the Papists would certainly have smelled out that monster nourished by the Augsburg theologians, and would not have dissembled; nor would Luther have written in the name of the Churches that the doctrine concerning the person of Christ had no controversy between the two sides, but that it had remained whole and intact among the Papists.

units.la: N.j. uersiæ,sed saluam & integram illam apud Papistas mansisse. Quia tamen sex isti Theologi hoc maximè agunt vt persua-deant se hanc doctrinam ex Lutheri scri-ptis hausisse, dissimulandum non est quid ab initio in suis Postillis Lutherus de dua-bus in Christo naturis earúmque proprie-tatibus ingenuè senserit, confessúsque sit. In Concione igitur de natali Domini hæc ipsius verba leguntur:
units.tr: Since, however, these six theologians labour above all to persuade people that they have drawn this doctrine from Luther's writings, it must not be passed over what Luther, at the beginning, in his Postils, sincerely thought and confessed about the two natures in Christ and their properties. In the sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, therefore, these words of his are read:

units.la: „ INTEMPESTIVAM quidam enarra-„ tionem adferunt, dicētes: Filius nescit, id„ est, non vult scire. Christus verus homo„ fuit, quare vt alius purus, sed sanctus, ho-„ mo, non quolibet tempore cogitauit, di-„ xit, voluit, intellexit omnia: sicut impesi-„ ti quidam omnipotentem ex eo homi-„ nem faciunt, permiscentes duas naturas,„ atque opera earum parum prudenter. Si-„ cut enim non quolibet tempore omnia„ vidit, audiuit, atque sensit: Ita etiam cor-„ de non omnia semper agnoüit, sed quan-„ tum eum duxit ac docuit Dominus.
units.tr: "Some bring forward an unseasonable explanation, saying: 'The Son does not know,' that is, he does not wish to know. Christ was a true man, and therefore he was not like another pure but holy man, who did not at all times think, say, will and understand everything. Some foolish men make him an omnipotent man in this way, mixing the two natures and their works rather unwisely. For just as he did not see, hear and perceive everything at all times, so also his heart did not always know everything, but as much as the Lord led and taught him."

units.la: „ Videmus scripturam multò dexterius„ & explicatius de Christo loqui, quàm nos„ soleamus. Pulchrè personam cum natura„ iungit, ac rursus naturas nequaquam con-„ fundit. Vt pauci sint (quod debemus humanis commentis,quibus ætatem nostrā attriuimus,& ingenium corrupimus)qui id percipiant,vt ipse profecto persæpe in his & similibus locis errauerim,& naturę tribuerim quod competit personæ, & contrà.
units.tr: "We see that Scripture speaks of Christ much more skilfully and clearly than we are accustomed to. It beautifully joins the person with the nature, and yet never confuses the natures. Few are able to grasp this (which we owe to human inventions, on which we have spent our age and corrupted our intellect). Indeed I myself have very often erred in such and similar passages, and have attributed to the nature what belongs to the person, and the reverse."

units.la: En candidum & apertum Lutheri testimonium,quo & quid de duabus Christi naturis sentiendum sit ex scripturis, & quomodo ipse sæpe in his distinguen-dis errauerit ingenuè fatetur. Sic etiam alibi aperte monet de Vbiquitate in hæc verba; De Vbiquitate,inquit,non est disputandum: neque scholastici Doctores quicquam hac de re tradiderunt. Quin obsequuntur igitur huic præceptoris sui admonitioni boni isti discipuli, potius quàm vt hoc nouum dogma illi affingen-do, turbas tantas excitent? Cur Eccle-siarum pacem quam tantopere optare se simulant, silentio suo potius non redi-munt? Scimus quid ad hoc vltimum.Lu-theri testimonium eludendum alicui re-sponderit Iacobus Andreas cùm illi in priuato colloquio obiiceretur: nempe a-diecta fuisse hæc verba à Philippo Melan-sthone,in Tomis wittembergicis. Verùm arguunt hominis versutum responsum Ienenfia exemplaria Colloquii Maulbrū nenfis iamprides edita, in quibus eadem verba leguntur.Ex his igitur fatis liquet, doctrinam hanc de Maiestate corporis Christi, realíque communicatione proprietatum essentialium diuinæ naturæ in humanam,itémq. Vbiquitatis dogma pro quibus in hoc scripto maximè laborant hi Theologi:nullo confessionis Augustanæ niti testimonio, ac ne cognitum quidem eo tempore à quoquam fuit fe. Itaque nouatores potius, quàm veteris doctrinæ assertores, merito dicendi sunt. Quod ex plerisque etiam aliis supra à nobis notatis capitibus apparet. Vbi enim habetur in Confessione,aut Apologia, Infantium animas à parentibus non minus quam corpora generari. Item vocationem quæ fit per Euangelij prædicationem vniuersalem esse, & ad singulos homines pertinere.Quod item de libero arbitrio tradunt,in rebus maximè externis, nonne aperte pugnat cum iis quæ scribit Lutherus in cap. x. Ieremiæ quæ sic habent ad illud Scio Domine quia non est hominis via eius?Si euentus,inquit,rerum
units.tr: "Here is a frank and open testimony of Luther, in which he freely confesses both what ought to be held from the Scriptures concerning the two natures of Christ, and how he himself often went astray in distinguishing them. Likewise he plainly warns elsewhere about the ubiquity in these words: 'Concerning ubiquity,' he says, 'there is no need to dispute; nor have the scholastic doctors handed down anything on this matter.' Why then do these good disciples not obey the admonition of their teacher, rather than stir up such great disturbances by attaching this new dogma to him? Why do they not rather, by their silence, preserve the peace of the Churches, which they pretend to desire so earnestly? We know what Jacob Andreae replied, to elude this last testimony of Luther, when it was thrown at him in a private conversation: namely that these words had been added by Philip Melanchthon in the Wittenberg Tomes. But the Jena copies of the Colloquy of Maulbronn, published a few days ago, in which the same words are read, argue against this clever answer of the man. From these things it is therefore sufficiently clear that this doctrine of the majesty of Christ's body, and of the real communication of the essential properties of the divine nature to the human, as well as the dogma of ubiquity, for which these theologians labour most in this writing, rest on no testimony of the Augsburg Confession, and were not even known to anyone at that time. Therefore they should rightly be called innovators rather than defenders of the old doctrine. This also appears from many other chapters we have noted above. For where is it found in the Confession or the Apology that the souls of infants are generated by their parents no less than their bodies? Likewise that the calling which takes place through the universal preaching of the gospel is for all, and pertains to each individual man? What they teach likewise about free will, especially in external matters, does it not clearly conflict with what Luther writes on chapter 10 of Jeremiah, which reads thus on the words 'I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not in himself': 'If the outcomes of those things,' he says, 'which are temporal, and in which man is constituted lord, are not in our hand, I beg you, how will that heavenly thing be in our hand, namely the grace of God, which depends on the will of God alone? Can the effort of free will obtain eternal salvation, when it cannot keep a penny, or even a hair of the head?'"

units.la: „ Ieremiæ cap. 10. rum istarum non est in manu nostra, quæ sunt temporales, & in quibus homo do- minus constituitur, Obsecro quomodo erit in manu nostra, res illa cœlestis, Gra tia scilicet Dei, quæ à solius Dei arbitrio pendet? An liberi arbitrij conatus, potest salutem æterna obtinere, qui non potest obolum, imo ne pilum capitis retinere? Et in eodem libro sequitur postea: Libe- rum arbitrium esse plane Diuinum no- men, nec vlli posse competere, quàm foli diuinæ Maiestati: Ea enim potest & facit (vt Pfal. canit) omnia quæ vult in cœlo, & in terra. Quod fi hominibus tributitur, nihilo id fit rectius, quàm fi illis Diuinitas tribueretur: quo sacrilegio nullum maius esse possit. Proinde Theologorum erat hoc vocabulo abstinere. Hæc D. Luthe- rus. Ipsa quoque Confessio Auguftana hac in parte Actiones politicas & ad hæc vitam pertinentes gubernationi Dei sub iicit, & Augustini sententiam laudat, qua dixit: Omnia bona quæ ad vitam præfen tem pertinent, non fine Diuina guberna tione subsistere, imo ex Deo & per ipsum esse & esse cœpisse. Neque in hoc dog- mate igitur istis plane vel cum Confeffione Auguftana, vel cum Luthero còn-uenit: Quemadmodum nec in illis quæ de Prædestinatione ab istis asseri, suprà notauimus. Quinimo ex Commentariis & Locis communib. Melanđthonis (quiñ quennio ante Confessionem, ex consen-su Lutheri editis) apparere potest, nostrā doctrinam de prædestinatione commu-niter & expresse fuisse tum temporis receptam, & probatam. Eiusmodi igitur dogmata peregrina, apparet non esse ex confessionis Augustanæ formula deprompta, sed noua additamenta fucoso interpretationis titulo ornata. Quæ tamen si propter Lutheri vnius authoritatem nobis importunius obtrudantur: licebit haud dubiè nobis aliorum contra sententium expositiones, istis opponere: atque etiam in plerisq. à Luthero irato ad Lutherum pacatum appellare: & in aliis etiam à discipulis ad magistrum prouocare, à cuius doctrina isti sæpenumero longissimè discedunt. Vt exempli gratia quæ isti de descensu Christi ad inferos suo scri pto inseruerunt recipiùt quidem ea quæ Lutherus ex Papistarum scholis in concione quadam Torgæ declamauit. Tum enim exprimunt totam personam Chri-sti secundum vtranque naturam ad infe-ros descendisse: At alibi fatetur Lutherus plurimis in locis, se hunc articulum non intelligere neque quicquam de eo vel a-pud se certi constituere, vel alios cõsiden-ter docere posse. Hîc igitur non satis sibi constat præceptor, quem discipuli per a-uia sequuntur. Alibi verò contra præce-ptoris authoritatem (in cuius tamen ver-ba volunt omnes sine exceptione iurare) quædam probant, quæ ille improbat. Vt cùm in tractatu de iustitia fidei, Diui Iaco-bi Epistolam pro Canonica scriptura a-gnoscunt, & ex illa doctrinam fidei illu-strari, & confirmari contendunt: cùm Lu-therus plerisque in locis (ac præcipuè ad 22.cap. Genesꝋos) illius authoritatem e-leuet & quasi irrideat dum ait male con-cludere Iacobum, imò Iacobum delirare & cum Iacobo suo facessere iubet eos qui eius authoritate niituntur.
units.tr: "Jeremiah chapter 10. And in the same book he goes on afterwards: 'Free will is plainly a divine name, and cannot belong to anyone except the divine majesty alone. For it can and does (as the Psalm sings) all that it wills in heaven and on earth. And if it is attributed to men, this is no more correct than if divinity were attributed to them; no sacrilege could be greater than this. Therefore it was the duty of theologians to abstain from this word.' So says Dr Luther. The Augsburg Confession itself, in this part, subjects political actions, and those pertaining to this life, to the government of God, and praises the saying of Augustine, that all goods which pertain to the present life do not subsist without divine government, indeed that they both are and have begun to be from God and through him. Therefore these men do not agree plainly, in this dogma, either with the Augsburg Confession or with Luther, just as in those things which they have asserted about predestination, as we noted above. Indeed, from the Commentaries and Common Places of Melanchthon (published five years before the Confession, with the consent of Luther), it can be seen that our doctrine of predestination was then commonly and expressly received and approved. Such foreign dogmas therefore evidently are not drawn from the formula of the Augsburg Confession, but are new additions decked out with the specious title of interpretation. Yet if they are forced upon us more insistently on account of the authority of Luther alone, we shall undoubtedly be free to set against them the interpretations of other opinions; and also, in many points, to appeal from the angry Luther to the calm Luther, and in other matters to appeal from the disciples to the master, from whose teaching these men very often depart far. For example, what these men have inserted in their writing about the descent of Christ into hell, they indeed accept what Luther declaimed from the Papists' schools in a certain sermon at Torgau. For then they express the whole person of Christ as having descended into hell according to both natures. But elsewhere Luther confesses in very many places that he does not understand this article, nor can he either establish anything certain about it for himself or teach it consistently to others. Here the teacher does not agree with himself sufficiently, and his disciples follow him in the byways. Elsewhere, moreover, against the authority of the teacher (in whose words they wish all to swear without exception), they approve certain things which he disapproves. For example, in the treatise on the justification of faith, they acknowledge the Epistle of the divine James as canonical Scripture, and strive to illustrate and confirm the doctrine of faith from it; whereas Luther in very many places (and especially on chapter 22 of Genesis) extols its authority and almost mocks it, saying that James concludes badly, indeed that James raves, and bids those who rely on his authority to go away with their James."

units.la: Ex his igitur patet falsum esse funda-mentum, & authoritatem quam ex Au-gustana Confessione & Apologia, item, ex scriptis Lutheri huic suo scripto sub-sternunt: cùm plurima sint de nouo ab ipfis excogitata, & pro arbitrio adiecta, multa etiam illis contraria: alia depravata & in contrarium sensum detorta. quod ex eorum maxime scriptis apparet, qui tum Confessionem, tum Apologiam scripserunt.
units.tr: "From these things it is therefore evident that the foundation and authority which these men lay under this their writing, from the Augsburg Confession and the Apology, and likewise from the writings of Luther, are false: since very many things have been newly devised by them, and added at their pleasure, many things too are contrary to those documents, and others are corrupted and twisted into the opposite sense. This appears especially from the writings of those who wrote both the Confession and the Apology."

units.la: Neque hoc silentio praeterire possumus (ut constet quantum auctoritatis tribuere tam ipsi confessioni, quam Apologiae eius conveniat) palam esse, ex D. Philippi Melanchthonis (a quo utraque conscripta est) Epistola ad Lutherum Norimbergae scripta & Vvittembergae excusa: Non fuisse ab initio, vel Confessionem, vel Apologiam, eo compositam atque editam, ut certa & immota ac generalis essent omnibus, totius Religionis ac fidei Christianae Regula & fundamentum: sed ut instar iustae defensionis Caesari adversus Pontificiorum calumnias exhiberentur: qui Germanicas Ecclesias, tum primum renascentes, tamquam impias & haereticas variis scriptis & vociferationibus damnabant: eaque omnibus ordinibus exosas reddere conabantur.
units.tr: "Nor can we pass over in silence (so that it is clear how much authority both the Confession itself and its Apology properly deserve) that it is plain, from the letter of Dr Philip Melanchthon (by whom both were written), written at Nuremberg and printed at Wittenberg, that neither the Confession nor the Apology was from the beginning composed and published in such a way that they should be a fixed and unchanging and general rule and foundation of the whole religion and Christian faith for all; but that they were presented, in the manner of a just defence, to the Emperor against the calumnies of the Papists, who, as the German Churches were then first being reborn, condemned them as impious and heretical in various writings and outcries, and tried to make them hateful to all orders."

units.la: Sic enim ille scribit (tam de confessione quam Apologia loquens) Vellem percurrisse risses Articulos fidei. In quibus si nihil putaueris esse vitij, reliqua vtcunque tra ѓtabimus. Subinde enim mutandi sunt, at que ad occasiones accommodandi'. Et in alia Epistola ad quendam amicum ista le- guntur: Ego conatus sum eam senten- tiam in Apologia explicare: sed ibi pro- pter aduersariorum calumnias, non sic lo qui licet, vt nunc coram loquor, & reipsa idem dico. Nonne ergo Philippus ipse te stis erit idoneus suorum scriptorū, quo-modo scilicet, & in quem finem ab ipso scripti fuerint?
units.tr: "For he writes thus (speaking both of the Confession and of the Apology): 'I would have wished to run through the articles of faith again. If you think there is no fault in them, we shall let the rest go on as it is. For they must be changed from time to time, and adapted to occasions.' And in another letter to a certain friend these words are read: 'I have tried to explain that opinion in the Apology; but there, on account of the calumnies of our adversaries, I did not speak as freely as I now speak in your presence, and in fact I say the same thing.' Will not Philip himself, then, be a fit witness to his own writings, of how and to what end they were written by him?"

units.la: Ex hoc ergo testimonio, ad superiores firmissimas rationes addito, duorursus ne cessario concludimus. Primùm huius libri authores, nullum habere vel ex Confes-sione Augustana, vel ex eius Apologia fundamentum, in præcipuis illis doctri-næ capitibus, in quibus nos tanquam hæ reticos condemnant. Secundò cùm tam Confessio quàm Apologia adeo va-riè ab illis ipsis exponantur à quibus fue-runt conscriptæ: neutram vel posse, vel debere pro certa fidei Regula & Norma aut præscribi aut agnosci: ex qua omnia cõtrouersa dogmata decidi legitimè possint. Sed contrā subiiciendā esse vtràque (non secus ac reliqua omnia vtriusque partis scripta) examini verbi Dei, vt secun dum illud in œccumenico sancto, ac legi-timo aliquo conuentu, iudicium de illis omnibus fiat.
units.tr: From this testimony, added to the firmest arguments above, we necessarily conclude in two ways. First, the authors of this book have no foundation, either in the Augsburg Confession or in its Apology, for those principal heads of doctrine on which they condemn us as heretics. Second, since both the Confession and the Apology are explained so variously even by those very men by whom they were written, neither can or should be prescribed or acknowledged as a certain rule and norm of faith, by which all controverted doctrines might legitimately be decided. On the contrary, both (no less than all the other writings of either party) must be submitted to the examination of the Word of God, so that judgment on all of them may be made according to it, in some holy and lawful ecumenical assembly.

units.la: In summa, quod ad authores huius libri spectat, qui tantopere confessionis & Apologiæ autoritatem prædicant, vr-gent & nobis obiiciunt, hoc postremò ad dere cogimur non sincerè ac cordatè ab ipsis, sed malitiosè & per inuidiam sum-mámque ingratitudinem fieri, quòd Phi-lippi Melanƈthonis nomen in hac tota scriptione supprimát, quum præcipuam ille in Apologia & confessione conscri-benda operam nauauerit, & ideò doƈtri-næ in eis comprehensæ certiorem cogni-tionem & intelligentiam habuerit præ o-mnibus. Quum denique vir ille nō solùm de Ecclesiis omnibus, sed & de literis tam Diuinis quàm humanis, apud omnes gen-tes, & Nationes, optimè sit meritus, quæ iusta causa fuit his sex Theologis, vt eius ne minimam quidem mentionē toto hoc libro fecerint, nisi impia in communē pa-rentem ingratitudo, & maleuola quædā etiam in mortuum inuidia? Alibi enim non dissimulant odium. At longè aliud fuit D. Lutheri de hoc summo viro iudi-dium cum quo in fine vsque iucundam, gratam atque indelebilem amicitiam & familiaritatem coluit: Cuius encomium etiam(aduersus omnes ingratos discipu-los)nunquam obliterandum in præfatio-ne omnium operum suorum sculpere, & ad posteros in omne æuü transmittere vo-luit. Hæc enim sunt postrema eius encomij verba: Quod operatus sit Dominus per hoc organum(Philippum scilicet) nō in literis tantùm,sed in Theologia satis te stantur eius opera,etiamsi irascatur Satâ, & omnes eius squamę.
units.tr: In sum, as far as the authors of this book are concerned, who so greatly proclaim, press and throw in our faces the authority of the Confession and the Apology, we are finally compelled to conclude that they do not do this sincerely and wisely, but maliciously, out of envy and the greatest ingratitude: that in this whole writing they suppress the name of Philip Melanchthon, although he laboured most of all in writing the Apology and the Confession, and therefore had a clearer knowledge and understanding of the doctrines contained in them above all others. Finally, since that man has deserved well not only of all the Churches but also of literature, both divine and human, among all peoples and nations, what just cause was there for these six theologians to make not even the slightest mention of him in this whole book, unless it was impious ingratitude towards a common father, and a certain malevolent envy even towards the dead? For elsewhere they do not hide their hatred. But Dr Luther's judgment of this great man was far different, with whom he cultivated a pleasant, grateful and enduring friendship and familiarity to the end. Luther wished to have his encomium, which must never be forgotten (against all ungrateful disciples), carved in the preface of all his works, and transmitted to posterity for all ages. For these are the closing words of his eulogy: That the Lord has worked through this organ (namely Philip) not only in literature but in theology, his works bear sufficient witness, even if Satan and all his scales are angry.

units.la: Quos per squamas Satanæ intelligere voluerit Luther9, viderint isti,piissimi huius & eruditissimi nec vnquam satis laudati viri, inuidi obtrectatores: quorum hoc scriptum vel hac vnica de causa, suspectum piis omnibus esse debet.
units.tr: Whom Luther meant to understand by the scales of Satan, let those envious detractors see, of this most pious and learned man, never sufficiently praised. This writing of theirs ought to be suspect to all the godly for this single reason alone.

units.la: Habetis nostrum integrum de hoc scripro iudiciü. Quod vt à nobis denegari iustis vestris precibus non debuit:ita te stari possumus bona conscientia nos hæc collegisse,ac demum etiam vulgasse, vt in firmis conscientiis (quas isti, ad subscri-ptionē importunius virgēndo, mirum in modum turbant) quantū in nobis est consulamus: facile enim his perlectis intelligere poterunt omnes quicunque adhuc micam sani iudicij retinent, nec ab istis fascinati sunt: non solum non esse puram & sincerām horum Theologorum doctri-nam: sed etiam maximum impendere omnibus Ecclesiis periculum, imo certam perniciem, nisi illorum cōsiliis opportu-nè obviam eatur: & totus hic liber mandato & authoritate piorum Principū sup-primatur, nec illi patiantur à suis Doctoribus & Pastoribus subscribi, nisi prius cō-muni omnium Ecclesiarum, quarum præcipuē interest, consilio atque consensu libero, examinatus & approbatus fuerit.
units.tr: You have our complete judgment on this writing. Since it ought not to have been denied to your just prayers by us, so we may testify with a good conscience that we have gathered these remarks and also published them, so that we may do what lies in us to help firm consciences (which these men, by pressing subscription more importunately, disturb in a remarkable way). For once these pages have been read through, all those who still retain a grain of sound judgment and are not bewitched by these men will easily be able to understand that the doctrine of these theologians is not pure and sincere, but that it poses the greatest danger, indeed certain ruin, to all the Churches, unless their counsels are opportunely resisted; and that this whole book should be suppressed by the command and authority of the pious princes, and that they should not allow it to be subscribed by their teachers and ministers unless it has first been examined and approved by the free counsel and consent of all the Churches, whose interest is chief in the matter.

units.la: Quod ad vos attinet, habetis exempla quę sequamini, earum scilicet Ecclesiarū quæ liberè & strenuē subscriptionem illis denegarūt: inter quas etiam quædam sunt, de quibus isti Theologi longè aliud expectabant. Valete in Domino.
units.tr: As for you, you have examples to follow: namely those Churches which freely and vigorously refused subscription to them, among which there are some from whom these theologians expected something quite different. Farewell in the Lord.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: FINIS.

units.la: N. N.
units.tr: N. N.

units.la: CHRISTIANO LECTORI
units.tr: TO THE CHRISTIAN READER

units.la: Salutem.
units.tr: Greetings.

units.la: QVVM instarent apud me nonnulli verae pietatis piaeque veritatis studiosi, vt Animaduersiones, quas Theologi quidam orthodoxi in nouum & clandularium Doctrinae corpus, quod per totam ferè Germaniam manu scriptum circumfertur, ante aliquot menses conscripserunt, typis excudendum curarem: oportunè accidit, vt eodem tempore non solùm totus Tractatus de persona Christi ex corpore illo doctrinae excerptus in manus nostras incideret, sed etiam illa ipsa Epistola qua corporis istius authores ac compilatores Illustrissimo & Clementissimo Duci Electori Saxoniae persuadere conantur, vt sine vlla legitima cognitione aut Ecclesiastico iudicio, ad illius subscriptionem, omnes tum suos tum vicinarum regionum atque ordinum Theologos, non modò inuitet sed etiam adigat. Itaque tam oportunam occasionem nacti, operaepretium duximus vtrumque illud scriptum, quasi Animaduersionum illarum basim & fundamentum, huic opusculo praeponere, quandoquidem integrum corporis illius volumen nondum nancisci potuimus. Id verò duplici potissimum de causa facimus,tum quod vtriusque huius scripti in animaduersionibus mentio fiat. Tum vt ex illis facile omnes iudicare posint quorsum vet gant omnia istorum consilia, & quàm confidenter piorum Principum autoritate abutantur: vt suam culpam omnem in eos deriuent.
units.tr: When several men devoted to true piety and sound doctrine pressed me to have printed the Animadversions which certain orthodox theologians drew up some months ago against the new and clandestine body of doctrine that is circulated in manuscript through almost all of Germany, it happened at the same time that not only the whole treatise on the person of Christ, taken from that body of doctrine, came into our hands, but also that very letter by which the authors and compilers of that work try to persuade the most illustrious and most merciful Elector of Saxony to invite, and indeed to compel, all the theologians of his own lands and of neighbouring regions and orders to subscribe to it, without any lawful examination or ecclesiastical judgment. Therefore, having found so opportune an occasion, we thought it worth the effort to place both of these writings before this little work, as the basis and foundation of those Animadversions, since we have not yet been able to obtain the complete volume of that body of doctrine. We do this chiefly for two reasons: first, because both of these writings are mentioned in the Animadversions; second, so that from them everyone can easily judge where all the plans of these men are tending, and how confidently they abuse the authority of pious princes, so as to shift all their own guilt onto them.

units.la: Addidimus etiam Heshufij epistolam, qua compilatoribus istis(quorum tamen nonnullos fictæ de suis erroribus pœnitentiæ tacitè insimulat,& suos interim ipse errores aperte pro dit,propter quos opera Wigandi à suo Episcopatu nuper expulsus est) præclarum hoc circumueniendarum & damnādarum Ecclefiarū artificium congratulatur: vt ex ea clarius confet veritas prouerbij, Similes habent labra la-ctucas.
units.tr: We have also added the letter of Heshusius, in which he congratulates those compilers on this clever device of deceiving and condemning churches (though he tacitly accuses some of them of feigned repentance for their errors, while he himself openly reveals his own errors, on account of which he was recently expelled from his bishopric because of the work of Wigand), so that from it the truth of the proverb may be more clearly confirmed: "Their lips are like lettuces" [Similes habent labra lactucas].

units.la: Postremò quia ijdem autores subinde in eo Tractatu de persona Christi, iactant suam illā nouam doctrinam de corpore maiestatico, & vbiquitate carnis Christi, iam inde initio Augu-stanæ confessionis à D.Luthero fuisse Ecclesijs traditam,cùm contrà constet apud omnes, (vel ex Lutheri ipsius testimonio quod in animad-uersionibus citatur) nullam fuisse ab initio de persona Christi controuersiam,inter Protestantium & Romanensium Theologos: superiorib. scriptis etiam addere visum est necesse Theses Pontificij cuiusdam de his dogmatibus aduersus Iacobum Andreæ, ante aliquot annos conscriptas. Quas tamen non ideò recudendas censuimus, vt à Pontificijs subsidium aduersus noua ista dogmata (quæ toties à nostris Th gis & quidē solidè ex verbo Dei refutata sunt) emendicare videremur, sed duntaxat vt ex his Thesibus appareat, quantum sit discrimen inter Pontificiorum de his capitibus sententiam cum pia antiquitate per omnia conuenientem & eam quam Luthero, atque Ecclesijs omnibus confessionem Augustanam profesis isti affingunt. At ne quis cauilletur, nos cætera quoque Papistica commenta de inuisibili præsentia Christi in Cœna (his Thesibus ab autore Pontificio immixta) perinde atque ea quæ de personali vnione aduersus Vbiquitarios, doctè & piè disputantur, probare, dedimus operam vt ea quæ Papismum redolebant expungerentur, & pura illa dūtaxat doctrina retineretur. Quod sicubi vestigia aliqua Papisticæ doctrinæ per incogitantiam remanserunt (vt in pag. 89. Thes. 5. sub finem, & p. 137. Thes. 99. deprehendimus accidisse) monemus, rogamúsque pium Lectorem vt illud erratis annumeret, & benignè cum reliquis quæ nobis inuitis inter excudendum excuderunt excusæt. Vale Christiane Lector & nostrum hunc conatum candido beneuoloque animo excipe.
units.tr: Finally, because these same authors repeatedly boast in that treatise on the person of Christ that their new doctrine of the majestic body and the ubiquity of Christ's flesh was handed down to the Churches by Dr. Luther from the very beginning of the Augsburg Confession, whereas it is clear to all (even from Luther's own testimony, which is cited in the Animadversions) that there was originally no controversy about the person of Christ between the theologians of the Protestants and of the Romanists, we also thought it necessary to add to the earlier writings the theses of a certain Papist on these doctrines, written against Jacob Andreae some years ago. We have not, however, thought them worth reprinting so that we might seem to beg aid from the Papists against these new doctrines (which our own theologians have so often and so solidly refuted from the Word of God), but only so that it may appear from these Theses how great the difference is between the Papists' opinion on these heads, which agrees in every respect with pious antiquity, and the view that those men attribute to Luther and to all the Churches, who profess the Augsburg Confession. Lest anyone object, we have also taken care, in regard to the other Papist inventions about the invisible presence of Christ in the Supper (which the Papist author mingled into these Theses), that those things which smelled of Papism should be struck out, and that only that pure doctrine should be retained, which is learnedly and piously argued against the Ubiquitarians concerning the personal union. If any traces of Papist doctrine have nevertheless remained through carelessness (as we have found happened on page 89, Thesis 5, near the end, and on page 137, Thesis 99), we give notice of this, and ask the pious reader to count it among the errata and to pardon it kindly, along with the other things which, against our will, were allowed to slip through in printing. Farewell, Christian reader, and receive this our effort with a candid and kindly mind.
